NATURAL GAS FOR MOTOR-CARS.

A novel exhibition of the use of natural gas has been demonstrated in the United States on a race-course, when a small motor- car was driven three miles, using natural gas as power. The test is etatecl to have shewn conclusively that automobiles can be driven by natural gas. The total'amount of gas used in running the car for the three miles was about 10ft. At 15 cents per 1,000 the cost of this amount would be 3-20ths of a cent, or 1-20th of a cent per mile. The car with its load of two passengers and tank weighed 1,6001 b., and the speed attained in the teat varied from three to twelve miles an hour.
EFFECTUAL TREATMENT FOR WARTS.

It is now fairly established that the com- mon wart, which is so unsightly on the hands and face, can be easily removed by small doses of sulphate of magnesia taken inter- nally. M. Colrat, of Lyons, has drawn atten- tion to this extraordinary fact. Several chil- dren treated with three-grain doses of Epsom salts morning and evening .were promptly cured. M. Aubert cites the case of a woman whose face was disfigured by these excres- cences, and who was cured in a month by a drachm and a-half of magnesia taken daily. Another medical man reports a case of very large warts which disappeared in a fortnight from the daily administration of ten grains of the salts.„ ,

This nightgown is made high to the throat, and is finished at the ;ke ck with a neat turn-down collar, edged by a tiny frill of good torchon lace, and finished with a row of feather- stitching. COIFFURE ORNAMENTS.

Greek filets for the coiffure are now in the heyday of their popularity with the vraie elegant°, and are usually of gold or silver tissue embroidered with old-world designs, the fashion- ing of which, says a railer writer, whether for pleasure or profit, is a charming occupation for the home worker. Frequently the filets are sur- mounted with lilies, roses, and butterflies of jewelled net, which give height to the wearer. The Greek filet of diamonds is of exalted merit for the woman who has passed the meridian of life, and is often arranged with a wheatear or Louis design. Genuinely artistic are the twisted ribbon schemes, which are so easy to manipulate with the assistance of a hair needle. The ribbon is attached to the needle, and is passed in and out of the hair after it has been dressed. This increases the size of the coiffure in a very be- coming manner, and gives a pretty effect.

div.head: SMART _SHIRT BLOUSE.
div.p: A SMART _SHIRT BLOUSE.

There is a perfect rage just now for the sleeve out in one with the garment. The very smart shirt blouse illustrated in our sketch has this sleeve, which really forms its distinguishing fea- ture, and makeS it a particularly new and origi- nal model. This sleeve has two seams, one down the back and one down the front of the arm, and ie set into a plain shirt cuff at the wrist. Down

the front of the blouse rot a box-pleat of mode- rate width, edged with a line of machine-stitch- ing on either side, and further adorned with buttons. On either side of this centre pleat come two groups of tucks, three in each group, which are released just about on a level with the arm- hole, the resultant fulness being allowed to pouch a little at the waist. This design would look very well carried out in flannel, cashmere, delaine, nun's-veiling, or wancev, or for more dressy wear in washing silk, taffetas, velveteen, or soft satin.

div.head: FRIAR Tux CLOAKS.
div.p: FRIAR Tux CLOAKS.

France has set an excellent example in dis- covering the usefulness of a monk-like robe as an outer wrap. Nothing could be more comfort- able, says a Globe writer, than the warm, light, ample folds of such a gown; and accordingly they are being worn for many purposes, motor- ing, walking, boating, bathing, &c. Even the hood is kept, and very sweet and pretty does a n young feminine face look, peeping out from the hood of a friar's gown on the moors in e. Sooteh mist. Grey, brown, black, and white, v.II the orders are represented. The white are only sliitable for quite young girls; but they are not as perishable as they sound, since they wash so well. These robes are quite dreadnoughts, and slip on over any costume, and the hoods go over any hat of reasonable size, thus avoiding the necessity of carrying an umbrella, and leaving one's hands free.

div.head: AUTOMATIC WALNUT GATHERERS.
div.p: AUTOMATIC WALNUT GATHERERS.

A correspondent sends to the Times a de- scription of a walnut-gathering machine which is used in California. Two; men are re- quired tO operate the machine, which is said to do, the work of 100 pickers and packers. The &whine consists of a two-cylinder gaso- line engine, which is hung between 41t. wheels, close to the ground. The truck which the engine propels carxies the: nut-picking apparatus. There is an exhaust-blower work- ing as a suction-pump at the front which sucks up the walnuts from the ground. The nuts, leaves, and twigs thus sucked up are dumped into a tank, and the blower sepa- rates the debris and bad nuts from the good ones, ind blows, the waste" material out on the ground behind the machine, the , nuts passino,..er to the huller. They are then sent through a tube to the sacks.

div.head: HAVE YOU CAT SENSE?
div.p: HAVE YOU CAT SENSE?

Can a cat, see in the dark? In the dusk it can see better than human beings, but in total darkness neither the cat nor any other animal can see at all. It is the cat's whiskers and extraordinarily, acute hearing which help it in the dark. He can hear the faintest pos- sible noise, and can even measure its distance from him; so that the cat can spring in the dark with as much certainty of alighting on his prey as he can in broad day. In the brain of the cat the pee connected with hearing is very largely developed. In the dog's brain there is a similar development with regard .to smell—the dog's best sense. Fishes have practically no part of the brain devoted to smell; this faculty would be useless under water. Carnivorous animals find their prey chiefly by the aid of smell and hearing. Her- bivorous animals depend mainly on sight.

div.head: CONCERNING SELENIUM.
div.p: CONCERNING SELENIUM.

Selenium, fdiscovered by Berzelius in 1818, is a non-mdtallic element closely 'elated to sulphur and tellurium. In darkness it is practically a non-conductor of electricity, but when lighted it passes current readily, and it is this unique variability that gives to the substance great possibilities of future import- ance. The curious property has been applied experimentally in various ways. It has given a means of transmitting speech along a ray of light, a method of guiding and exploding torpedoes by light, and it is employed for sending pictures ,by wire. It has been used also for measuring the Röntgen rays applied in medicine. Selenium is a rare substance in little demand; but in the United States it has been produced experimentally, from the anode slimes of the electrolytic refining of copper, and it is probable that a moderate supply can be obtained in this way.

div.head: 110 W WE ARE KEPT WARM.
div.p: 110 W WE ARE KEPT WARM.

In a lecture on "How the Earth is Warmed," Professor Poynting chewed that the earth was chiefly warmed by sunshine, by the burning of coal, which was the sun- shine of past ages stored up, and from the earth's internal heat. Having demonstrated that the heat from the sun, by comparison, rendered the two other sources insignificant, he explained the methods by which heat travels—namely, by conduction or travelling from the hotter part of one body to the cooler part, or from a hotter body to a cooler one in contact with it; by convection, .or the movement of hot matter, .as in a heating ap- paratus; and by radiation. Radiation was the Way in which heat comes from the sun. It is heat in the sun. It is converted, as it issucs from the sun, into a travelling form of energy—not heat—and it is •converted into heat again when it falls on a surface which absorbs it and is warmed by it. It does not appear to need ordinary matter to carry it, but passes quite freely through the almost empty space between the sun and the earth. It resambles light in travelling in straight lines, in being reflected by mirrors, and in being refracted by lenses, and it is present always with light.

div.head: MIRAGES ON LOCH NESS.
div.p: MIRAGES ON LOCH NESS.

A kind of mirage is one of the most familiar phenomena on Loch Ness, especially in winter and spring. It is best seen in the morning. Dia twit objects, such as the steamers plying on the lake, appear as though raised above the surface and floating in the air. The most constant feature of the Loch Rasa mirages is seen at promontories seven miles distant, says, the AS'cottish Geo- graphical Magazine. The shore line at the promontories, though really nearly parallel with the horizon, is caused by the mirage to appear to form an angle with the horizon. When this angle is great the promontories appear like overhanging cliffs. When the angle is very acute they seem to be sus- pended over the horizon. Objects which are known to be below the horizon are brought into view. The receding steamer, after sail- ing out of sight, will reappear miles further away raised high above the loch and looking very large. The promontory at Dores appears as a conspicuous island in the middle of the loch. The fathers in the Benedictine Monastery at Fort-Auglistus tell that on one occasion a snow-covered mountain appeared over the end of the loch. These phenomena are best marked at a distance of several miles from the observer. The steamer, sail- ing away from the observer, seemed at a dis- tance of a mile or more to leave the surface of the loch and sail up into the air.

div.head: HOW A COMET'S TAIL GROWS.
div.p: HOW A COMET'S TAIL GROWS.

No bridal veil was ever so filmy -as a comet's tail. Hundreds of cubic miles of that wonderful appendage are outweighed by a jarful of air, writea Waldemar Kaempifert in Harper's Magazine. By means of the spec- troscope we have magically transported this fairy plume to our laboratories, and have dis- covered that it is akin to the' blue flame of our as stoves; for the gas by which we cook and the delicate tresses of a comet both con- kist of combinations of hydrogen and carbon, appropriately called by chemists " hydrocar- bons." When it first appears in the heavens, far removed from the sun, a comet is a tail- less blotch of light. As a comet swims on to- wards the sun, the hydrocarbona of the tail split up under the increasing heat into hydro- gen gas and hydrocarbons bf

- - HIGHER BOILING - POINT. With a still closer approach to the sun, these more resistcat hydrocarbons eventually yield to th 3 increasing heat, sand are decompoccd in the form of soot. Inter-planetary space is airless. Hence the soot cannot burn. It most pursue the comet in the form of a duet train. Ths particles constituting that train are small enough to be toy-Td with by the pres- sure' of sunlight. NO matter where the comet may be in its orbit, whethor it has just en- teiptt the solar system or is sneeding away, that plume Is inevitably tossed away from Vie, sun, just as if a mighty wind were blow- ing it from the central luminary. The a?peri- (lige of shining dust is the symbol oY the triumph of light over solar gravitation, -

div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

Queen Elizabeth and the Comet.—" Old Moore's 1 Almanac" for 1009 predicts very troublesome times are , in store for as. "Old Mcore ' contrary to popular conception, does not invoke the aid of the stars for his powers of prevision, so that the near apprcach to the earth of Halley's comet cannot be responsible for his gloomy predictions. But in former times,the comet was regarded as cue of those signs that" forerun the death or fall of Kings." Queen Elizabeth alone, and to the amazement of her courtiers, held this super- stiticn in contempt. It was thought that if the Sovereign would refrain from looking at the comet no harm would come, but when the Queen's attendants curtained her windows, she ordered them to be opened, saying that there "is no warrant in Scripture to portend the mishaps of princess." Women and Pension Committees.—Women are not being invited to serve upon old-aee pension committees, but they might render very useful help, and one would think that they ought to have some part in this administrative work. A Ceuncillor on one of the Metropolitians Borough Councils, opposed the idea of making such an appointment on the ground that there were enough" old women " in the Council already, but he might be reminded of a retort which a Duchess of Gordon once made to such a remark. A statesman of her time, in once referring to some unwise act of his, apologetically remarked, " Really madam, I feel I am growing an o woman." "lam glad to hear that that's it all," replied t e Duchess—" for I really thought you were growing an old man, and that's a much worse thing.' An Anti-Kissing League.—The proposal to start an anti-kissing league reminds one that the old adage " kissing goes by favour " is one of the most commonly misconstrued saying. It is not, as is often supposed, an allusion to favouritism, but to good looks, in the sense that in former times handsome people were called " well-favoured." Whether an anti-kissing league would have any chance of becoming popular is open to i doubt. There s much to be said against the habit on hygienic grounds, but the custom is so general between women and girls, that even that objection has little effect. But boys, as a rule are tot fond of being kissed by their relatives, especially before "the other fellows" nor are men. Eing Edward probably has this insular prejudice, and one can only admire his courage when he submits to being kissed by the Emperors of Germany and Austria, or other Sovereigns of Europe by way of greeting or saying adieu. The Tipping System. One can never get away from the tipping system, either in a public hotel or as a guest in a friend's house. An Austrian, himself a hotel pro- prietor, and his family, recently tried the experiment of touring through Switzerland as a non-tipper, but his experiences do not encourage others to follow his example. He found that certain marks were placed on his luggage, and at subsequent stopping places this would lie about untouched, and there would not only be delay but vexatious mistakes, moreover at table he would be placed near a draughty window that, for some or other reason, could not be closed, and he would be the last in the room to be approached by the waiters. At ()eel y turn he was met by difficulties and objections whenever be 'slanted any little attention, and at last he bad to abandon the non-tipping principle, when life once more entered upon oiled wheels. Centuries of protests against the system have been quite unavailing for we find our old friend "Constant Header" writing to the Times in 1705, complaining that if a man put up at an inn, he must give at least Is. to the waiter, 6d. to the chambermaid, Gd. to the ostler, and Gd. to the jack-boot, making with 2s. 6d. for himself for the night altogether ss. Nowadays one would want some courage to offer a hotel chambermaid 6d., even if staying only for the night. Miss Carev's New Hook.—Yet another volume has been added to Miss Rosa N. Casey's list of works, which delight and charm all readers. The title chosen is " The Sunny Side of the Hill " and Messrs. Macmillan have published the book. Concerning Millinery.—Certainly leading milliners are running to extremes with a vengeance this autumn in the matter of trimmings. When flowers are used they are Use size of dinner plates, and wings are of enormous dimensions. At close quarters one is always in fear that an eye may be permanently damaged, or a cheek scratched by the sharp pin-like points of wings and quills alike. Then we have several curiosities in the feather line, among them " ostrich fringo " which surrounds the huge hat in weeping-willow fashion. So long as the fronds are soft and fluffy' the effect is only funny, but after a shower or the heavy mist La dgecended upon them it is extremely ludricrous. Another form of ornamentation beloved by the smart milliner is the uncurled clipped, and perfectly fiat ostrich feather, which closely resembles the backbone of a herring. The woman who possesses a " creation " trimmed with at least half-a-dozen of these" feathers" may certainly consider herself in Fashion's van. Fur and Satin Necklets.—The high collar-band of fur, edged at the top and base with a frill cf satin, and fastened at the side with a full satin bow, has appeared again in shopland—but it is to be doubted whether it will be seen very often about our necks this coming winter. It is almost impossible to wear this fur and satin collar unfsstened as one would a boa or stole and unless it is quite tightly-fitting—when it is much too hot and stuffy to be healthy—it is doe dy. The Ermine Tie.—VChite furs promise to be less Wont this winter than last, white fox being generally given over to young girls and children. White fox is undoubtedly the most trying of all furs, while ermine, if worn in a mass, may be said to come next in this particular way. Such a verdict cannot however be passed upon the long, rather narrow ermine ties that are being offered us in such vast quantities. The average complexion should easily he able to tolerate these little wraps, always prov hied some colour that suits the wearer, appears about the neck and front of the blouse beneath. The Door-Knocking Nuisance.-To householders in populous neighbourhoods, the itinerant salesman and others, who call at the door, are often a very great nuisance. Half the men who profess to be willing to buy rags and bones, are mgre prowling thieves, whose object is either to steal :Scything that they see lying about or to persuade servants to sell their employers' property at a twentieth of its value depending upon the fact that there are probably only women to deal with them. Another class of men who require strict surveillance, het who receive little or note, are the travelling tinkers. If they believe that there is nobody in the house but women they will refuse to return an article unless an outrageous price is paid for repairing it and the housewife generally submits to the extortion in order to escape being bullied. The flower-Feller who puts his foot in at the door and refuses to remove it tmtil something is purchased is another nuisance, and dill worse are the touters for the Bele of rubbishy tea, and men who seek to delude servants into buying sew- ing machines, watches and books on instalment systems, the aggregate of the instalments being far in excess of the value of the article sold. The legislature would confer a great boon ,upcn householders if they would find time to deal with these pests and meanwhile the police would increase their indebtedness to them if they could discos er a way of protecting the public from such persors, who are a far greater nuitatce than the ordinary beggar. . MADGE.

PHOTOCRAPHIC NOTES.
By Veronica.
A PHOTOGRAPHIC GALA DAY.

At the Franco-British Exhibition, arranged by Mr. Ernest Human and the London and Provincial Photo- graphic Association, for Saturday, September 260, promises to be a busy and interesting day. Cheap trips are being run from almost all parts of the country, and very special reduced terms have been arranged for almost all the attractions and the side shows. THE NORTHERN PHOTOGRAPHIC EXHIBITION.

This most interesting of professional shows has just issued its prospectus, from which it is evident that Manchester intends to beat its own record, as well as that of its sister towns, Leeds and Liverpool. The exhibition will be from the 6th to the 27th of January, 1909, in the City Art Gallery, Manshester. The secre- tary is Mr. S. L. Coulthnrst, Broadoak-road, Worsley, Manchester, who has as his chairman of committee, Mr A. T. Lakin. There will be one judge, Mr. J. C. S. Mummery, A.R.1.8.A., president of the Royal Photo- graphic Society, and he will be his own selecting com- mittee. This Is, of course, an enormous responsibility to place upon one man, and Manchester is distinctly to be congratulated on having induced Mr. Mummery to undertake it. There will be four open sections, dealing with (1) pictorial photographs, (2) ditto, in colour, (3) pictorial lantern slides, ond (4) colour slides, auto- chromes, etc. Fifteen handsome plaques will be at the dispcsal of the judge, and there non be no doubt that those who win them will have very great reason for pride.

div.head: TRADE EXHIBITS.
div.p: THE TRADE EXHIBITS.

On entering the fine handsome Fountain Court, one comes at once upon the stands of the leading photo- graphic manufacturers and dealers, and finds a series of , exhibits and demonstrations that afford quite a liberal education in photography. Each of the stands is under the management of one or more experts in the 119.3 of the apparatus or materials displayed, and many a photo- grapher spending an hour or so chatting over his difficulties with these gentlemen has saved himself weeks of hopeless expEimenting and any amount of wasted material, time ai. patience. In the centre of the court is the Ilford stand, well supplied with prints made upon the firm's various papers from negatives made , upon their plates, and I noted that with a generosity worthy of full reward, the specimen prints are being fairly freely given away to those who take real irterest in them. Sample packets of quarter. plates end half-plates are also being given ta those who have not already used any particular Ilford brand and who may be interested in testing it. On the left, near the entrance is the stand of Wellington and Ward, where the demonstra- tions are always of great interest and where the transparencies and prints are exceedingly fine. J. H. Dallmeyer, Limited, have always someone at their I stand who can tell anyone everything about lenses, shutters, &c.. and the adjoining place fitted up by the Sanger-Shepherd Company is always fascinating by I reason ett its fine example of three-colour work. 0. Sicbe'.i and Co., show cameras, lenses, printing papers, etc., and it is whispered that during the exhibi- tion they intend to give away fifty high-class quarter- plate reflex cameras as presents to visitors. C. P. Cioerz shows cameras, lenses and some wonderful examples of work done with the Naturalists and Goerz-Ansehiltz cameras, lenses and stands. Burroughs, Wellcome and ! Co., are showing the results of, and evil away speci- mens of, their Tabloid photographic chemicals. Adams and Co., have a collection of apparatus that is roost tantalizing to any one who has not ample means, and , Wratten and Wainwright have an illuminated show case I for demonstrating a series of cptical and colour problems, and for proving the advantages of ortho- ! cromatic and panchromatic plates. The Platinotype I Co., always has some very capable and experienced demonstrators who give useful instruction every after- noon at 4.30 and on Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday at Kodak, Ltd., on the right of the entrance shows i a full range of Kodak cameras, developing tanks for roll I films, plates and film packs, and examples of work done on the firm's materials. Of especial interest are the four entirely new patterns of camera w hich are included.

div.head: R.P.S. EXHIBITION.
div.p: THE R.P.S. EXHIBITION.

The venerable " Parent Society " open its 53rd Annual Exhibition on Thursday, the 17th September, and it is quite safe to say that never since the great Exhibition held by the same society in the Crystal Palace, has so much interesting photographic matter been brought together in one collection. The impres- sion one receives at the New Gallery this year is some- what the same as is given by a first visit to the Franco- British Exhibition, for the wealth of material is so great that one feels as if a single visit is not nearly enough to allow of the proper inspection of the many things one wishes to examine carefully.

div.head: LECTURES.
div.p: THE LECTURES.

Lantern lectures have always, been a special feature of the it show' and have been given on three nights in the week. This year they are being given on six nights, and there can be little doubt that everyone will be crowded. The great attraction will be the lectures illustrated with autochrome slides, prepared and delivered by the Secretary, Mr. J. Mclntosh, on "The Thames from Source to Sea." This is dealt with in three sections, of which the first will be shown every Monday, the second every Wednesday, and the third every Friday, from the 21st September to the 23rd October inclusive. Cirencester to Maidenhead, Windsor to Richmond, and Kew Gardens to the sea, am o the three sections. The programme of ordinary lantern lecturn is an unusually interesting and varied one, the lecturers including W. Fan en, A. H. Blake M.A., Rev, T. T. Norgate, W. L. W. Westell, F. Martin Duncan, A. H. Duncan, A. H. Dunning, C. H. Oal.den W. Biclserton F.Z.S., M.8.0.U., G. E. Thompson, E. W. llarvey Piper, Hon. M.S.A., Arthur Marshall, A.R.1.8.A., Ernest R. Ashton, Henry NV. Bennett, E. Seymour, Vaughan C‘rnish, D. Sc., and' F. J. Mortimer.

div.head: FATTENING THE RAY CROP.
div.p: FATTENING THE RAY CROP.

Mr. Ernest Parke records the results of his seventh years' experience in the improvement of poor grass land on his farm at Kinston, in Warwickshire. The unmanured portions of his fields continue give small yields of poor hay—about lOcwt. to 12cwt. per acre. In one field the portion annually dressed with super- phosphate alone (Bcwa. per acre) has this year yielded 28icwt. of hay per acre, and the portion dressed with nitrate of soda alone (fl cwt. per acre) has given 27cwt. per acre. Where both -fertilisers are used together the yield has been 34owt. of hay per acre—an increase of 23icwt. over the natural yield of the land in return for an outlay of less than 255. On another field where, owing to difference in soil, Dr. Dyer, who acts as Mr. Parke's adviser, considers basic slag more suitable than superphosphate, very similar results are recorded The natural yield of hay was l2lcwt. per acre. Basid slag alone (scwt. per acre) gave'3olcwt. of hay, and nitrate of soda alone (lott. per acre) gave 283cvrt.. while Lasio slag and nitrate of soda together gave 26icwt.9 being an increase of 24cwt. of hay per acre over the mow/lured plot in return for an outlay of under 30s. The ay. rage increase in yield from phosphatic and nitrogenous manure together on both fields over the seven years has been over lj ton of hay per acre, hut the hay crop in Warwickshire generally has been lighter than usual this year. Mr. Parke con- siders that the quality of the herbage is best on the land receiving the mixed dressings, and the appearance of the manured and unraanured and, all of which is alike grazed during the autumn, affords during any time of year a striking contrast.

div.head: DONT'S FOR FAT FOLKS.
div.p: DONT'S FOR FAT FOLKS.

Here are the dont's for fat folks if they want to get thin again : - Don't drink too much water, don't eat rich fo6d, don't indulge in .spirituous liquors, don't eat sweetmeats ; don't take it easy," but keep moving. Take long walks, eat starch), food, driLk little and sleep seven hours or less —no more. If you don't fancy that programme there is an alternative which has most certainly proved a blessing to the fat In the first place, it is inexpensive ; second, it is per: feet!), harmless, and third, no dieting, is necessary— you can eat what you like. Nevertheless, it takes off the fat without causing wrinkles, at the rate, it is claimed, of a round a day. Here is the recipe in full: Step over to your chemist and ask for one half-ounce of Marnaola, one ounce of fluid extract of Glycyrrhin MP ,ote ounce cf pure Glycerine D.P.,and reppe.rinint Water to make six ounces in all. Get the Martnola in a sealed half-ounce package, and mix it with the other three ingredients at home, or your chemist will mix them fcr you. It is necessary that ,the mixture should be fresh to get the best results. Thenitake one dessertspoonful after each meal and at bedtime until your fat is gone. Simple, isn't it ? Yu can eat, drii.k and sleep as you please and yet be just as slim as you wish without risk of injury to your health and at ithout the least trouble or discomfort.

It was only since his last return home after a long absence that he had been attracted by Lady Rhoda's beauty, which had now just reached its youthful perfection, and he had made up his mind to marry her. He had spared no pains to discover her tastes, and to gratify them when possible. This was his first present, but he had taken trouble to please her so plainly that it was quite as eloquent as the giving of many. And now there could no longer be any doubt of his object in doing so, nor any further delay in its being made clear. This evening must settle the fate of Rhoda's whole life. Her heart beat fast as she thought of it. But much can happen •in a single day, and much was to happen in this day, the most event- ful of any Rhoda had yet known. In the morning she had enough to do with receiving some of her girl friends who lived near and who brought her presents, and a deputation from the village school with a wonderful gift devised by the children themselves. She snatched a moment now and again to look in upon Sophia and see that her work was getting on well. At lunch she said to her mother, "I should like to go down to the village now with some things for some of the sick people. And then I might go to the school and thank all the children. Next year I should like to give everybody presents instead of their giving presents to me. It would be so nice if I were going to take some- thing to everyona, of these children." Her mother looked at her with a little smile. Probably by next year she would be married, and all the world would look different ,to her, and she might even have forgotten the village school- children. She went off very soon, with a multitude of little treasures packed away in her coat pockets. She was a ,3vell-known and -welcome visitor at the bedside of every invalid, rich or poor, within reach of Vernon Hall. Half-way to the village her heart suddenly seemed to stop beating, and she paused with eyes dilated and hands unconsciously clasped, watch- ing an alarming sight. It was a furious struggle between a wild young horse and his driver. When Lady Rhoda first caught sight of it the horse was rearing in such an extraordinary way that it seemed to be trying to get out of its harness; it literally writhed in its passionate efforts to escape from the strong hold on the reins of the man standing up in the dog-cart behind . it. As soon as its 'forelegs came down he began to thrash it so furiously that Rhoda cried out for mercy where she stood, though she was too far off to be heard. Then she began to run, with only one idea—to somehow take the part of i this poor wild creature. And as she ran she saw something else—a little child that had caught sight of her from the window of a cottage on the roadside and was toddling off to meet her. If that horse bolted the child. would be right in the way! Oh! what should she do? What could she do? And the man seemed to see nothing, to be blinded in his rage. She ran swiftly on, not noticing the sound of wheels behind herb The horse was now standing, shivering, for a moment, and the driver, with great agility and skill, sprang from the cart, seized the rein close to the bit firmly, and then began to kick the horse , violently in the side. The animal sprang back- ; . wards in its desperate effort to escape from him, and in doing so knocked down the child, and one . wheel passed over it. div.head: OLD AGE PENSIONS.
div.p: OLD AGE PENSIONS.
First Meeting of the Warrington
Committee.
NO OUTSIDE REPRESENTATION.

The Warrington Old Age Pensions Committee, which , consists of the whole of the members of the Town Council, bss got to work, the first meeting being held at the Town Hall on Monday afternoon under the • presidency of the Mayor (Alderman Smethurst). After the Deputy Town Clerk bad explained the provisions of the Act; there was onsiderable discussion as to whether the committee should delegate their duties to sub-committees or not. Eventually it was decided by a large majority not to delegate any powers, • but that the Act shoeld be administered by the committee. A letter was read from the Trades and Labour Cauncil raking for representation on the committee, but seeing that the committee had resolved not to delegat a their r Jwers, the question of the co-operation of outriders could not be considered, as the Act states that t'm nt—nbers of the committee must not exceed that of the appo'tting Council. The Mayor was elcated chairman of the committee pro tem., and the Town Clerk was apr Dinted clerk. The next Mt iting will be held as soon PS the pension officers have sent in the result of their investigations and the claims received by them. REPORT BY THE TOWN CLERK. The Town Clerk had prepared the following report on the Act :—The Council on the 11th August last con- stituted and appointed the whole of the members of the Council the Local Pension Committee. The immediate questions for the committee to consider are: —(1) Whether sub-committees are necessary, rod if so how many. (2) In what areas such sub-committees should rat, and (3) What powers and duties of the committee should be delegated to them. In speaking of "the committee," it will be understood that reference is made to the Local Pension Committee, and that the functions of the Town Council are practically at an end. The committee have power to appoint sub-committees. which may consist either wholly or partly of the mem- bers of the committee. The number of members of a sub-committee must not be less than five nore more than nine. With regard to the constitution of the snb- committees,the Local Government Board suggest that representatives from the local branches of trades unions or friendly or other societies might be appointed, whose services may he utilized if desired. If such l suggc lticm should be acted upon it might be advisable ' to appoint sub-committees, consisting of nine members, five of whom to be elected from the committee and two nominated by the United Fliendly Societies and two by • the Trades and Labour Conncil. The committee have power to delegate to the sub-committees, either abso- lutely or under such conditions as they think fit, all or any powers and duties of the committee under the Act. Beating in mind that the duties of the committee are mainly ministerial, there appears to be no advantage in their re-considering the work none by the sub-com- mittees, and it is, therefore suggcstc I that they should delegate ribsolut—.ly to Vie sub-committees all their powers and duties. Acting on the advice of the Local Government Board communication has been or.e.ncd with the local super- viser of Inland Revenue with regard to the division of the borough into art -1 for and in which the sub-com- mittees will act and it hos been suggested that the borough be divided into two areas as follons :-13y a line drawn from Longford Bridge on the north to the Stockton Heath Swing Bridge on the south, via. Winwiek-road, Winwick-street, Horsemarket-stre at, Bridge-stree, Wilderspool-causeway, to the level crossings, thence along the L. and N.-W. Railway to the Runcorn and I atchford Canal,and thence along that canal in a south-westerly direction to the Stockton Heath Swing Bridge. The areas might be called east and west districts respectively. The east district it is sug- gested, should include both sides of the streets named, as this boundary would enable the pension officers (of whom there are two in Warrington) to carry ant their duties without having to traverse the same ground as each other. The committee and each sub-comntittee is entitled to use free .of charge (except each as may be approved and paid by the Treasury for heating, lighting or cleaning) any <Mines of the Council at all reasonable times. The Council were empowered to "make regu- lations as to the quorum, proceedings and place of meetineof the committee," but as suitable provision • has been made in the regulations of the Local Govern- ment Board as to therm matters it is considered unnecessary for the Council either to amplify, extend or restrict them.

The general scheme of the Act is, as the committee is aware, to provide old-age pensions for poor persons of 70 years of age and upwards. The qualifications 1 end statutory conditions which will entitle a person to s, pension are set out in the Act and the regulations issued by the Local Government Board. A further report as to the manner in which claims for peosjons will be made und dealt with by the pension officer, /Ind ultimately considered and decided by the committee or sub-committee, may be found necessary,

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, September 26, 1908. OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, September 26, 1908. OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
ST. BARNABAS' CHURCH.

The harvest thanksgiving services in connection with this church commenced on Thursday evening when a large congregation assembled. As usual, the church had been beautifully decorated, an abundance of flowers, fruit and cereals being arranged with artistic effect. The altar, font and pulpit received special attention. The service was of on appropriately festal character, and the musical portions were creditably rendered. The choir had the assistance of an orchestra recently formed under the title of St.Barnabas' Musical Society, with Mr. H. J. Iddon as conductor. The anthem was " When thou hest gathered in thy corn " (Shaper), the solos being sung by Mr. T. Evans (tenor) and Mr. J. Green (bass). The Rev. P. Latimer Davies, of Liverpool, preach.d, taking for his text " And I will restore you the years that the locnst hath eaten " (Joel ii. 25). After describing the circumstances of the time to which the text referred—viz., the plague of locusts which devastated the land of Israel—the preacher said that year was not only unproductive, but the plague destroyed the stored-up harvests of previous years. In this, there could be found a parallel to present day events. The accumula- tion of wealth derived from years of successful enter- prise in business was very often swept away by an unfortunate piece of Er. eulat ion. In the religious world the same thing obtained. More moral fibre was destroyed in a single day than had been acquired in a lifetime. Not only was this true, but years which might have been successful from a worldly point of view, were very often spiritually barren. The ques- tion for each one to answer was : " Have I tried to make my little corner of God's world happier and brighter ? Have I tried to contemplate the Cross of Jesus Christ as God's crowning mercy to a lost world ? " God promised to give back to the Israelites the fruit of past years which had been destroyed. In a sense this could not be done. , The past was irreparable. We could not undo the mistakes of the past, but by making use of the experi- ences which the past held out to us, the years could be restored. The sticks and straws which were left from the harvest died and fructified the soil for the harvest of a future year. So in the spiritual and moral life, the experience which might be derived from the mis- takes of the past, could be used to produce, with God's help, a rich harvest in the coming years. We must remember, however, that the restored years would not be quite the sane as the first days of childhood's innocence. There as ould not be the exhilaration and swing as in former times. Something was gone ; some power, some capacity which we could never recover here, but even though it could not be regained in this life, in the larger life which began when this life ended, 1 in the richest and fullest sense, would the locust-eaten years be restored. The offertory was on behalf of the choir fund.

div.head: St Paul's Church.
div.p: St Paul's Church.

At this church on Sunday the annual church choir services were held, when the special preacher was the Rev. A. Wood, vicar of Packington, whose discourses were listened to with considerable interest. There was a very large congregation in the evening, and a sub- stantial sum was realized in aid of the choir funds. Spacial music was rendered by the choir, the anthem being a feature at each service. Mr. E. Wilkes presided at the organ. A united Bible Class service was held in the afternoon when the sermon was preached by the Vicar, the Rev. W. Bracecarap.

div.head: HARVEST- FESTIVALS.
div.p: HARVEST- FESTIVALS.
SALVATION ARMY.

The No. 2 Corps, West-street, harvest thanksgiving services last week-end. The barracks were nicely decorated with fruit, flowers arid vegetables. On Saturday miscellaneous items under the direction of Miss Jessie Keen were contributed by the following children: Janet Urmston, Jeanie Coyne, Ada Klan, Minnie Fogg, Ruth Wilkinson and Hannah Cla3lon. On Sunday afternoon there was a thankoffering meeting, and in the evening a" Salvation meeting," Staff-Captain Sewell, of Liverpool, officiating. Monday night brought the meetings to a close with a harvest home festival aud sale of fruit, conducted by Captain Charles Harper, officer-in-charge.

ST. PETER'S CHURCH. The harvest thanksgiving services were commenced on Thursday evening. The decorations of the church were in the best of taste and reflected great credit upon the following ladies who were responsible for them:— Choir stalls, Mrs. Young; chancel screen, Wm. Steel and Mrs. Tnnstall; font, Mrs. Clayton; windows and pillars, Mrs. Percival and Mrs. Hughes; pulpit and general decorations, Mrs. Greaves and Mrs. Meacock. There was a large congregation, the preacher 13ing the Van. Archdeacon Spooner, Rector of Walton, Liverpool, who based a powerful sermon on the words "Like as a shock of corn cometh in his season." (Job v.. 26). The choir gave a credit- able interpretation of the anthem All Thy works praise Thee," the soloists being Mr. W. Clayton and Master J. Greaves, Mr. E. A. Padmore presided at the organ. The offertory was in aid of special church expenses.

div.head: ELLESMERE S MEET WESLEY &N _MISSION.
div.p: ELLESMERE S MEET WESLEY &N _MISSION.

Harvest thanksgiving services were held at the above place or worship on Sunday. The interior of the building had been prettily decorated with a goodly display of corn, fruit, flowers and vegetables. Despite the inclement weather, there was a fair congregation at the morning service, which was oonducted by the Rev. T. Miller. A musical service was held in the afternoon, presided over by Mr. Edward Taylor. The Rev. F. W. Kernick delivered an address, and the vocal items included a solo by Miss May Isherwood, a duet by Miss S. Lee and Mr. J. Conway, and a quartette by Messrs. Powell, Tonge, Fletcher and Conway. In the evening the congregation was unusually large, wben-the pulpit was occupied by Cho Rev. F. Welwyn Remick, M.A., who had the undivided attention of his hearers whilst preaching from the text " The Lord is my Shepherd, I shall not w t "(Psalm xxiii. 1). The choir rendered the anthems "Gifts of Beauty "and "Consider the Lilies." A fruit banquet was held on Monday evening, the Rev. E. Blanshard Keeling pre- siding. Songs were rendered by Miss May Isherwood, Mr. G. Bennett and Mr. B. Sprive, a recitation by Miss M. Whitmore and violin selections by Miss E. Chadwick. Miss P. Taylor was an efaoient aclom- panist. Refreshments were served during an interval, and later in the evening there was a sale of fruit and vegetables. BAPTIST CT:MOH, COLBORNE-STREET.

div.head: ADDRESS BY AIR. ROBERT CAMERON, ALP.
div.p: ADDRESS BY AIR. ROBERT CAMERON, ALP.

The harvest services were oontinned on Sunday, when the interior of the church presented a very marked contrast to the dull conditions of the weather. The Ladies Committee adopted a very pleasing scheme of decoration, and the generous gifts of fruit, flowers, &c., were displayed with charming taste. In the morning the Rev. R. E. Letheren preaohed from Jeremiah v., 21, "The appointed weeks of the Harvest." The recently- formed choir acquitted itself very creditably indeed under the conductorship of Mr. C. Dawsou, and rendered the anthem "Ha watereth the earth," the solo part being taken by Miss Bather. Mr. S. Rickers presided at the organ. Very heavy rain interfered with the attendance in the afternoon but the chapel was fairly full when Mr. James Dodds took the chair. It was twenty-five years, he said, since he had last paid a visit to the church. It seemed to him that the Baptists had not taken that place in Warrington which was worthy of the denomin- ation ; but from what he had seen and heard of the work of Mr. and Mrs. Letheren the church at Golborne- street had now a better chance than ever before of making an advance; and if they were prepared to go forward he was sure there were friends outside who would help to see them through. He had not come to speak himself but he had very great pleasure in intro- ducing to them a Baptist veteran, who had for many years exerted a great influence upon his life and who at the age of 83 was one of the foremost fighters in the ranks of Temperance and was soon going back to the House of Commons to help the Licensing BUI through —his revered friend, Mr. Robert Cameron, M.P. Mr. CAMERON had an enthusiastic greeting, and, asking Mr. Dodds how he was to address him, hoped that as chairman he would keep the meeting iu order but especially the speaker who had the reputation of being" rather Inng-w;nded." He first addressed the boys and girls, and hoped that, however much they loved play, they would also early acquire a love of read- ing. He had himself excelled at football up to the ago of 28, but had then dropped it because he thought play was for boys and work for men. He hoped that they I would play themselves and not be content to pay six- pence to watch geown up men iplay. He had been stay- ing recently at a faem house n Yorkshire, and he had noticed that when the farmer went out into the yard with a basket of corn the fowls and chiekens rad even the geese all knew what was to happan and ran to be fed. That suggested his text "The eyes of all wait upon Thee." With the ripe wisdom of age and yet with a winsome simplicity that betokened a heart still young he spoke most beautifully of the" Great Farmer" for all His creatures. He sr Ate of the multitudinous swallows gathering for flight and how they are fed. He bed recently seep in the Canadian Hall of the Franco- British Exhibition immense pictures of the great prairies cover: I with golden waves of wheat • had recently recognized with great delight a butterfly he be had not seen for years. Upon this followed an account of the wonders revellved by the microscope. He then showed how the influence of the sun upon the sea and the soil lay at the sour of the rich harvest we reaped. And then with a graphic and delightfully tender recital of the "most wonderful story in the world," the story of the Prodigal Son, he rivetted the attention of his hearc: .; with thoughts of God's Father- hood and what it means for the sons of men. The scholars had been asked to bring to the service some Bible object and to attach some appropriate text to each. 11T-. Latheren conducted this part of the service and congratulated the audience upon having a chairmae who had entered so heartily into the spirit of the occasion that he had even brought his "object" with hire. The speaker hesitsted, he said, to speak of a Member of Parliament as an object and hoped he might not be called to the Bar, of the House of COM- MODS to apologize for his temerity; but might he be allowed to copy the example of the children and supply that object with a text? It should be these words— "A man more precious than fine gold . . . than the golden :wedge of Ophir." No one enjoyed the ministers use of the situation more than Mr. Cameron himself. _ _

Miss Mulkey, Mr. W. Tynan and Mr. Bailey sang solos that were very much .enjoyed and Mr. E. Wynne Jones in thanking the Chairman and Mr. Cameron for their presence and help assured Mr. Dodds that twenty- five years should not pass before he MS asked to come again and encouraged Mr. Cameron with the fact that there was a solid body of support in Warrington in favour of the Licensing Bill. In the evening the church was so crowded that extra accommodation bad to be provided wherever space was available. The choir very belutifnlly rendered the anthem " The earth is the Lord's " the solo parts being taken by Miss Emily Bates, Mr. W. Tynan and Mr. Herbert Barnes. „ . .

Mr. Letheren pren from Hosea 7-3 " A cake not turned," He said that among all classes in the East i and especially under conditions requiring haste there was much in dame-id a round fiat scone which was i baked by being laid on hot stones and the art of baking consisted in turning it over at the right moment. If this were mismanaged, one side might be burnt ! to a cinder while the other remained raw. ! He then sketched the historic background of the text and showed that it was a description of Society, one half of whose members wore too rich and the other half too poor ; that it described the unequal distribution of religion through life ; that it describ:d a political situation sc_ arched on the side of futile scheming, and raw as regardcd faith in God and righteousness; that it was the symbol of a nation in the furnace of atiliction half ruined by calamities and not re-cued. We are a Christian nation, said the preacher, and yet one-sixth of all British born children die within twelve months of birth, and of the remtining five 7ixths thousands are handicapped from the start through living in conditions that rob them of sullicient air, food and clothing to ensure their sound development ; one-third of the population exists on an income insufficient to supply the ' family with the bare necessaries of a healthy life . . yet one of the greatest of living political economists tells u-, that there is a margin of at least one or two hundred millions in our yearly expenditure which might be diverted to social uses without causing any great distress to those from whom it was taken. Hosea's word was equally true of churches that put ritual and formality in the place of the service of God and man; and also of individuals whose character was full of inconsistencies. Mr. H. BUCKBV (Church secretary), expressed the thanks of the church to all who by their generous gifts and willing service had made the gathering so successful. The series of engagements concluded with a harvest supper on Thursday evening.

div.head: .. A FATAL GAME.
div.p: .. A FATAL GAME.
Warrington Girl Falls Into al Acid
Vat.

Mr. F. A. Jones, deputy coroner, held an inquest at the Warrington Police Station on Tuesday, touching the death of Beatrice Wainwright, the eight-year-old daughter of John Wainwright, 221, Winwick-road, who died as the result of falling into a vat of acid at the Longford Wire Works on Thursday night. Mr. Sumner, ILM. Factory Inspector, was present: Mr. Draper (Robert Davies and Company) represented the Company, and Mr. Browne appeared for the relatives of the deceased.

_ Deceased's father stated that the girl went out with a companion named Hilda Spilling about 7.30 p.m. last Thursday. He knew they had been In the habit of going to the Longford Wire Works with supper, hut he was not aware that they were allowed to enter the works. Deceased was brought home at eight o'clock and her condition was such that she was removed to the Infirmary where she died. She told witness that she was playing "I spy" and fell into a vat of acid at the works. She went over-head and swallowed some of the acid. She added that she thought tho vat was a plank of wood and stepped on to it. Mr. Browne: Isn't it common knowledge that chil- dren have been allowed for COMO years to go and play in these works? Witness • I believe it is.

Hilda SI;illi-nma7g,e-d—ten, said that deceased accom- panied her to the works. They went to see if witness's brother George wanted his supper bringing. The works door was open and they went in. After seeing her brother they played hide-and-seek. Deceased" jumped on to a shadow ." and found herself in the acid vat. They had gone to the works together at night many times and had always found the gate open. No one ever stooped them from going in. There were other girls taking suppers into the works. George Spilling, SO, Foster-street, a block minder in the galvanizing shed at Longford Wire Works, said his sister had been in the habit of bringing his supper to the works for the past two years. She was generally accompanied by the deceased. After leaving the supper they used to play about for a minute or two and then he would send them home. He did not think it was .dangerous for them to play in the galvanizing shed, but it was certainly dangerous to play in the vicinity of the acid vats. On the night in question hesaw the children playing in a sand heap in the works. After they bad spoken to him about the supr 3r he told them to go borne and he thought they had left the works, but about a quarter of an hour later his sister came and told him that deceased had fallen into the vat. In cross-examination by Mr. Browne, Spilling stated that there was no lodgeman at the works gates at night. It was a fact that a large number of children went into the works with suppers. He had seen as many as four with one supper.—Questioned by the Cororer, witness said as far as he knew the girl Wainwright had no right on the prom:ism—By Mr. Draper : The large gates of the works were closed, but the small gate was open all night. Joseph Lee,the works manager, said the nearest point to the vat in passing through the acid room to the galvanizing department was Cat. Gin. It was not correct that the works were always open. The wicket gate was only open at meal times.—ln answer to Mr. Browne, witness said a notice was put up IS months ago prohibiting children going into the works for any purpose,but that notice had not been up for some time. George Worthington, potman at the works, said he was in charge during the night. He saw the two girls on Thursday playing about, end ha told them to go home to bed. They ran away towards the clearing house. The wicket gate was open from six o'clock until 9.30 p.m. Dr. Russell said the girl died through having got some of the muriatic acid in her lungs ; otherwise he did not think she would have died.

The jury returned a verdict of " Accidental death," and suggested that better precautions should be taken with a view to preventing any parson except workmen entering the premises. Mr. Draper, on behalf of the directors of the com- pany, expressed sympathy with the deceased's relatives that the accident had occurred. The works had been going for 30 years, and that was the first fatal accident. Although it had been the custom for fool to be taken into the works, the company had already taken pre- cautions and made other arrangements.

div.head: RUN-DOWN AFTER THE SUMMER.

A Wife's Heart Pains, Nervous Weakness, and Headacne.

Mts. Susan Chapman, of London-road, Hertford Heath, Herts., for two years was terribly run down and felt constantly sleepy, just as hundreds of women do after the hot, debilitating summer. "I had a con- stant aching between the shoulders," says Mrs. Chapman, "feeling as if a heavy weight were pulling my neck down backwards. Every morning I felt very heavy, my head aching, and severe palpi- tation starting immediately on my getting out of bed and on to my feet. This fluttering at the heart caused me much distress at all times. div.head: COUNTY REVISION COURTS. -- Mr. J. HMS, jai., Obtains a Li
div.p: COUNTY REVISION COURTS. -- Mr. J. HMS, jai., Obtains a Li
Vote.

Mr. C. H. M. Wharton, ravising barrister, hell the annual Revision Court for the townships of Penketh, Sankey, Cuerdley, and 13)1d, at Penketh Institute, at noon on Tuesday. The Conservatives were represented by M. J. EL Bottomley and Mr. Mawdsley, and the Labour Party by Mr. Forshaw. The following assistant overseers wers present :—Messrs. E. Foster (Penketh), J. Smith (Sankey), J. Fairclough (Bold), and 11. B. Wright '(Cuerdley). LIABLE TO A .£5 FINE.

Mr. Wright had not brought his rate book, awl the Revising Barrister informed him that he was liable to a fine of £5, He (the Barrister) had no right to take his word without his books. Another time that he did not bring his book he would have to go and bring it, and also pay the fine of £5. MR. BOTTONILEV'S AMBITION.

- - Several passages of arms took place between the Revising Barrister and Mr: Bottomley owing to the latter supplying information which Mr. Wharton con- sidered should be given by the assistant overseers. • I On one occasion Mr. Wharton exclaimed excitedly : 1" Really, Mr. Bottomley, you seem to waiit to be agenlo assistant overseer of all the parishes, and revising barrister all at once. If that is so it would be as well if you came and took this chair and conducted the revision yourself." Among the applications for the lodger franchise was one in Penketh by Mr. T. H. Owen. Mr. Bottomley said this was yeally an old claim, as Mr. Owen had been on last year. Mr. Wharton: I don't care. It is a new claim now. Mr. Bottomley: But it is the custom that whep a claim is once allowed it is always allowed as a mattef of course unless there is some objection to it, and there is no objection to this. Mr. Wharton: I am going to inquire into the cases myself, no matter what my ,predecessor did. He may have had his reasons for acting as he did. Mr. Bottomley: This applicant has been for many years a lodger, and it has been the practice in every court in Ragland that when a man has once got on the list he should be kept on unless there is some change or objection. Mr. Wharton: Nothing of the sort. That is not my practice and it won't be my practice. Mr. Bottomley It is so every where fits.. I have bad 25 year's experience, and it has always been the practice. Mr. Wharton: I dare say it is the practice in a good many coui s to get all the information from the agents. I intend to be different. I am not going to do it, Mr. Bottomley, so don't let us squabbled Mr. Bottomley: I am-entitled to tell you that there are two lists here. One is a list of new claimants and , the other is a list of old claimants. 'lee applicant in this case has been on tto list in•previous years, though I for a certain reason he is on the list of new claimants. , He is, therefore entitled to have his vote. A SUCCESSFUL LODGER CLAIM.

All the lodger claims in the various townships were struck out except the one of Mr. Owen. In reply to the Revising Barrister, Mr. E. Foster said the ratable value of the house in which Mr. Owen had apartments was £25. It was occupied by his mother. . Mr. Wharton: Do you think.thli is a good claim? Mr. Fostrr : I do. , Mr. Wharton: On what grounds? Mr. Foster: If the lodger pays sufficient rent, I should consider be has sufficient value for a vote: Mr. Wharton: It that t 4 only reason you have? Mr. Foster : Yes sir. Mr. Wharton: That is not the law. I have already I ruled that the amount of rent paid by the lodger is a I very small item indeed in the consideration of this matter. I Mr. Foster : You allowed the claim last year on the ground that he was a supporter of the house. Mr. Wharton: Never in this world. I have never allowed a claim on that ground. You must have put into my judgment something which came out of the mouth of an agent. Mr. Foster: That' was a point which had some influence with you in the matter. Mri Wharton: Never! The fact that a man is a supporter of the house is absolutely a matter of indiffer- ence to mee It is a sentimental reason, and I am not influenced at all by that. The only consideration to me is whether this one bedroom is worth £lO. That is what is bothering me. It is a genuine lodger case. The only thing is this : Ts the room worth £10? Ultimately the Revising Barrister granted the claim on the ground that there were very few houses in Penketh which claimant would be able to get for lodgings. Therefore, there being none, they could ask a bigger price for one room. " nutlet it be understood" he added, " that omtimental reasons about breed winners, supporters of families and that kind of non- sense are absolutely outside the law, and I will have nothing to do with them."

div.head: WARRINGTON.
div.p: WARRINGTON.

• • -- On Tuesday afternoon Mr. Wharton attended at the Warrington Borough Police Court, to revise the lists for the Warrington polling district of the Newton Division, which comprises the townships of Poulton, Rixton, Martinscroft and Warrington tcounty).
OWNERSHIP CLAIMS. "GROSS IRREGULARITY."

There was a lively discussion with reference to several ownership claims to which, in one or two cases, objec- tion was raised by the assistant overseer for Warring- ton (Mr. W. H. Woodcock). The Conservative agent's usual official form of claim was put in, but the barrister held that if Mr. Bottomley signed for a claimant, a pro-curation must be put in. Mr. Bottomley replied that what he had done was approved by every Barrister in the country., Mr. Wharton: I don't bare if I wore the only, Barrister in tbe country who objected to the form, I should still object. Mr. Bottomley read extracts from the "notice of claim" addressed tn the claimant which said among other things: "I believe you are entitled to claim a vote for the Newton Division and will be glad if you will kindly send me (Mr. Bottomley) back both these forms signed, so that I may in due course take the necessary steps to sc lure you your vote. Will you kindly answer the oinc-,tions below, for my information and guidance By doing so your owner's vote is pre, tically secured without further trouble." Mr. Wharton: Are you going to argue the case, because I shall use strong language if you do? The sooner you stop writing other people's signatures the better, and lam going to put a atop to it. Someone in the office has written the whole of the claim, signature and all, in the same writing, and it does not say " by authority." Mr. Bottomley explained that the applicant signed the official form sent to him. • Mr. Wharton : If I were to examine all the claims— I hive not done so because it has been the custom to take a good deal from agents—l should find that the whole of the system of the registration courts has been based on the grossest irregularity. 'lois is gross irregu- larity vid it won't do for me. 1 don't suppose for a moment it hrs been done except in a perfectly straight- forward manner so far as intention is concerned. When you sign another man's name put something in to show by whose authority you do so. 11R. JOSEPH BOWES, JUN., OBTAINS A LODGER VOTE.

Mr Joseph Howev, jun., Liberal agent for Warring- ton, claimed a lodger vote in respect of apartments at Eddie House, Fearrhead. Mr. Fred Wright, essistant oversor for the town- ship, said the grors value of the horse was RIR. Mr. Howes : Gat of deference to your honor* I have come to suprert the claim. I have left my holicTays on purpose to greet you again. I occupy a bedroom and a sitting-room, which 1 considered to be the best room. _ .
„. Mr. Wherton I,Nve Ton the enelusive re of the rooms ?
Mr. Howes : Ye", sir. My sitting-room will he up while I am here. I generally turn the key in the door, ellhough I always leave the key in the door. _ _ .

.Mr.Bottoroley : Mr.Forshaw and I strongly support the claini. We think it is a very deierving one (Laughter.) Mr. Howes : Thank you. Mr. Wharton (to the Assistant Oveh;eer, Mr. F. Wright).—Woulcl these rooms., if empty, be worth .£lO. Mr. Wright : Yes, sir. The Barrister : On the evidence of the Assistant Overseer I shall allow the vote. Mr. Bottomley : We take it as a great compliment to the political agents. The Barrister : No, I have evidence on which to grant it. EVIDENCE OF DEATHS REQUIRED.

Mr. Bottomley asked for a man to be struck off the list because he was dead. The Assistant Overseer said he had not rc 7,eived any information to that effect. Mr. Bottomley said the case was referred to a local correspondent in the parish, and he reported the man to be dead. Mr. Wharton said it was very kind of the agents to do what they did to supply the Court with information, but he thought it would be a dangerous precedent to strike a man off on evidence like that. It was not strictly legrl evidence, especially if it was not known by the Assistant Overseer. Mr. Bottomley should com- municate the facts to the Assistant Overseer and let him verify them. Under the circumstances, he must allow the name to stand.

div.head: PRONOUNCED HIS CASE INCURABLE
div.p: PRONOUNCED HIS CASE INCURABLE
Whole Body Raw with Eczema--- Life was Intolerable—Was Even incased in Piaster—Discharged from Hospitals as Hopeless.

div.head: SUFFERED 14 YEARS CURED BY CUTICURA
div.p: SUFFERED 14 YEARS CURED BY CUTICURA

"From the age of three months until fifteen years old, my eon Owen's life was made intoler- able by eczema in its worst form. He was all right until a red rash broke out on his fore- head, but we were lot alarmed at first. "ery soon, however, ho rash began to spread over his head and shoulders, and It caused him great discomfort. I took him _,2tor and tried half a dozen other treatments, all with the same result: no improvement at all. The disease gradually spread until nearly- every part of his body was quite raw. We had to strap him down in bed, for he used to tear himself dreadfully in his sleep. The agony he went through is quite beyond words. No one thought we would rear him. The regimental doctor, a very clever man, pronounced the case hopeless; at least, he said the only hope was that he might, if he lived long enough, outgrow it to some extent. We had him in hospitals four times and he was pronounced one of the worst cases, if not the worst, ever admitted. From each he was dis- charged as incurable; in fact he got worse under the successive treatments. At one hospital they incased him in plaster, and this seemed to aggravate the soreness terribly. He looked so badly that no one liked to go near him and his life was a burden to him. We kept trying remedy after remedy, but we had got almost past hoping for a cure.
