So we have lost Newcastle ! NEWCASTLE The combination of forces ELECTION, has proved too much for the Liberal, pretty much as it did in Peckham and North West Manchester. Brewers, licensees, coal-owners and Tariff Reformers joined issue to mislead the electorate and render the Liberal position untenable. They were helped by that spirit of discontent arising from bad trade and unemployment which always goes against the party in power; and the inter- vention of a Socialist candidate with no chance of success for himself, but certain to split the Progressive vote. As a matter of fact the I Socialist drew oft just enough Progressives to turn the scale. In a straight fight between Liberal and Conservative, the former would probably just have won, seeing that the difference between them is one of only 2,143 out of a total poll of 28,631, and that the Socialist had 2,971 followers. It must be remembered that at the General Biection in 1906, there were four candidates for two seats, and the Liberal-Labour combination proved irresistible. The death of Mr. CAIRNS, the Liberal member, created a vacancy which the Socialist firebands of Newcastle have conspired to play into the hands of the Tories.

The number of those who will find any satis- faction in the S3cialist achievement is small out of all proportion to the importance which the candidature assumed in view of the fact that the Liberal candidate found himself opposed by the Irish influences in the constituency. Mr. HARTLEY may be regarded as expressing in its extremest form the doctrine that of the two great parties in the State the one is as bad as the other. To extravagance of that kind there is no reply but a shrug of the shoulders. That man has some common sense on his side who says that he is not concerned about parties if he can get out of one what he could get out of another. Bat does that ever happen? Putting the case on the narrow and selfish ground of personal advantage, does it ever occur that the country gets from th 3 Con- servatives what it would have got from the Liberals, or vice versa% ? "The answer is in the negative," as Mbaistera are wont to say in the House of Commons. It is the reply of history and experience.

The -main and essential difference between all Liberal and all Tory legislation is that Liberalism never legislates for a class or for an "interest," and that Conservatism almost habitually does. It is contrary to every Liberal principle to confer bene- fits on a section of the people at the expense of the whole. Bat in how many cases did the late Conservative Government make itself respon- sible for measures which contemplated the advantage of the people as a whole, or which were not, in fact, measures of partial appli- cation, designed to assist the landowning class, or the clerical caste, or some other hungry section of applicants, at the cost of the gensral taxpayer? The simple truth is that the differ- ences between parties are so deep that they go' down to the very roots of human nature. We must look for the origin of these contending opinions in the human problem itself, in the character of mankind, and in the constitution of the individual man. We may choose our party for one reason or another. We often sort our selves for very indifferent reasons, the real charcter of which we do not acknowledge or admit; but here, there are concerned motives into which it is not at present necessary to inquire. These accidental attachments have nothing whatever to do with the real differences which divide us. The original basis of one's Liberalism or one's Conservatism will be found in the mental constitution which dominates one's outlook on life and one's view of one's fellow-creatures. The truth has never been so concisely and so trenchantly put as by Mr. GLADSTON :when he said: "Conservatism is distrust of the people, qualided,by prudence."; This is the real and only reasonable ground for the differences between the two great parties in the State. There is the popular and progressive influence on the one side, and there is the resist- ing influence on the other. The spirit of progress contending with the spirit of resistance to pro- gress—that, in a nutshell, is our whole system—a beneficial system, in the main—of party government.

Mr. Herbert Gladstone's THE CASE OF explanation of the course DirsY LORD. the Home Office propose to take in regard to the girl Daisy Lord, lying under sentence of penal servitude for life for the murder of her infant child, should satisfy all reasonable persons. The authorities propose to deal with her in the manner which Mr. Gladstone assures us is customary in cases of this kind. That is to say, she will be detained in a place where she will be brought in contact with reclaiming influences, and he will have a free hand to subsequently modify the sentence in accordance with the circumstances of the case and the disposition and progress of the ptisoner. In all probability she will not be detained more than three years. We do not agree with those who claim that the girl should be hastily or unconditionally released. The Home Secretary points out, quite rightly, that action of that kind would tend at once to minimise the seriousness of the crime of infanticide—a result which could not but be deplorable. It is far better that an attempt at the social salvation of the mother should be made, and there is no ques- tion that in this case, if the Home Sectetary sees his way by reason of the girl's conduct to give her freedom, she will find many ready to give her a new start in life. Similarly a definite reduction of the sentence to a fixed term would prevent

him from exercising that discretion which is placed in his hands, and which we are sure will be used humanely and mercifully. The coarse taken in this case does not affect the reasonable claim which is made by a very large section of the community that a reform should be made in the criminal law, by which a Judge should have a power in cases-of this kind, where it is obvious that the death sentence could not be carried out, to pass some other sentence.

Th eGarden Saburbs scheme GARDEN is out of its swaddling SUBURB!. clothes at last, and on Thursday next, the first garden suburb will make its bow to the priblic at Sankey. It is less than two years since the scheme first took shape in the minds of cectain influential local people, who wrote to the press, and followed the matter up with a meeting at which it was decided to form a local company. Matters then progressed with some rapidity and £5,000 were subscribed towards the nominal I capital of the Company. As most of our readers will be aware, sites were quickly secured lat Sankey, and Moans Brook, Grappenhall. The former is the one which has been most rapidly pushed forward, and on Thursday next the corner stones of the first two houses will be laid with fitting ceremonial. In another page we publish plans of the two estates showing the scheme for laying them out as Garden Subunbs. The houses are to be held under a Co-operative Society, affiliated to the Co-partner ship Tenants' Housing Council, about which Mr. THenry Vivian, M.P. has told us so much in recent years. It is hoped that in course of time the tenants will own all the houses built by the Society. In fact this is its raison d'etre, and tho progress made at Ealing on similar lines encourages the hope. A ring of Garden Suburbs girdling the town is contemplated. Warrington is, so far, the only town in Eagland to make definite and material progress in this direction, and the idea of the "good old town "leading the way to a better new town is appropriate and stimulating. The idea of Beautiful Warrington inside, and even more beautiful suburbs outside, seems to possess a resemblance to the millennium, but we believe it will prove a little easier to attain. The ceremony of next Thursday is to honoured by the presence of Mr. Ebenezer Howand, the pioneer of the Garden City ideal. Mr. Howard was scoffed at as a dreamer when he first broached his scheme, but he was firm in h's faith in the collectivist and associative idea. His persistent effort attracted valued helpers and the dead weight of public apathy was overoome. Letchworth —the first Garden City—is the sequel, and Mr. Howard may be considered fortunate in seeing his ideals so well on the way to realization in such a' short time. The Letchworth estate covers 3,318 acres, has 1,110 houses already, and a population of 6,000—t0 look after whom requites the attention of only three policemen. Tne Garden City tenants own 250 houses ranging in rent from 41. 6d. to 16s. per week. For 4s. 63. a week a workingman can have a house with two bedrooms, living room, scullery, and bath, together with a garden 120 ft. by 12ft. All this is due, in the main, to Eoenezer Howard who has, in the words of Blake, " built Jerusalem in England's green and pleasant land."

Thursday was a day to WARRTNGTON which the aged poor PEN4tosinas. throughoutthe.country had been anxiously looking for. ward, for they were able to take the first step to- wards that long-cherished goal—the old age pension —by filling in their forms of application at the various Post Offices. Batches of forms were sent out to Post Offices all over the country a week ago, and from the stroke of eight on Thursday morning the officials were authorised to supply them to would-be pensioners. The eagerness which great numbers of toil- worn veterans of both sexes manifested to complete the necessary preliminaries gave the lie to any suggestion that the beneficent provision made for their declining years by the Liberal Government—which will be an accomplished fact by January Ist—would not be appreciated. It was only on August let last that the Act received the Royal assent, so that no time has been lost in getting to work. The proceeding under the Act has been made as simple as possible. The applicant, who must be over seventy, walks into a post office and fills in a form of application. The form is then posted to the officer of the Inland Revenue. All the information on these forms is then verified as far as possible by the pension officer. Should he decide that the applicant is not entitled to the pension, the latter still has a right of appeal to the Local Pension Committee, before whom he I can plead his case. The old folk of Warrington and district have not yet come forward in strikingly large nembers, but a good start has been made. On Thursday there were 41 applications at the General Post Office, Warrington, and 139 in the whole of the Warrington district, which includes Frodshain. , Yesterday 17 applications were dealt with at the head office. As was only to be expected, some pathetic and humorous scenes were witnessed. Most of the applicants appeared to approach the, office in fear and trembling, but went away rejoicing when their claims were duly made out, the officials doing all they could to help them in the task. The oldest applicant at the Warrington office was a man of eighty-three. One old lady of seventy-seven took the trouble to produce her grandmother's marriage lines "to show" to use her own words " that she was genuine." One man who has reached his seventy-first year informed the officials that he had been discharged from work a fortnight ago because he was too old. On the form of claim appears the question" Have you lived in the United Kingdom for the whole of the last twenty years ?” and to this one lady of eighty returned the prompt answer than she had never been more than two miles out of Warrington. A female applicant of seventy-eight had a pathetic tale to tell. Eight years ago she had the misfortune to slip and fall on a piece of glass and in consequence had entirely 'lost the use of her right hand. A would-be pensioner whose birth place was a village several miles away told how she had communicated with the Rector of the parish to 'obtain something of the nature of an official record of the date of her birth and had received a reply to the effect that he was unable to find the desired inforthation in the church books. She was told that the entry in the family Bible would no doutt be sufficient and gratefully exclaimed " You have taken a load off my mind !" adding that at her advanced age she did not want to have to make a visit of inquiry •to her birth- place. A singular fact was that most of the men appeared to be supported by their sons, while the women had relied upon their daughters' help.

div.head: WESLEYAN QUARTERLY MEETING.
div.p: WESLEYAN QUARTERLY MEETING.

The quarterly meeting of the Warrington Wesleyan Methodist Circuit was held at Lymm on Thursday. Tea was provided by the Lyrnm friends for a company of between fifty and sixty, and a vote of thanks was accorded to them for their hospitality, on the proposi- tion of the Rev. E. Blanshard Keeling (superintendent minister). The business meeting was afterwards held, the Rev. E. B. Keeling presiding. All the local ministers and the circuit stewards (Hr. R. H. INleldru m and Dr. Bennett) were present. At the commencement a vote of condolence with the family of the late Mr. R. 11. Silcock, a devoted worker in the cause of Methodism, was passed on the proposi- tion of Mr. Meldrum seconded by Dr. Bennett, the members standing as a mark of respect. The accounts were passed, the financial position being considered satisfactory. There was some discussion on the foreign missionary programme for the coming winter. The services of missionaries from various parts of the foreign field have been secured for practically all the places in the circuit. The following officers were re-elected :—Treasurer, Mr. William Silcock ; secretaries, the Rev. T. Miller, Mr. M. Silcock and Mr. J. G. Withiashaw ; treasurer of the worn-out ministers' fund, Mr. .1. E. Richardson. Arrangements were made for the visit next week of the Rev. W. Kingscote Greenland and for the circuit guild rally on November Bth and 9th, both events to be held at Bewsey-road Church. This completed the business and afterwards there was an innovation in the form of a devotional meeting which was conducted by the Rev. E. B. Keeling and the other ministers with much fervour and benefit. The next meeting will be held at Bold-street on December 17th.

The residents of Padg,ate and Fearnhead are wroth with the Cheshire Lines Committee. The 10.3 a.m. train is rarely, if ever, up to tiine and season ticket holders are considering whether it is worth their while to take a season ticket and then be compelled to walk to town. Padgate has some pretensions to becoming the best residential suburb of Warrington but we are afraid that there is not much likelihood of that becoming an accomplished fact so long as the • railway service is so shockingly bad. The Parish Council must be alive to the disadvantages, and if it values its reputation, it must insist upon a remedy. * *

The Board of Agriculture has issued an order threatening with severe pains or penalties anybody who harbours, without notification to the Board, such pets as the Ceratilis capitata Wiedemann or the Doryphora decemlineata Say, or who encourages Rosellininia necatriv Prillieux et Delacroiv or Chrysophlyctis euclobiotica. These things would seem so much less picturesque that nobody would want to make pets of them if they were known, respectively, by their every-day names —Mediterranean fruit-fly, Colorado beetle, white root-rot, and warty disease of potatoes. * * *

Our confident friend Councillor Broadhurst, is not to be allowed to escape the persistent attention of his critics, and particularly "Red Rose," who has been busy for some time nailing the Councillor's Tariff Reform fallacies to the counter. * Mr. Winston Churchill's brilliant wedding ceremony the other day reminds "T. P.'s Weekly" that St. Margaret's Church, Westminster, has witnessed many great nuptials. In this church John 1111 ton married his second wife, Katherine Woodcocke, and here this lady as buried after a very short married life. The great Lord Chancellor Clarendon also married his second wife, Frances Aylesbury, in this church. Two other poets, Edmund Waller and Thomas Campbell, met their wives at the altar of St. Margaret's, and here also Samuel Pepys was wedded to the penniless girl of - fifteen whose wifely ways are immortalised in the Diary.

* * * The school accommodation question on Monday progressed another stage in its slow journey towards solution. After much pow-wowing and some priceless pearls of wisdom from the lips of Alderman Bolton, the recommendations of the School Attendance Com- mittee were confirmod. This means that the Sites and Buildings Committee will proceed at its best pace— which is not hair-raising—towards the provision of a school for the West end of St. Austin's Ward. They ' I are also instructed to secure sites fn. new schools iaA Fairfield, Orford, St. John's, and Whitecross Wards. The Committee may be considered to have its hands -, full. Meanwhile we note with interest the opinion. expressed by Mr. John Upson that "there was no-, immediate intention un the part of the Board of Education to reduce accommodation by reckoniag - school places on a 10ft, basis instead of Sit." 1* * *

Sarasate has passed away some thirteen months after Joachim. In temperament, the two greatest violinists of the day were strangely unlike. Joachim's was a profound genius. Sarasate was unequalled among his contemporaries for the brilliant wizardry of his bow, but his interpretation of the great master- pieces of the old school lacked the poetry and depth of Joachim's playing. Those who have experienced . the spell of Sarasate cannot forget it. His tone was superb, his executive powers amazing beyond descrip- tion, and his style full of Spanish fire. In London he had a great following from the day of his debut in ISM, but in recent years his appearances have not been numerous. His income from his playing is said to have been £lO,OOO a year. He owned a "Strad" presented to him at the age of ten by Queen Isabel of Spain, but the instrument he has made doubly famous reverts at his death to the State.

* * The big beer picnic takes place to-morrow in Hyde Park. We don't know how many of the brewers' conscripts will be assembled there, but there won't be many left at home, unless they are deserters from the ranks. From what we can hear the deserters

will be " fired " as usual. It is not quite certain that the death penalty will be inflicted on those brewery employ-6s who don't want to " demonstrate " in Loudon, but they are quite likely to find themselves among the unemployed before the echoes-of the great shout "We want our beer, our bitter, .bitter beer have died away. The pay of the conscripts is pretty good, however. Some get free railway tickets and os. to spend (on their own product of course). The 800 who are being despatched from Warrington will, we hear, have free railway tickets and free dinner and tea. We wonder how many will " deTonstrate " independently when they next enter a polling booth? * * * The death, at eight-four, of Dr. Walter Chalmers Smith, ex-Moderator and minister of the Free High Church, Edinburgh, and author of " Olrig Grange" and other poetical works, will have been heard of by many with deep regret. Thirty years ago he was certainly, north if not south of the Tweed, among the most widely read verse-writers of his time, and the " Spectator, ' which then reflected the literary judg- ments of Mr. It. H. Hutton, thought him "perhaps the most uniformly equal of living poets." After Olrig Grange," which was published in 1872, Dr. Smith's best known work was " Hilda among the Broken Gods," and in " Kildrostan " he made an essay in dramatic poetry. Dr. Smith was a teacher of liberal theology in verse, and in a day when the novels of George Macdmald were eagerly read, he found his public without difficulty. * * * ' There's nothing like a bankrupt father to make a son succeed.—Maartens. Great men dislike being disappointed in little things.—Joscple Conrad. It is not silly to love. It is unwise, or wrong, or heavenly, or mad, but silly, no.—Barottes3 ran Ilutten. It takes some grit to be a practical philosopher in the corner of a stuffy 'bus at ten o'clock at night.-- Margaret Baillie-Saunders. Woman invented persuasion.—Geo,.gc Calderon. A lie which is half a truth is ever the blackest of lies.—Tc)ln yson. Silence is better than speech.—Long fellow. A. woman admires a good man and loves a bad one.

* * * A great point has been made by the Trade in the opposition to the Licensing Bill of the statement that the Inland Revenue authorities have been adopting the practice of valuing publicans' estates for death duties on the assumption that the licence " will con- tinue to be renewed." This statement has been widely used in otder to emphasise the injustice of levying duties on the licence as if the renewal were a certainty, and then of proposing a time limit, But an interesting light is thrown on this by a letter from Mr. C. Smith pointing out, by quoting from a letter written by the Chancellor of the Exchequer's instructions, that the augument used by the Trade is based upon a document issued from Somerset House prior to the Sharp v. Wakefield judgment of 1891. Since then the only principle recognised in valuing has been that which applies to probate duties—viz., that the value is taken to be the amount that "interest would fetch if sold in the open market at the time of the death of the decelsed." Thig entirely disposes of the fiction that any exceptional methods have been used in the case of licences. If the Trade has at any time created an Milted markep that has been their business, and the Inland Revenue; authorities are not responsible.

'Alderman Bennett entertained the Parliamentary "Debating Society with some of his lightning oratory on Thursday evening and the members were rather amused when, having bounded along in his usual Style for nearly ten minutes, he remarked with a fiance at the clock, "I see my time is nearly gone, so, must hurry on!" * ** .Ater a few months' holiday, the members of our local Parliament re-assembled on Thursday and were son tackling the affairs of the nation once more in real earnest. We must congratulate the Cabinet „ill?ou the bold progressive policy outlined in the "-Ing's Speech. The problem of unemployment naturally occupies a prominent place and the Cocain- rn,ent hope to submit for the members' approval plans , which they trust will go far towards a ion. It will be interesting to hear on what lines they propose to deal with this pressing national tronble which at present looms far above all other Political questions. But this is not all. Railway , nationalisation, taxation of rand values, and electoral • and registration reform all find a place in the Govern- ment's ambitious programme. They have only until : 'this end of December in which to carry it out—for , 'whether they are defeated or not they are bound to : relinquish office then —but they are determined to ; 'Put forward every effort to pass sound measures , embodying their strong views on these important , subjects. With a leader of Mr. John Upson's tried 'arabilities, they should have another successful session.

[FROIt OCR LONDON CORRESPONDENT.] The need of some better way of settling trade disputes than by the cm ule and wasteful methods of the strike and the lock-out is, perhaps, the most Prominent subject occupying public attention at the present moment. Startling revelations of the corrupt influence of the great Trusts in American politics furnish an object lesson in the demoralisation caused by the facilities which a protective system offers for the over-riding of the interests of the cammunity by Powerful combinations. STRIKES AND LOCK-OUTS.

Although the lock-out in the Lancashire cotton ' trade is not expected to last very long, the very large lianlher of operatives thrown cut of work —some 120,000 cotton-spinners, card-room ht.nds, and others ---atnoclrt the overwhelming proportion of the British tot trade affected—nearly three-quarters of the whole number of spindles idle—bring home in a l'emarkable manner the enormous possibilities of evil In the existing rough-and-ready methods of settling Points in dispute between employers and employed. Against the failure of the Lancashire trade dispute to adjust itself can at any rate be set the decision of theizen in the North-East Coast engineering industry to accept the terms arranged at the recent conference called by Mr. Churchill, as President of the Board of 'Trade, at Whitehall, on September Bth and 9th. The executive have communicated the result of the ballot 10.1.1 r. Churchill, and expressed their gratitude for Ts services in bringing about a settlement. It is, nowever, lamentable to think that seven months of unnecessary suffering and dislocation of trade might easily have been avoided if the men had not rejected the advice of their leaders. Sir Christopher -rurrress's intimation that, unless some arrangement be entered into for the avoidance of disputes in the future, the great company over which he presides 13'111 find it necessary to close its ship yard at Middle- -I°o, may mean disaster to the Hartlepools. On the Other hand, it may be that the conference at which, tha October 7th, Sir Christopher hopes to inset the ;ePresentatives of the trade unions on the North-East ~aast, will succeed in doing away with a constant loTree of friction. Evidently Mr. Churchill's scheme a permanent Arbitration Court, which has been more well received, could not have been launched at a `ll:re appropriate time. It goes as far as it can and will i'tarr.v along with it the approval of organized labour,and will give both employers and labour an opportunity of forming a mature opinion whether, when the full extent of what can be achieved by voluntary arbitra- tion has been realised, it would be desirable to accept any form of compulsion. REMEDIES FOR UNEMPLOYMENT. Herbert Samuel has been speaking on nnemploy- tent at Skelton, and he stated very emphatically a Yie \a' of the Labour Party's Right to Work Bill which !a shared by very many serious thinkers noon_ dustrial problems. That Bill, he said, did not help Vorliament an inch along the road towards a solution the Problem; it simply passed round the problem and did not touch it. To "make" work for the nnerriployed, either, by leading to uneconomic pro- duction, tends eventually to increase instead of decreasing unemployment, or else it does nothing more than the present Poor Law, which sets a test of The to work before the paupers that it relieves. Ina real problem is to enlarge the field of remunerative ' Znoployment, and Mr. Herbert Samuel declared himself '°Peful of a solution. He made the interesting 4,ooooncement that when the Commissions on Canals, anfforestation, Coast Erosion, and the Poor Law, report d they will do shortly, it is the intention of the _l:memo:lent to take them into immediate consideration,' Eiith the purpose of devising some practicable scheme. oar' Asquith has sent a message to the Liberal ,inr.lidate, in which he states that the Government is 'aged to deal with unemployment, and is giving the ri,u;.etstion " the most earnest and anxious consideration, Ito"., a view to the framing and the early presentation arliament of practical legislative proposals." THE EIGHT HOURS BILL. t. There is often confusion in many minds at election ar as to what constitutes an effective and legitimate I,,Peal and what amounts to sheer misrepresentation. ,Z Conservatives, no doubt, have persuaded them- ., es that they were making quite a legitimate ?Peal to the Newcastle electors when they paraded 'twe streets with coal waggons, on each of which were tai° Lacks of coal. The big one was supposed to con- 'lr. Renwick's hundredweight, and the small one s labelled " Shortt's sack." A gigantic placard aetakeed the question," Why is Shortt the poor man's ~BtaY ?.' and another placard gave the reply, coal ?Pse the Radical is pledged to vote for dearer r_ Of course, there is nothing surprising in this. tia•eY fluty be expected to ignore altogether the i_ ins which the Government tool to have the question injestigated whether the reduction would be likely to c'rease prices to any. appreciable extent ; the o ntention of the miners representatives that is the time actually worked, not the time ;IJtO. nt in the pit which determines the output shut Mr. Churchill's appeal to the miners to try to' • ow that shorter hours did not mean injury to pro- ‘'tion. Nor is it surprising that the Conservative ov?rtY, after giving a Platonic support to the principle the Eight Hours Bill when in office, should in uPp-Aition attack the Government for taking the raessnre seriously in hand. In a few years' time we haay expect to see the Conservatives posing as the tniners' friends because they will say, they advocated at' eight hours' day for miners long before the Liberal Government passed it into law. But it was rather surprising to find the Conservatives, when their hopes of success at Newcastle were chiefly based on the scontent of some sections of the local Labour party Liberal what they regard as an excess of caution in the -tAberal policy, thinking to improve their position by 4_ll attack on the Eight Hours Bill. The favourite remedy of the Labour party for unemployment is a 'eduction of working hours. Why, then, should they %to the poll for a candidate whose return would be inned as a protest against the Eight Hours' Bill ?

PICNIC OR DEMONSTRATION ? t The organizers of Sunday's demonstration against ' e Licensing Bill forget that the mere size of a igoazthering is not impressive if it lacks earnestness of I 'Pose. A demonstration, the numbers of which tiavLe been swollen by the attraction of free railway free rations, and a five shilling bonus for .oevuits, bears almost as much resemblance to a t':rtic as to a public meeting. The organizers have ;-'en obliged to make the stipulation "that those who tteeire free or specially reduced tickets must walk in ,64, Procession and vote for the resolution." Mean- -1118 a much-used argument against the Licensing has trgtbeen completely. exploded. The brewers' nizations have industriously circulated a docu- ignta issued by the Inland Revenue Department in el purporting to show the practice of the Inland of-venue authorities in valuing at his death the estate b 5 aplbliCan. In that document it was directed that 1, ficenee was to be valued on the assumption that it that continue to be renewed." But it now appears I,as that paper was issued before Sharpe v. Wakefield e pecided by the House of Lords. Since that (171,1t.8'0n, licence values have been assessed, like all ci forms of property, at their market value. 'I,I)REN's COURTS AND PREVENTION OF CRIME. ChAiliP:lt the value of the reforms embodied in the 'reres Bill° and the Prevention of Crime Bill,

which passed through the Committee stage in July, and will be pissed into law in the A.utunan sitting, there cannot be two opinions. But the annual report of the Commissioners on Prisons, which has just been issued, supplies an instructive commentary. In Birmingham, where there is a Children's Court, the number of juveniles recaived into Birmingham Prison during the year 1907-8 has fallen to eight, and there was no case at all from the city of Birmingham itself. On the other hand, there were 03 juveniles committed to Newcastle Prison, and one of these, a boy of fifteen, had seventeen previous convictions, while the longest sentence he had ever served was for five days. It is, as the Commissioners point out, against the admitted evil of this unnecessary and unwise commitment of young persons that the main provisions in the Chil- dren's Bill are directed. The Commissioners also express the satisfaction that they feel, as a conse- quence of their experience of the Borstal system, that la Bill is now receiving the consideration of Parliament 11 for giving effect to the principle of a long period of detention for reformatory purposes, with a free power of conditional licence, where in the opinion of the authorities a young offender might be released with the prospect of his criminal career being broken.

div.head: ROYAL COURT THEATRE.
div.p: ROYAL COURT THEATRE.
" New Frivolity."

1 Those who desire a full evening's rollicking fun should make a point of seeing Mr. John Leopoid's Company in the farcical musical absurdity " Now Frivolity." It has been a source of unbounded mirth at the Royal Court Theatre this week and has proved an excellent draw. The far-famed Leopolds have been on the road a considerable time, but their entertain- ment loses none of its brightness. As acrobats and tumblers they would be hard to beat and the extra- ordinary mrrnesuvres in which they indulge, make the audiences gasp with astonishment. The first act of " New Frivolity " centres in two rival seminaries, and there is love-making over the garden wall, an elopement and other interesting doings, the old pedagogue's life being made miserable by the exploits of his frolicsome students. For the other acts the scene is laid in Paris and the fun continues fast and furious. The company is a very capable one, special praise being due to Mr. Watson Hulme, as Oliver Buckwheat, the love-sick stockbroker. Mr. Charles Goff, as Samuel Vermiglio, the deserted husband, is the personification of wrathfulness, and Mr. Willie Leopold takes the part of Samuel Vermiglio his son, in first-rate style. Mr. Tom Leopold is a highly amusing Professor Fumble and Miss Kathleen Kavanagh does full justice to the role of Madame Cobweb. A fine representation of Roman statuary, pretty songs and dances are amongst the popular features of the progragnme.'

div.head: NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAIIME.
div.p: NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAIIME.

Next week Messrs. Dauncey and Leveaux present Mr. Arthur Bouchier's principal company in Alfred Sutro's wonderfully successful play " The \Valls of Jericho," which was such a great attraction on its last visit to Warrington, ia fact the play has been most successful all over the world. Most of our readers will probably know the story and it is sufficient to say that the play is a powerful satire on the manners and morals of the "smart set." The role of Jack Frobisher is taken on this tour by Mr. Alfl Goddard, who has baen a leading man with Mr. Beerbohm Tree, was specially engaged to support hirn on his recent visit to Bailin to play before the Kaiser, was leading man with Mrs. Patrick Campbell, and has been specially engaged to play this part. NESS Nancy Beresford,another well-known and gifted artiste, plays Lady Alethea. The company is an exceptionally strong one of marked ability, and the play is staged exactly as it was in London on its original production. The strong cast also comprises Mesdames Ormonde Wynne, Pauline Straus, Millie Emden, Elsie Ross, St. Vincent, Gladys Merrick and Mabel Mears, Messrs. Russell Barry, Ben Levia, A. W. Tyrer. Geo. Psrcy, C. Steele, F. Drake, 0 Gen and William Fletcher.

div.head: NOVEMBER ELECTIONS.
div.p: THE NOVEMBER ELECTIONS.

Already the November elections are beginninc, to engage attention but it is too early to forecast ;hat contests there will be. One fight is, however, assured—in Orford Ward where the Indepandelat Labour Party will make efforts to retain the seat previously held by Councillor Stott who has gone to New Zealand. Their candidate is Mr. J.Hampson of Garabaldi-street,and this week the Conservatives have selected as their nominee Mr. James R. Rushworth who contested the ward unsuccessfully three years ago. Mr. Peter Peacock has been mentioned as a probable candidate, but so far the Liberal Asso - elation has not taken any steps in the matter. The following is a list of the membars of the Town Council who retire on November Ist : Town Hall Ward—Mr. W. Benson (N.T). Whitecross Ward —Mr. James Evans (L). Bewsey Ward—Mr. James Dickenson (N.T). Orford Ward —Mr. Fred Stott (Lab.) St. John's Ward—Mr. Councillor Ball (Lab.) Fairfield Ward—Mr. J. G. Craik (Ind.) How ley Ward—Mr. T. Chantler (C). St. Austin's Ward—Dr. G. W. Joseph (C). Latchford Ward —Mr. John Pemberton (N.T). At a meeting of the Conservative Comtnittee for St. Austin's Wald held on Monday evening, under the presidency of Alderman Forshaw, it was decided on the motion of Councillor BrtomnurtsT, seconded by Councillor ROGERS, and supported by Councillor LORD, "That the best thanks of. the meeting be given to Councillor Dr. Joseph for his valuable services as one of the representatives of the ward." The Cil URMIN moved, and Councillor Ro.-.Etts seconded, a motion to the effect that the Doctor be asked to seek re-election, and he promised to do so, the meeting pledging itself to do all in its power to secure his return. rt The Conservative Committee of Howley Ward ha resolved to support the candidature of Councillor I'. Chantler. Councillor W. Benson will stand as a Non-Trader in the Town Hall Ward.

div.head: FAME AND HIPPODROME.
div.p: FAME AND HIPPODROME.

The supply of talent to the music-halls is as varied as it seems to be unending nowadays. Week after week an excellent programme is supplied and it is only on rare occasions that the artistes make a return visit. The Macaaghten Circuit seems to have endless resource and can always be relied upon to provide a first-rate show at the Warrington Palace and Hippodrome. This week that famous trio of comedians, Cullen and earthy and Little Cluley have been one of the main attractions. The two former are cross-talk men of the highest class and keep the audience in a constant roar of merriment, while Little Gluley is a second" Little Tich " and winds up the turn with a most expert big boot dance. Fritz Don I Listen has made a speciality of animal and bird mimicry, and we can honestly say we have never heard anything better in this line. Fritz even essays to imitate the nightingale with success, while his I lion-like roar and tigerish snarl are quite thrilling. Good dancing always makes a popular feature, and in Bertha Winder we have a world's champion at the heal and to style. Among her feats is to perform on the back of a large-sized dinner plate. She is also an accomplished musician and can skirl the pipes like a Scotchtnan. Kelly and Ashby produce a lively item entitled" Fun in a billiard Saloon." The " table" comes in for some rough treatment and would hardly suit the average player as well as it does its present possessors. Their "breaks" are chiefly of an acrobatic character, but they beat the anchor-stroke as a spectacle completely. The Tally !_To Trio can be complimented on the possession of capital voices and a knowledge of how to combine harmony with humour to good effect. Jock Walker, as a Scotch comedian and whistler,gives satisfaction, and the three Sisters Silcott are both seen and heard to advantage as dancers and vocalists. Dolly and Elsie are an attractive pair of duettists and dancers. The orchestra does its full share in an entertaining programme, which is concluded by biograph pictures, illustrating the remarkable adven- tires of " The Stolen Overcooat."

div.head: NEXT. WEEK'S PROGRAMME.
div.p: NEXT. WEEK'S PROGRAMME.

Some excellent attractions are announced for next week, the bill being headed by H. 0. Wills, the Water Rat, described as "The Pick of the Pack." Kurkamp, the original singing conductor, who won golden opinions on the occasion of his previous visit to Warrington, will again appear, and the other artistes will be :—Sisters Cora, vocalisis and dancers : Gregson Comedy Trio in their original absurdity " The Dummy "; Harry Milton, Dutch comedian and dancer; Five Vernons, the great xylophone specialists, from the Empire, London ; Burns and Bentley, the premier dancing team • Twin Sisters Erlwardes, vocalists, dancers and drummers.
The Examiner Saturday, September 26, 1908.
The Mayoralty. A meeting of the General Purposes Committee to consider the selection of Mayor for the ensuing year will be held on Monday.

Ambulance Work. The Warrington Corps of the St. John Ambulance Brigade announce a course of instruction in first aid to commence at the headquarters, Central Police Buildings, about the middle of October. Police Force Changes. At a meeting of the Watch Committee on Thursday Inspectors Smith and Williamson, of the Borott,gla Police Force, were promoted to the rank of first class inspectors. P.C. Clough was appointed a detective officer and P.C. Holland a plainclothes officer.

Forthcoming Guardian's Election. The vacancy on the Board of Guardians for Howley Ward, caused by the resignation of Mr. Samuel Davies, has been declared, and Thursday next is the last day for receiving nominations. We understand that Mr. William Clegg, ex-member of the Town Council, has been asked to allow himself to be nominated.

Policeman Assaulted. At the Warrington Police Court, on Thursday, John Glynn, of Mersey-view, was fined .20i. and costs, or one month's imprisonment; for being drunk and disorderly in Knutsford-road, and assaulting Sergeant Cooper.

Death of Mrs. Pugh. We regret to announce the death of Mrs. James Pugh, formerly of the George Hotel, Sankey-street, which took place after a short illness on September 14th at Stilians, Cornwall, where she had been living since tier ietirement. The reaains of the deceased lady, who was 80 years of age, and was the widow of Mr. Edward Pugh, a former landlord of the hotel, were interred in Stilians Parish churchyard on the 17th inst.

Wyciffe , The meeting of the above society on Sunday was presided over by Mr. D. M. C. Dechern. Mr. T. Prince, of Warrington, gave the' address, upon " The Spirit of God, its workings upon the spirit of man, and its loadings to right, purity and righteousness." The Secretary welcomed four new members into the Brotherhood, and expressed the hope that there would be a largo gathering at the open meeting next Sunday, the p; ize day. He announced that about 250 prizes were ready for distribution. Since the formation of the Brotherhood close upon 14,000 books have been disposed of, which must have a lasting effect upon the lives of all those who have received them.

Warrington and District Cricket League. By winning the championship of the Warrington and District Cricket League the St. James' team have become the proud possessors for twelve months of the handsome Challenge Shield ,presented by Colonel J. Reid Walker. the formal presentation was made by Councillor Fulton-Smith at a smoking concert held at the Crown and Sceptre Inn, Buttermarket street, on Tuesday evening. Mr. J. F. Foster, captain of the winning team, presided over a large attendance of members. The successful team was composed of Messrs. J. F. Foster (captain), C. Holt (sub-captain,) J. Hallam, J. Lester, P. Knight, P. Cummins, J. Sherratt, T. Tole, C. Hackney, H. Booth, J. Cartwright, A. Green and W. Minards. The runners-up tbe Cheshire Lines Engineers' Club —are as follows : —Messrs. J. Duckworth, G. Chamberlain, H. Brown, W. Hill, E. Deeley, W. Chamberlain, H. Reline, A. Hill, J. Monks, J. McKay and S. Howard. In addition to the shield the members of the winning team received silver medals with gold centres and the runners-up were also the recipients of similar medals. Order of Rechabites. The North West of England Juvenile Conference of the Independent Order of Rechabites has just been held at Sonthport. The delegates from the Warring- ton district were Bros. Benjamin Warburton, D.S.J.T. Wm. Baxendale, D. treasurer, and David Sutton, D.T., and the Visitors included Bros. Thos. Massey, J.D.S.,Chas.Ftllows, D.G., Jas. Lawton, D.T., and Hill, D.C.R. (Wigan). The delegates presented reports on the progress of the Order in their respective districts. Bro. Baxendale (Warrington District) said since 1891, when his district was opened, they had enrolled 3,000 new members, and established 15 tents. They had transferred 751 to adult tents. On December 31st their district fund only amounted to £7. To-day they had close on 2.500. It was interesting to note that their first new tent was opened by their esteemed and respected Bro. Dimond, and was named the John Vincend Tent.

div.head: LOCAL NEWS.
div.p: LOCAL NEWS.

Coming Events. The Rev. Jolla Grinnell will preach a memorial sermon to the late Mr. R. IL Silcock, at Bold-street Wesleyan Church to-morrow (Sunday). The Rev. J. F. Matthews, who has just entered upon his twelfth year at the Latchford Baptist Church, resumes his ministry to-morrow (Sunday). Harvest sermons will be preached at Legh-street Primitive Methodist Church to-morrow by the Rev. J. B. Buglass. In the afternoon a cantata ` Esther, the beautiful Queen " will be rendered, and on Monday evening a fruit banquet and concert will be held. Harvest festival services will be held at Bewsey- road Wesleyan Church to-morrow (Sunday), when the preachers will be :-10.30, Rev. E. Blanshard Keeling; 6.30, Rev. Thomas Miller. A fruit banquet will be held on Monday evening. In connection with Bold-street Wesleyan Methodist Men's Bible Class an " At Home " will be held on Thursday evening next to celebrate the re-opening of the classroom after decoration. On the walls of the room ate to be hung a portrait group of the members of the class and enlarged photos of past superinten- dents and officers of the Sunday school. Six grand performances of the opera " Merrie England" will be given at the Royal Court Theatre from October 12th to 17th. The plan of reserved seats opens at the theatre on Wednesday next A smoking concert will. be held at the Liberal Club on Thursday evening, when Mrs. A. H. Crosfield will present the bowling prizes. Mr. A. H. Crosfield, M.P., will also attend. All Liberals are invited. Alleged Thefts from Golf House. At the Warrington Police Court, yesterday, Peter Grady and Patrick WCreese, both of Widnes, were charged with breaking and entering the pavilion of the Mersey Golf Club, at Penketh, between August 22 and 24, and stealing nine pairs of gentlemen's boots, twelve jackets, four caps' and a number of golf balls, the property of William Stanley Knowles, solicitors and others.—The prisoners were committed to the Liverpool Quarter Sessions.

CUTLERY by best Sheffield makers.—J. S. GARLA.ND, 31, Bridge-street, Warrington.—Advt. Sunday Night in Sankey-street. Joseph Barton, 42, Nicholson-street, and Willidm Robinson' 149, Mersey-street, were charged at the Borough Police Court on Monday with creating a disturbance, by fighting in Sankey-street on Sunday night. Detective Holland, stated that he saw defend- ants exchanging blows and rolling about the parapet under the feet of people who were watching. Both defendants admitted the offence and said it was caused through having a few words. The Mayor said it was a most disgraceful scene for Sunday night and defendants ought to be ashamed of themselves. They were fined iss. and costs or seven dais.

On Saturday the remains of Father William Francis Stanley, aged forty-seven, parish priest for New Brighton, and formerly stationed at St. Mary's, Latchford, were laid to rest, in Wallasey Cemetery. An imposing procession of school children, members of the Children of Mary, and the Young Men's Society preceded the hearse, an the obsequies were conducted with all the imposing ceremonial attaching to the interment of a Roman Catholic dignitary.—The inter- ment was preceded by Requiem Mass at the Church of SS. Peter and Paul. The celebrant was the Very Rev. Canon Barry (Church of Our Lady, Birkenhead), Father Mullins officiating as deacon, and Father Mottrain ( West Kirby) as sub-deacon. Father Kinsella was master of ceremonies.—The diocesan clergy present included the Right Rev. Monsignor Canon Marsden, the Right Rev. Provost Clegg, the Very Rev. Canons Keel an and O'Toole, D.D., the Rev. Fathers J. Thompson, McGreever, Pagett, Reid,Roche. Marrs, McGuire, O'Leary, D.D., Baines, Leahy, Al'Afanus, Walsh, J. Kelly, Cronin, Miller, T. Lowery, Thompson and Welch. Mr. Willie Byrne (chairman of the General Council of the Young Men's Societies of Great Britain) was amongst those present.

div.head: Presentation.
div.p: Presentation.

- - ------------- There was an interesting gathering at the War- rington Post Office when members of the staff assembled to say gooddrye to Mr. P. Jarman, until recently a town postman at Warrington, and who was about to proceed to New Zealand. At the same time the opportunity was taken to mark tha occasion by presenting Mr. Jarman with a red morocco writing case. Town Postman J. 11. Osley asked Mr. 11. C. Jones (who is acting postmaster in the absence of Mr. Lister) to make the presentation on behalf of the staff. In doing so, Mr. Jones pointed out that this was the first time that one had left the Warrington Post Office for the purpose of going abroad, and eulogized the sterling qualities possessed by Mr. Jarman. In making the presentation he (Mr. Jones) wished him every success in his now sphere of life.—Mr. A. B. Mellor heartily supported Mr. Jones's remarks.— Mr. Jarman, in reply, said he should never forget the kindness shown to him by the various members of the staff. Mr. Jarman left Warrington by the night mail on the 17th inst., and as the train moved out of the station 30 or 40 members of the staff gathered and sang " Auld lang syne."

Loyal Order of Ancient Shepherds. The quarterly meeting of the Rosebud Lodge No. 1031, was held on Saturday evening at St. James' Schoolroom, Latchford. The accounts read by the Secretary (Bro. J. Mather) showed a satisfactory state of affairs were passed as read. An interesting presentation took place of a beautiful framed Emblem of Merit to Bro. J. H. Eckersley P.M. by Bro. W. Box P.M. who congratulated Bro. Eckersley on being the recipient and hoped it would remind him of the pleasant time he had spent amongst the members. He urged all young members to try and follow in the footsteps of Br:). Eckersley. These remarks were supported by the District Officers, P.C.S. Gillooly, D.C.S. Miles, P.P.C.S. Edgar Parr, Gresty, Eckersley Mather, also by Bro. Leatherbarrow, Champion' Blythe, Artley, Hough and Wills. P.M. Bro' Eckersley feelingly replied and thanked all for the kindness they had shown to him. He hoped that the lodge would prosper in the future as it had done in the past. The quarterly meeting of members of the late Spring Rose Lodge No. 82,3 was held on Saturday. at the house of Bro. James Gleave, Barley Mow Hotel. A very creditable report of the past quarter's working was given by the auditors P.U. William Taylor and Bro. G. Ratcliffe. The balance sheet showed after meeting all expenses a gain of over :COS, bringing the total worth of Lodge to 52,281. After the election of Lodge and District Officers P.P.C.S. Fred S.lfassey presented P.M. Robert Fairbrotber with a framed emblem of merit for services rendered to the Lodge. In making the presentation Bro. Massey spoke very highly of the great assistance and interest taken by Bro. Fairbrother during his term of office and he sincerely hoped other brethren would follow his example. Bro. Fairbrother suitably responded.

div.head: WARRINGTON SWIMMING CLUB. AnnUiiGala.
div.p: WARRINGTON SWIMMING CLUB. AnnUiiGala.

The twenty-fifth annual swimming gala in connection with the Warrington Swimming Club, took place on Thursday evening at the Corporation Baths, Legh-street. The Mayor (Alderman James Smethurst) presided, and was accompanied by the Mayoress. There was a large attendance, all parts of the building being packed to overflowing. An excellent programme had been arranged and passed of£ without a hitch. The first event was the 50 yards Schoolboy Champion- ship and Warrington and District. Prizes.—lst, " Thornton" perpetual challenge bowl and gold medal; 2nd, gold centre medal; 3rd, silver medal. R. Atkinson, who was the holder last year, was beaten by Reginald Chalmers, Arpley-street school, who won by 2 yards. Samuel Roberts, Arpley-street school, was second, and William Cooper,Arpley-street school, third; distance between second and third, 1 yard ; time 40 secs. I Much interest was taken in the final for the Works Squadron Championship. The winners become the holders for a year of the Sir Gilbert Greenall Perpetual Challenge Shield, and they also received four gold medals(presented by Sir Gilbert Greenall.) The holders, the Co-operative Stores team, swam exeellently, and after a keen struggle were again victorious by a few , inches. Crosfields' were second. Time 2 min. 21 secs. 50 Yards Members' Handicap—The prizes for this event were: Ist, oak clock ; 2nd, knives and forks in case ; 3rd, pair of hair brushes in leather case ; 4th, silver photo frame. The first and second in each heat to swim in semi-final. Winners of Ist heat : 1 R Atkinson, 2, M Aukland ; 2nd heat, 1 P Higifam, 2 G Corlett ' • 3rd heat, 1 H Horrabin, 2 A Wright; 4th heat, 1 G Molyneux, 2 H Furnival ' • sth heat, 1 R Silk, 2 NV Goodenough; 6th heat, 1 G Baird, 2 J Wilkinson ; 7th heat, 1 W Gibson, 211 Beaman ; Bth heat, 1 , Jolley,2 C Woods. Final ; 1, W Gibson ;2, G Corlett; 3, G Molyueux ; 4, R Silk. The distance between lst and 2nd was yard. The race for the 150 yards Championship of War- rington and District was the chief event of the night. A splendid exhibition was given by the winnerft Allen. The prizes were : Ist, Licensed Victuallers Perpetual I Challenge Trophy and gold medal (presented by the Warrington and District Licensed Victuallers' Associa- tion); 2nd, gold medal ; 3rd, gold medal. The com- petitors were : R Pepper, H Sisson, R Beaman A Smith, Ii Allen and S Inca. After the first length It Allen, the holder, was leading by half a length, but he I quickly increased the distance and came in an easy , winner by a length. The second was Inca who led by a yard, and R Beaman and A Smith tied for the 3rd. The time was 1 min., 55 secs. The comic event was a very amusing feature. Each competitor had to start from the shallow end of the bath carrying a lighted candle and swim two lengths,the candle to bo kept alight all the time.lf a candle went out the competitor bed to retire, re-light it and begin the raceagain. Winners of heats were : Ist heat, 1 R Atkin- son. 2 II Horrabin ; 2nd heat, 1 J Sanders,2 H lournival; 3rd heat, 1 W Donn, 2 E Baker. Final : Ist, Woods ; 2nd, It Atkinson ; 3rd, J Sanders. Much interest was taken in the exhibition of orna- mental swimming given by I'rofessor G. A. Barlow and Miss M, Barlow. The former gave a number of unique representations, such as porpoise at play, the human torpedo, singing under water, and the sinking ship ; and created much amusement by imitating a monkey up a stick, while in the water. Miss M. Barlow gave examples of various methods of swimming, includ- ing the breast stroke, the over-hand stroke, and floating. WATER POLO MATCH.—WARRINGTON v LEIGH.

For this match the teams were :—Warrington : C Woods ; W Sutton, S Walker ; W Ashton, R Allen, T Pemberton, and C Turner. Leigh : Hewitt ' • Rams- dale, Williams ; C Ashton, Collier, Tiscornia, and Craft. , In the first half Leigh were called upon to defend the deep end. After a few minutes of exciting play It. Allen opened the score for the home team. I Warrington were continually making attempts at scoring, but the Leigh goal-keeper, Hewitt, was on the alert and stopped many hot shots. Half-time : ‘Varrington 1 goal, Leigh 0. In the second half, the , game became keener, and fouls were repeatedly indulged , in. The Warrington goal was continually in danger and but for the quickness of Woods would have fallen early. Tiscornia after dribbling up the ball, made a hot shot at the Warrington goal which evaded the goal-keeper. This placed the teams on level terms. After repeated attempts by both sides to score the game was brought to a close. Final : Warrington I goal, Leigh 1 goal. During an interval the Mayor gave a short speech. He said swimming was greatly encouraged in Warring- ton and he was pleased to see the excellent matches which took place from time to time. Alluding to the improvements which he had advocated during his Mayoralty, the speaker expressed the hope that the much needed widening of Warrington Bridge and the erection of a new bridge at Howley would shortly be accomplished. The prizes having been distributed by the Mayoress, a vote of thanks was accorded to the Mayor and Mayoress on the proposition of Councillor Fulton- Smith.

div.head: WIDNES RUFFIAN SENTENCED.
div.p: WIDNES RUFFIAN SENTENCED.

At Widnes on Monday, John M`Leavy, of St. Helens and Widnes, was sent to gaol for six months' hard labour —one month for being drunk and disorderly, two months for assaulting Police Constable Huntingdon, and three months for deserting his wife and children and leaving them chargeable to the funds of the Prescot Union. On Saturday night he attacked the constable in Albert-road without any provocation, and outside had to be requisitioned to bring him to the police station. He had a bad police record, particularly for assaults on the police, both at St. Helens and ‘Vidnes

div.head: WIDNE.Y MILK' AND THE ATMOSPHERE.
div.p: WIDNE.Y MILK' AND THE ATMOSPHERE.

At the Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, John Johnson, dairyman, of Primrose Farm, Cuerdley, was charged with selling milk to Sergeant Donald Ross, on July SOO, which was not of the nature demanded by the purchaser. On July 12th, Sergeant Ross purchased a supply of milk from a milkman named Hewitt, which upon analysis was found to be wrong. Hewitt com- plained that he had got some milk from Johnson and mixed it with his own. On July 30th a sample was taken of flewitt's milk from his own cows and a sample taken from Johnson's cows. Hewitt's milk was found to be good and Johnson's was found to contain 9 per cent. added water upon analysis. Defenduit pleaded that he had farmed on the outskirts of Widnes for forty years, and had lived sixty years in the same farmhouse. The land was almost barren through the chemical atmosphere and he had to.,,feed his cows upon potatoes to make them give milk: He had never watered milk in his life, and the only reason he could assign for the deficiency was the barren feeding land. The bench imposed a fine of £5 and costs.

SAILORS ENTERTAINED. On Saturday by the kindness of Mr. J. Rogers, of Liverpool, Mr. W. Shaw, ruissioner, was able to invite a party of sailors to the Institute of the Runcorn branch of the Mersey Mission. Upwards of SO sailors and workers attended, and during the afternoon an excellent entertainment was provided by bowls and skittles. A substantial tea was then served in the Institute. Mesdames Kirkham Druce, J. Shaw, Gibson, Evans and other ladies presided at the tables. After tea the party adjourned to the Mission Recteation Field, where an interesting programme of sports was gone through. The events included fiat, egg and spoon, throe-legged and other races. There was keen competi- tion and plenty of amusement and excitement. Mr. Kirkham acted as secretary, Mr. C. Johnson as starter, and Mr. Shaw as judge. Returning to the Institute, Mr. Shaw presided and distributed the prizes. On the motion of Captain Longmaid, seconded by Captain Salt, a vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Rogers for the splendid treat he had provided, and a similar vote was passed to the ladies who presided at the tea tables on on the motion of Captain Wilcock seconded by Captain Scanterbury. Several of the party contributed songs and recitations, and after the singing of " Auld lang syne "and" For he's a jolly good fellow," the com- pany gave hearty cheers for Mr. Rogers and Mr. and Mrs. Shaw, and the enjoyable proceedings closed with the singing of the National Anthem and cheers for the King. ----------

WIDNHS REPROBATE SEVERELY PUNISHED. John Macaleavy, of no fixed abode, was charged at Widnes, on Monday, with having been drunk and disorderly on Saturday night. He was further charged with having assaulted P.C. Huntingdon whilst in the execution of his duty.—He pleaded guilty to the first charge and said he remembered nothing of the assault.— Constable Bruce Huntingdon said that at 7.30 p.m. on Saturday he saw the prisoner in Albert-road very drunk He came up to witness and used filthy language. Witness ordered him away, but as he would not go eventually took him into custody. Ile then threw witness down and kicked him on the right knee and left leg. With the assistance of A civilian named James Tasker he was brought to the Police Station. He was very violent all the way. Witness saw the doctor later in the evening and was ordered off duty.—lnspector Burton said that the prisoner had been before the Widnes aud St. Heleqs Courts seventeen times. That was the sixth time he was charged with having assaulted the police.

ANOTHER CHARGE. Prisoner was then charged with neglecting his wife and four children, leaving them chargeable Lo the Guar- dians of the Whiston Union.—Prisoner said he had been forced to go away to get work.—Mr. Ratcliffe, reliev- iug ofilper to the Whiston Union, said that the prisoner left Widnes on the 24th June without leaving word where he was vbs.'. On the 29th his wife and family had to be removed to the workhouse, where they still were. Their maintenance had cost the Guardians £l2 12s. Prisoner had not communicated with them in any way. For the last five years his conduct had been a source of trouble to the Guardians.—The Chairman (Councillor F. Neil) said that the prisoner had a very bad record. For having been drunk and disorderly he must pay a floe of 20s. and costs, with the alternative Of a month's hard labour. For assaulting the constable he must go to gaol for two months without the option of a flue. For deserting his wife and family he must serve a further period of three months. FRIENDLY SOINETIES CHURCH PARADE AT RUNCORN.

The annual church parade of the combined Friendly Societies of Runcorn and District took place on Sunday afternoon. The members, who assembled in Devon- shire-square, represented the Grand United Order of Oddfellows, the Manchester Unity of the Order of Oddfellows, the Duke's Club, the Rechabites, the Sons of Temperance and the Ancient Order of Shepherds. The principal officers who attended were Bro. Dudley (president of the Council of the Societies), Bro. Lambert (vice-president), and Bros. Evans, Grand United Order of Oldfellows ; Groome, Manchester I Unity of the Order of Oddfellows; 0 ven, Duke's , Club ; Lsadstone, Rechabites ; Holt, Sons of Temper- ance ; and Malinger, Ancient Order of Shepherds (committee), H. Millington (treasurer), and A. Shaw ' (secretary). A procession was formed. It was headed by the Volunteer Baud, and the following members and officials of the Urban District Council : Messrs. T. Dean (chairman), who wore his chain of office, T. Jones, W. Carroll, G. Hewitt, R. H. Posnett, G. Duckett, D. Bisbrown, E. Imison, NV. Handley, John Littler and R. H. Pringle (members), and E. Marshall, F. A. Lake, J. Wilding, W. Jones, J. Percival, J. T. Shaw and G. Howard (officials). The number in the procession was about 500. The route was curtailed in con- sequence of the unfavourable weather. It was by Egerton-street, Waterloo-road, Church-street and High-street to St. Paul's Wesleyan Church, where the , service was held. It was conducted throughout by the Rev. T. Galland Hartley, superintendent minister and chairman of the Liverpool District Wesleyan Synod. The hymns sung were " All people that on earth do dwell," " Through the night of doubt and sorrow," and "God bless our native land." The choir sang the anthems "Lord, I have loved " and "0 Lord our Governor." The soloist in the latter was Mr. T. N. Johnson. Mr. R. Johnson presided at the organ. The offertory was in aid of the Cottage hospital. The Rev. ,T. Galland Hartley preached from the text," One is your Master, even Christ ; and all ye are brethren Matthew xxiii. 8.)

div.head: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
div.p: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
OLD-AGE PENSIONS.
Mr. J. F. Clarke has been appointed clerk to the Old - Age Pensions Committee for the Newton-in-Mak eraeld District Council.
DAHLIA SHOW.

On Saturday a dahlia show was held in the Club Room of the Victoria Hotel, Wargrave, by the mem- bers of the social club. The benching was very artisti- cally done. There were 43 exhibits of the doe ble dahlia class, the prizes being awarded as follows : —l, Mr. Rayer ; 2, Mr. Littler ; 3, Mr. J. Humphries ; 4, Mr. J. Foden. The show proved highly successful, and the variety of dahlias staged, together with their size' caused much comment.

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.
SERIOUS CHARGE AT ST. HELENS.

Joseph MLA well-known character, was remanded at St. Helens on Monday, on a charge of committing an aggravated assault on a married woman named Mary Ann Southworth. It was stated that while the woman was asleep in the house the man got through the window, struck her heavily on the head, and committed the offence complained of. When arrested by Detective Anders he admitted the offence. DEATH OF SIR JOSIAH GAMBLE. Sir Josiah Christopher Gamble died at his residence, Windlehurst, St. Helens,on Thursday night at the age of 60.—He was ths second baronet, succeeding to the title , last year. He took a prominent part in municipal work in I St. Helens, and, entering the Town Council in 1874, he I became alderman and Mayor in 1889, and in 1893 was made a freeman of the borough.—The deceased baronet who leaves four sons, had been ailing with a heart affection for some months, and recently returned from a month's rest in Yorkshire. He was suddenly taken ill on Monday morning and never recovered.—The new baronet, Sir David Gamble, who was born in 1876, is a town councillor and member of the St. Helens Board of , Guardians.

div.head: LIFE FOR A LIFE.
div.p: A LIFE FOR A LIFE.

Thomas Wright, of Park-road, St.lielens,a married ma with seven children, met his death early on Wednesday morning, at Baxter's Chemical Works. It is reported I that a workman named Harry Jackson, who was engaged 1 on the sulphur plant, fell down a hole in his section of the works, where there was a large quantity of chemical liquor and deadly fumes. A man named Maguire endeavoured to rescue him, but was obliged to leave the place on account of being overpowered. Wright then went down to Jackson's assistance, and succeeded in lifting him up out of the hole and put him on the ladder which led to the surface. He was then assisted by some men on the top, but Wright unfortunately fell back into the chemical liquor and died,

div.head: ASSAULT ON A ST. HELENS WOMAN.
div.p: ASSAULT ON A ST. HELENS WOMAN.

At St. Helens, on Tuesday, Joseph Hill, a well-known character ,pleaded guilty to an aggravated assault on Mary Ann Sudworth. Hill had been locked up on a more serious charge, but the Chief Constable now said that there wassome doubt as to whether the more serious offence was committed. The evi-lence was that Mrs. Sud worth had for some time been separated from her husband, and she had lived with her uncle and two brothers at 10, Mount-street. On Saturday night last she fell asleep in a chair in the kitchen, and was awakened between one and two o'clock in the morning by being struck a violent blow on the right eye, which knocked her on the floor. The man then held her by the throat and assaulted her. When arrested he said he would reserve his defence, bat later he pleaded guilty, and said he was drunk, and did not know what he was doing. Hill was sent to prison for six months with hard labour.

DRUNKEN ORGIE AND ITS SEQUEL. David Bates, a colliery day-wageman,of Carter-street, Peaseley Cross, was charged at St. Helens on Tuesday with assaulting his sister and brother-in-law, Elizabeth and Amos Bull.

_ Mrs. Bull said that on Saturday afternoon she went to her brother's house, and they had some drink. Late in the evening she went back home to Sherdley-road, and she alleged that she was followed by her brother. He followed her into the house, and immediately attacked Amos Bull, knocking him to the ground and biting him. A young man pulled Bates off. He then smashed some crockery, and tried to use a poker, and struck her on4be head with a brick.

—Amos Bull said that without any prevocation Bates set on him and fixed his teeth in his eyebrows. He dared not move for fear that his eye would be pulled out. Afterwards Bates came back and bombarded the ' house with stones. One brick entered the bedroom window and struck Mrs. Bull on the head. Bates said that his sister came to the house on Satur- day afternoon and said she had been falling out with her husband. She had "fettled" his head with a brush, but he had been spending money on drink. If he could spend a shilling she said she would spend two, and she sent him for some beer. He fetched live quarts, and his girl fetched seven or eight. The Clerk: For how many people ? Bates : There were five of us. The Clerk : Do you mean to say you had thirteen quarts among five people? Bates: Yes ; and as soon as she got the first cupful she started dancing. (Laughter.) Prisoner further said that Bull and his wife were the aggressors. Bates was fined ,C 2 10s, and costs in each case, or two months.

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH.
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH.
.PAROCHIAL COMMITTEE.

The monthly meeting of the Stockton Heath Parochial Committee was held at the Hall Cafe on Tuesday even- ing. Mr. G. Pilliu,g presided, and there were present— Messrs. F. Pearson, J. Hallows, J. Whitley, F. Warburton, J. W. Bouchier' J. Mynekyme, H. J. Westbrook, J. McDermid, T. Baxter, G. F. Ashton (clerk), and J. Ssvintou (surveyor).

_ . STREET MAKING. The Clerk stated that Messrs. Wright Garnett, and Wright had written agieeine" to carry out the various duties in connection with the making of the whole of the various streets and passages included in their list on the same terms as previously. He (the Clerk) had written to ask them to get out the plans as quickly as possible for the Local Government Board.

FOOTPATH IN BEDFORD-STRETR. Mr. Whitley drew attention to the footpath in Cliff View, Bedford-street, which, he said, had been taken up more than twelve months and was in a very unsatis- factory state. The kerbstone had been taken away and the tiles were missing. WELCOME TO MR. BAXTER. Mr. Westbrook expressed extreme pleasure in having Mr. Baxter amongst them, this being the first meeting he had attended. Mr. Baxter was a valuable addition, and they felt that to have a County Councillor amongst them was a great thing to be able to boast about. Mr. Whitley endorsed that, and said he was the one who proposed Mr. Baxter. Mr. Westbrook : I was the one who told you to do it. (Laughter.) Mr. Baxter said he WRS pleased to have the oppor- tunity of taking part in the local government of Stock- ton Heath. He was not a Stockton Heath man, but he had always belonged to Cheshire, and he would have pleasure in doing anything he could to make the district better than it is.
PARISH COUNCIL. A meeting of the Parish Council followed, Mr. H. J. Westbrook presiding.

TH-F, DUST NUESANCH. The Clerk (Mr. Bradshaw) read the following circular letter from Mr. Reginald Potts, clerk to the County Council :—" The County Council have again had under consideration the complaints made as to the nuisance occasioned by reason of the dust -raised on the main roads by the motor car and other traffic, and I am authorised to intimate that the County Council are prepared to treat the main trunk roads with calcium chloride or other dust laying material, conditional upon either Urban Councils, Rural District Councils, Parish Councils, parish meetings, or other persons interested along the routes of such roads, contributing two-thirds of the cost and providing and laying down such dust- laying material. If, therefore, your Council are desirous of availing themselves of the offer of the County Council you should communicate the same to the County Surveyor at his office at Chester Castle." Mr. Hallows proposed that the letter should lie on the table. It was not satisfactorily explained that the dust-laying material was ea improvement and that it it would be worth the expense. Mr. Pearson said laerhad been told that Sir Gilbert Greenall went to the expense of putting it down in Higher Walton and it had not proved a success. He thought they ought to wait a little while. Mr. Bouchier seconded, and the proposition was adopted.

div.head: EVENING CLASSES.
div.p: THE EVENING CLASSES.

Mr. Bouchier said it had been decided to carry on the evening classes during the winter, and they were hoping for as much success as at the last session. The Chairman said they bad a class for the first time on home nursing, which was a very valuable subjent. Mr. Hallows added that it would be well taken up. Mr. Whitley said they were hoping to open the extra classrooms added to the day schools in a week or a fortnight. Mr. Davenport was anticipating that he would commence building the new Council school in about a fortnight.

div.head: Charge Against an "Auditor."
div.p: Charge Against an "Auditor."

James Morgan, or Huttoned, a smartly dressed man, was charged at the Borough Police Court on Monday with stealing from the Lion Hotel, Bridge-street, on September 18th,a mackintosh, a pocket-book, a pair of gloves, a cheque book, and some cash, valued at 10s., the property of John Lee. It was stated by the Chief Constable that prisoner on September sth engaged a room at the above hotel, representing him- self as a chartered accountant engaged in auditing the books of a local wire firm. During the following week prisoner was presented with an account for apartments, &c., but excused himself by saying he had not quite finished his work in the town and would pay when he was going away. On the morning of the 18th of September a hall porter at the hotel found that prisoner was missing, also the above-mentioned goods. After investigation it was found that prisoner had left the town by the six o'clock train to Birmingham. Fortunately Detective Meacock of the Warrington Force was travelling by the same train, going to Birmingham un business. The detective got in con- versation with prisoner and heard him ask a porter to show him a Gist-class hotel. Returning to Warring- ton, Meacock was informed of the affair and communi- cated with the Birmingham Police, who arrested prisoner, in whose possession was found a dressing case containing some stolen property. He was after- wards transferred to Warrington. The Chief Constable said it was neceseary to ask for a remand as prisoner was only arrested on Saturday. A remand for eight days was granted.
