div.head: CROSFIELD'S BAND.
div.p: CROSFIELD'S BAND.

SACRED CONCERT AP THE PALACE AND HIPPODROME. With the praiseworthy object of augnmenting the fund in aid of the sufferers from the \Cigna Colliery disaster Messrs. Crosfield's Brass Band gave a concert on Sunday evening in the Palace and Hippodrome, kindly lent for the purpose by Mr. F. Macnaghten, before an audience which filled to overflowing every part of the building. Mr. Mosse, of Crosfield's staff, who has been intimately associated with the band ever since its inception, ably carried out the arrangements for the concert, the enterprise resulting in the handsome amount of being added to the local fund which is being got together by the Mayor. The pieces performed by the instrumentalists and the manner of their performance served to mark the immense progress which has been made by the band within a very recent periodaind this year's achievements at contests in various parts of the country in repeatedly beating the winners at Crystal Palace last year, offer the fullest promise of success when the musical foemen . meet again in friendly warfare in London to-day. The programme on Sunday included some very inter- esting items in which was found work bringing into solo prominence instruments ranging all the way from the soprano cornet to the bombardom Absolute pre- cision in attack, neat and crisp execution, tasteful phrasinmend a grand scale of tone gradation, are among the high qualities uhich are now conspicuous in the playing of the band under Mr. Halliwell's conductor- ship. Never-ceasing vigilance is however the price which must be paid by every man if a triumph is to be eon such as success in this week's Crystal Palace Contest may be regarded, and in this connection it may be mentioned that a little slip obtruding an instrument at the wrong moment, as happened on Sunday when the latter portion of The Bohemian Girl overture was repeated. would ruin the band's chances at this important event. Except for this ordinarily negligible mischance, the band's performances were uniformly excellent, and, whether hue judges the band's capabilities by the manner in which massive ensemble passages were rendered, or by the soloist's interpretation of such a beruitiful theme as " I'll sing thee songs of Araby" or, yet again, by the playing of the cornet duettists, the impression is confirmed that Crostleld's hand must at the present moment, at any rate, be accounted one of the finest associations of brass instrumentalists in the kingdom. There was same extremely neat execution, some graceful phrasing, and an admirable unanimity of effect in the playing of Messrs. Ryder and Fairhurst, while the sweet cantabile tone and style which Mr. Byers evolved from the bombardon in the " Be Frieschutz " selection was nothing short of a revelation of the splendid potentialities of a most unpromising and unwieldy instrument. But the most exacting and at the same time the most interesting item was undoubtedly the" Polinto "of Donizetti, rich variety being here found in the occurrence of solos for quite a number of instruments—one of these, of the tenor born class, coming in for an especially big share of the work and of the honours. To the band pieces relief was given by songs con- tributed by Mr. J. Willett, a tenor vocalist handicapped in possessing a voice of somewhat hard and unsympa- thetic quality. The songs Mr. Willet sang had, more- over, little intrinsic interest. But they were sung ins manner which so far pleased the audience that the vocalist was constrained by continued applause to repeat one of them. At the close of the concert Mr. Mosse and the Mayor Came upon the platform. Mr. Mosse introduced his Worship who, he said, wished to say a few words to the audience, and to thank them for attending in such large numbers. He (Mr. Mosse) also desired to thank them for their support. The MAYOR, who was received with applause, said that that was the second occasion on which he had had to thank Mr. alacnaghten for his kindness in allowing the use of the Hippodrome for a sacred concert. They all thanked him heartily, as well as the manager, Mr. Bradbury, and the whole of the staff for their assistance. As Mayor of the town he was much obliged to Messrs. Crostield for their kindness in vtting up the concert. He had just been told what the probable receipts would be, and it was gratifying to know that Warrington was not behind any other town in Lancashire in the matter of the practical sympathy shown by them for the widows and orphans. The \Carrington fund now amounted to over £3OO. (Applause.) Thanks were also due to Mr. Mosse, who bad promoted the concert, but even his ingenuity would have been at fault had they not obtained the services of the band who had favoured them with some beautiful music; a band that was as near perfection as the article it was so intimated associated with—Perfection Soap. (Laughter and applause.) He was given to understand that the band had during the season won eleven first prizes. (Applause.) They were to play in London next Satur- day for the world's prize, and he trusted they would bring that prize to Warrington, and if they did so he was sure they would have a fine reception. (Applause). The Mayor's Thanks.

iTo Tier: EDITOR, " EXAMIVER."j Sir,—lt is with sincere feelings of gratitude to you for your kind assistance that I venture to trespass further and ask you to allow me space in your columns to thank all those who have contributed to the fund which I commenced in the Borough to assist the naTerers by this dire disaster. The result of the effort 1 highly satisfactory, there being a grand total of 6435 shillings (£321 155.) collected,aa I think Warring- ton may justly feel proud of this achievement. In addition it ought to be mentioned that several local firms have largely contributed direct to the Mayor of ,k/ igan's Fund, viz :—Messrs. P.Walker and Sons, Ltd., Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Co., Ltd.,and the Pearson nd Knowles, Coal and Iron Co., Ltd. May I also take this opportunity of thanking al/ those who have supported my efforts in raising funds- for various local charities which have benefited to the 'amount of nearly .£OOO during my Mayoralty. As my term of office as Mayor will shortly come to a close I desire to add my heartfelt thanks to the public of Warrington for the uniform courtesy, consideration and support which have been extended to me and mine during the two years I have occupied the Mayoral chair, . thus assisting me to carry out the onerous duties of my Ihigh office with confidence in the knowledge that 1 post-teszed the whole-hearted support and good wishes of the community. To the Press of Warrington I am also greatly indebted for their assistance and support in my various undertakings. —Believe me, yours faithfully, JAMES SMETLIERBT, Mayor. div.head: WARRINGTON EDUCATION COMMITTEE. THE ACCOMMODATION DIFFICULTY.
div.p: WARRINGTON EDUCATION COMMITTEE. THE ACCOMMODATION DIFFICULTY.
Five New Scho3ls Proposal

The monthly meeting of the Warrington Education Committee was held at the Town Hall on Monday evening. Councillor J. Fulton Smith presided and there were also prssent :—Aldermen Bolton, Ellison and Bennett, Councillors Sankey, Roberts, Ball, Toole, Lord, Singleton, Pemberton, Revs. Canon Stevenson, James Davies and N. Wilson, Miss Williams, Messrs. EL Itt.berts, A. J. Jolley, H. kingdon, C. E. Parker, R. T. Fairclough, C. H. Cnsworth, E. Plinston, 'l'. P. Bradshaw, J. Upson, J. Moore Murray (secretary and director), R. B. Roberts (assistant director), and J. Fairhurst (borough treasurer). A NEW SCHOOL MANAGER. Mr. T. P. BRXDSTIA W was elected a representative manager of the Hamilton-street school in place of Councillor F. Stott, resigned. SECONDARY SCHOOL. THE SALARY OF THE SECOND MASTER.

- --- At a meeting of the School Management Committee, a renewed application from the second master of the Secondary school for an increase of salary was sub- mitted, and it was resolved (a) That the maximum salary of the second master of the Secondary school be fixed at £lB3 per annum ; and (b) That the scale of salaries for the staff of the Secondary school adopted by the Committee at their meeting on the 17th July, 19C3,be amended accordingly. It was also resolved that the salary of Mr. Richard H. Albery, MSc., Second Master at the Secondary school, be increased from £173 to £lB5 per annum as from the 15th September, 190 E. The adoption of the minutes was formally moved by the Rev. Canon STEVENSON. The Rev. Father WIT:A-es seconded. Mr. PLINSTON in moving that the minute be referred back said that when the appointment of second master was made no increase of salary was granted, but he found that on two occasions when other teachers had been appointed to a position involving increased work and greater supervision, an advance of salary had at oace been given. It appeared to him that there had been preferential treatment. There had been a promise of some kind to Mr. Albery about twelve months ago that he should have an increase. The Committee would be wise in endeavonring to keep the teachers already on the staff of that important school and who were doing a very valuable work. He found that in a number of towns the average maximum salary for a position of that kind was £266 and Warringtcn was consider- ably below that. Councillor LORD seconded. He said that as a member of the School Management Committee he remembered that when the matter came forward twelve months ago it was thought that Mr. Albery should have some adequate financial recognition of the additional duties he was per- forming. He (Councillor Lord) was certainly of opinion that more would have been given than the committee now recommended. Even iii the neighbouring town of Widnes the maximum fur the second master was £220 and several towns offered amounts in excess of what the committee had thought fit to offer Mr. Albery. There was no doubt that he was a capable and willing worker and his valifications as a science master were second to none in the town. Apart from that, the interest he took in the school was deserving of better recognition. The Rev. Canon STEVENSON said that a year ago Mr. Albery made an application for an increase of salary. He had not then reached his maximum of £175 and the committee deferred consideration until he had reached it. This year they discussed it again and recommended the advance of £lO. He sympathised to a great extent with all that fell from Councillor Lord about Mr. Albery and he was sure all the members of , the School Management Committee recognized his ability and the earnest way in which he had carried on his work. But the committee had a delicate and difficult task in the matter. Sometimes in that room they were taken to task by no means lightly for the way in which they advanced salaries and now they were taken to task for not advancing them rapidly enough. (Laue,hter). It was a little bit difficult to know how to guide one's steps well and wisely. Ever since he became a member of the School i`tlnnagernent Committee it had always been a sort of smouldering fire and cause of complaint as to the way in which they ran lip expenses, especially in the matter of salaries, and therefore they had learnt to walk with a certain amount of caution. If the feeling of the Education Committee was that the salaries were not sufficiently high,he thought the School Management Committee would go hack with more cheerful feelings. (Laughter). There was no reason for Mr. Albery's advance not being larger except that they thought they ought to be careful and keep the salaries within due bounds. Councillor Loma said his remarks did not apply to the salaries generally, but only to the second master. On a vote being taken, there voted for the amend- ment :—Alderman Bolton, Councillors Ball, Lord, Pemberton and Toole, and Mr. Plinston. Against: Miss Williams, Revs. Canon Stevenson and Father Wilson, Councillors Singleton and Sankey, Messrs. H. Roberts, A. J. Jolley, R. T. Fairclough and C. H. Cusworth. The amendment was therefore lost.

div.head: FAIR FIELD SCHOOL.
div.p: FAIR FIELD SCHOOL.

At a meeting of the School MAnagement Committee, it was resolved that the engagement of Miss Ada L. Corbett as Mistress-in-Charge of the Upper Girls' department be extended as from the Ist August, 1908, pending the receipt of the decision of the Board of Education upon the proposal to amalgamate the two girls' departments of the Fairfield school. Mr. R. T. FA IfICLOCG If moved that this minute be referred back, contending that in the interests of good feeling the managers should have been consulted about the extension. They felt very sore about it. Mr. Fairclough strongly objected to the way in which the committee had treated the school and submitted that their action tended to depreciate its work. The Rev. .J. D k-VIES seconded and said there was no question of amalgamation but of closing the upper school. This was the second occasion on which the term of office of the mistress-in•charge had been extended. There was a very important principle at stake, because they were having the benefit of the services of a mistress who was doing more difficult work—because the school was nnder sentence of death —than if she had the appointment of headmistress, but she was receiving a lower salary. He believed the Board of Education, according to a late ruling, had decide 3 that it was not in the province of the Educa- tion Committee to force the managers to change the character of the school. -

-• Mr. ROBERT : If it is not in the province of the Committee to do as Mr. Davies suggests, the Board of Ed u cat ion will put us right, and there will be an end at once to this extremely unpleasant and certainly not in the interests of education, desirable discussion which has been going on so long between the managers of the school and the School Management Committee. I cannot for the life of me see what harm can come from the passing of the resolution which is only to continue the appointment in a tentative condition, pending the decision of the Board of Education. Continuing, Mr. Roberts said it would throw a considerable amount of light on the whole matter if the correspondence which was recently rec3ived by the School Management Com- mittee, were put in. He did not hesitate to say that instead of assisting the Committee to arrive at a proper, wise and sensible decision with regard to the school, all kinds of small, pettyfogging, narrow-minded ideas were being urged with a view to prolonging a condition of things which was not advantageous to the cause ot education in the district or to the school itself. The Committee would not allow the managers, so far as they had power to prevent it, to maintain in permanence— he would not say by means of a trick, but by means of misrepresentation of facts—a condition of things which the Committle strongly objected to. Alderman BOLTON contended that the managers were entitled to a certain amount of respect. The School Management Committee and other lub-committvas of the Education Committee seemed to bs always looking out for friction and mischief.

Councillor PEMBERTON suggested that the school managers, if they felt aggrieved, should wait upon the School Management Committee and stat 3 their case. Some managers appaared to think that the Committc ) should be like dumb dogs and pass whatever they lik( I to do, but ho would not agree to that. The Committ: ) bad tried to do its level best for the school and had probably spent more time and trouble on it than cm any half-dozen schools in Warrington. The Rev. CANON STEVENSON said he could not help thinking that they had drifted into a state of mutual misundersanding for which there was no occasion. In conference with the managers and with their vnction and agreement, it was' arrange I that a mistress in- charge should be appointed by the managers. .It was understood that that should be a temporary appointment to see whether the numbers of the school would increase sufficiently to justify its being continued in the same way as in the past. When it was found that the members did not increase to that extent, the Committee decided to propose to the Board of Education that the two schools should he placed under one head. There was no intention on the part of the Committee to do anything that would close the school. Their idea was that it could be more economically worked and fulll a better and more useful purpose instead of having two head mistresses there was only one and the whole of the spice was occupied as one school. There is only one change in the Rochdale Hornets' team to visit Warrington on Saturday from that which was defeated by Huddersfield. Farrar, who up to the present his been engaged at cricket, is now available and will displace Rigg at centre. The selected players are as follow : Hollinrake : Hartley, Farrar, Robinson, Threlfall ; Scholfield, Ledgard ; Daarden' Richardson, Turner, Thomas, Walker, Crabtree and Pearson.
Hornets "A "v. Warrington "A " at Rochdale— Charles, E. Mullen, Henderson, English, Latchford, E irnshaw, °tad rink, Hammand, Wormald, Marshall, Cockle, Liley and Thomas.

The Wsrrington team for to-day differs little from that of last week. Dowell cnnes in for Chester, and the backs remain the same as Taylor has not yet recovered from his injury. Team : Tilley, full-hack; Fish, Dickenson, Cartwright and Jordan, three- quarters; Jenkins and Brooks, half-backs; Dowell, A. Boardman, P. Boardman, Belton, Naylor and Hewitt, forwards.

The " A " team will be Mclntyre, full-back: Harries, Landor, Oakes and Bradshaw, three-quarters; Lloyd, and Daintith. half-backs; Hamer, Chester, Harrison, Forster, Fairhurst and Jolley, forwards. It was expected that Knox Gibbs would have been available for the forwards, but a suspension under the Rugby Union has to be dealt with first.
The South-West Lancashire up-to-date is as follows:

div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATilLEnc s.
Rilby Football.
131 " Onlist."

rue \Varrington Committee are losing no time in the process of team-building, and have made import- ant captures in a playing sense this week. First and foremost they have signed on a real live international in the porson of W. 11. Dowell, a forward who repr..3- sented Wales last season against Eigland, Ireland, Scotland, anl France. This is something like enter- prise, and I hope that Dowell will prJva such an acquisition that the anamittee will feel amply rewarded."

A few personal details of the new roan will be read with interest. Dowell was formerly a member of Newport, but last year assisted Pontypool. lie is 23 years of age, stands nearly six feet, and scales 134 t. ilbs. His action in signing a professiohal form has caused consternation in South Wales. Dowell will assist Warrington against Rochdale Hornets to-day, and should attract such a gate as will help to pay his transfer fee.

The signature has also been secured of a young Stockton Heath three-quarter, Bradshaw, rey.arded as the best junior in the Warrington district. He is fast and tricky, and has been one of the most consistent scorers. Knox Gibbs, the stalwart Stockton Edelth for ward, has also thrown in his lot with the " Wire- pullers," and these captures are also regarded as likely to considerably re-inforce the playing strength of the Club. The new men all have the great advan- tage of youth.

I believe I am correct in stating that the Committee are not going to rest on their oars juet yet. One forward does not make a teem, and hopes are enter- tained of two more players of international rank being secured at an early dete. ole is a forward and the other a full back—but more I must not say at present. -- Warrington have yet to record their first victory of the season. It mast be a long time since they opened with three successive defeats, and everyone hopes they will never do it again. By way of a change they might follow on n ,Nv with four consecutive victories. It's by no means an impossibility, as a glance at the fixture card will show. To-day Warrington are at home to Rochdale Hornets and most certainly ought to open their account with something handsome. Then comes S ilford (away), and as the Rs are doing worse than Warrington there is a prospect of success here. The Welsh trip is next, and if the Wirenullers don't get the better of Merthyr and Ebbw Vale they will be spoken to plainly when they return. I won't go any further, because I see Wigan are the next on the list. At present they are a bit above our class, but things might be different by Osetober 17. Its lucky for Warrington they haven't met their old foes from the banks of the Douglas river within the last three weeks!

There was a noticeable improvement in Warrington's form at Swinton. The changes in the team were all for the best and there was more than one glimpse of the old form. It was decidedly hard luck to be beaten on the post by a goal-kick, and that from the foot of Jack Preston. The ex-Warrington man doesn't often kick goals from half-way, but he landed a beauty on Saturday and it won the match after Warrington had had rather the better of the game. Such is the i••ony of Fate. Preston is not the forward of yore in midfiehl work but he can kick goals —as witness the discomfiture of Brought° n Rangers and Warrington. By the way, Warrington are as badly in need of a goal-kicker as of anything. They are going to drop valuab!e poiats from this cause alone, unless some expert placer is secured. .

Ine struggle was exceptionally keen at Swinton and it was refreshing to see the way the Warrington lads went about their work. They gave Swint m a rare fright by scoring first and holding the lead until well on for three-quarter time. The forwards held their own, and the backs were better at combination than their opponents, but if anything Swinton had it in pace. Fish played a moderate game, and seems to be good only spasmodically. He is not the man he was by a long si ay and I don't sea much hope of him going out to New Zealand with the first N.U. tourists unless he shows very much more activity. Dickenson worked like a horse on S tturday, and was well supported by Carte right aid Jordon, but as I have said, they are not fast enough to put on the finishing touches. There was a big improvement in half-back play with Jenkins and Brooks together, and these two ought to prove equal to any emergency when they have had practice. Tilley did some fine defensive work and punted strongly, but even he cannot go the pace like he used to do.

Oa the Swinton side there was nothing very brilliant. The team is keen, and has youth in plenty in the ranks, with a few veterans like Preston, Wallwork and Simister to do the drilling. The Swinton " Lion " hardly looks strong enough yet to swallow any tough meat away from his own den!

They have scored already 15ei points and should easily put up a new record. Warrington have lost every match but they have had less scored against them than the Wiganers. The team with the best average is Keighley. Lucky for them they don't come much into Lancashire !

Warrington's solo representative in the County trial match on Monday was Brooks,wha distinguished himself and his club by a fine display. He was easily the best half on the field, and well earned his selection to play in the match against the Champion County at Workington next Saturday. The selected side to meet Cumberland is

H. Gifford (Barrow) ; G. W. Smith (Oldham). right centre, B. Jenkir,s (Wigan), left centre, G. Tyson (Oldham), right wing, J Leythana (Wigan), left wing ; J. Jolley (Runcorn), scrumrnage, half E. div.head: LOCAL WEDDING.
div.p: LOCAL WEDDING.
Jones-Blair.

The marriage was solemnized at St. John's Church, Irlam, of Mr. Harold Jones, only son of Mr. Hugh Jones, of Manchester, and Miss Gertrude Blair, only daughter of Mr. Thomas Blair, of Cadishead. The Rev. Dr. Robert Martin was the officiating clergyman. The bride who was given away by her uncle (Hr. Robert Jones), was tastefully dressed in slate blue, trimmed with the same colour of silk and cream lace, and wore a gold watch, the gift of the bridegroom. She also wore a white felt hat, and carried a bouquet of white roses, white asters, and white lillies with streamets of white , silk ribbon. Her bridesmaids were Miss Eva Bridge (cousin of the bridegroom), who wore a crushed strawberry dress, trimmed with the same colour of silk and cream lace, with hat to match, and Miss Emily Thomas, (cousin of the bride), who wore a white dress with slate blue hat. Both young ladies carried bouquets of lilies, red roses and asters, and their ornaments were a gold watch guard and gold brooch respectively. Mr. Robert Jones, the bridegroom's uncle, was the best man. The ceremony was partly choral and Mendel- ssohn's " Wedding March ' was rendered by Mr. E. Hampson, of Cadishead. The reception at Cleveland, Moss Side-road, Cadishead, was a very hearty one, the bride and bridegroom being well knows to the Musical inhabitants of Cadishead. The bride is a brilliant pianist and the bridegroom a highly accomplished violinist. The bride's travelling dress was a dark violet costume, trimmed with black and white silk with black picture hat to match. After the honeymoon the happy pair take up their residences at Urmston. • The following is a list of the presents; Bride to bridegroom, gold and ("amond scarf ring and smoking cabinet Bridegroom to bride, gold watch and gold broooh ,Bridegroom to bridesmaids, gold watch chain and , brooch and dressing case Parents of the bride, drawing-room suite, organ, grandfather's clock, copper kettle, toilet set, silver cruet, set of vases with shades, ' pair of otaaments with shades, linen basket, counterpatri, curtains, celery glasses, wino decanters, salad bowlr, fruit dishes, cake stands kitchen utensils, salt cellars, antique crockery, blankets and bed linen, hot water jug and tea pot Parents of Bridegroom, cheque each from father and mother, dining-room suite, piano, Chippendale bookcase and secretaire, hall clock, warble clock, hat stand, writing desk, barometer, drawing and dining room pictures, music cabinet, dinner service, tea service, set of carvers, cutlery, decanter, cruet, mirrqr and parr of pictures, tea urn, two sets of toilet mats, toilet set, trinket set, black and copper fire suite, brass and black Are suite, silver cigarette case and match box, table centre.

ORGAN RECI/AL.—ln connection with the opening of the new organ at the Wesleyan Chapel an organ recital was given on Friday evening by Mr. 0. G. Smith, organist at the Oughtrington Parish Church. In spite of the inclement weather there was a fairly good attendance. Mr. Smith entertained the congre- gation with the following music : Chorus "For unto us a Child is born" (Handel) ; Offertoire in D (Baiiste) ; "Prayer and cradle song," "Marche religeuse 'on a theme by Handel " (Guilmant) ; Organ Concerto No. s—moderato, allegro, siciliano, presto (Handel) ; "The lost chord" (by request) (Sullivan) ; 0 Sanctissima (Lux),(organ fantasia on Sicilian Mariners' Hymn) ; march, "Schiller " (Nlyerbeer.) A collection was was made for the new organ and school improve- ment fund. __ _

DRAM OF MR. WALTER FURNESS.—We regret to announce the death of Mr. Walter Furness, son of the late Mr. Josiah Furness, which took place at his residence, Highaeld, Great Sankey, early on Tuesday morning, at the age of 32 years. Though it was not apparent, except to those who knew him intimately, his health had been failing him for some months, but it was only a fortnight ago that his illness developed into a serious nature, when meningitis set in and he died as stated. He had been attended by Dr. Joseph, sen., and Dr. Joseph, jun. The family have the sympathy of a large circle of friends in their sad bereavement.

DEBATE AT THE LIBERAL CLUB.—An interesting evening was spent at the Liberal Club on Tuesd ty when a debate was opsned by Mr. A. T. Clay on the Licensing Bill. Mr. Clay read several clauses of the Bill at the opening and offered to supply anyone with a copy of the Bill. He said a great number of those who opposed the Bill did not know what the clauses were and he asked them first of all to read for themselves and then speak of the Bill as they saw it and not from what they saw on the placards on public-houses. There were several questions asked and answered by Mr. Clay. The debate, which is the first of a series of debates arranged for the winter months, proved highly satisfactory. Mr. H. Davies occupied the chair in the absence of the President, Mr. R. Routledge.

How ck you like the *twits about animals which I print in the Children's Corner" this week. If you keep your eyes open, you will very soon be able to read some of the essays I have received about kindness to animals, and perhaps if you will sit down to-night and write yours, and get one of the big folk to post it, you may have the great joy of finding that you have won a prize.

_ JUST A WORD TO THE OLDER MEMBERS. Do you know it is such a long time since I heard trom you that I am almost beginning to think that you have forgotten your poor old Uncle, but surely that would be impossible. Now that the dark evenings are coming on, I am thinking of giving you some more puzzles to solve, so if any of you have got one which you think would interest the other member's, send it along, and I will print your name underneath it. I wonder if any of you have ever been to Felixstowe. It is quite a nice place on the East Coast, and when I was there last week I saw such a lot of little boys and girls enjoying themselves. that I began to wonder if any of them belonged to the "Children's Corner." I could only stay one day, but I had such a lovely drive, and per- suaded one of the Coastguardsmen to show me over a real fort, which was built in the time of Napoleon to keep away the enemy. I think this is all for this week, Your affectionate UNCLE NED.
OLD RHYMES IN NEW DRESS.
"There was a man in our town and he was
wondrous wise." There was a man whose wisdom was immense, He was our neighbour and we knew him well; But after I his story to you tell, Perhaps you'll think him quite devoid of
sense, And if you do, I shall not take offence. This man was on a walk, and jumping, fell Into a sprawling bramble-bush, pell-mell. He scratched out both his eyei, but " acc4-

dents Will happen," and this fall was nothing more. And now he had no eyes, but he had sight 1 The paradox, however, I'll explain: 'Twas foresight that he had, and as before, He boldly made the fearful plunge again, And. lo t the next time he came out all right. " Little Miss Muffet sat on a tuffet

Eating of curds and whey." There was a maid, Miss Muffet was her name, As maidens do, she liked her curds and whey; And so, one sunny beautiful June day, he sallied forth to eat them. What a shame (Though for for what followed she was not to

Edaiue.) she chose a spot where one would like to stay, A mossy knoll, all decked in green array, And then she said, " I am so glad I came." Into the luscious cup she dipped her spoon, A horrid spider crept from out his lair; "Oh! oh!' she sereamed and ran away . .
(Was't wise?) Nor came she back:in all that afternoon; Though 'twas a spot as sweet as it was fair, But for the spider's trail, a Paradise!
" This little pig went to market. This little pig stayed at home."

A certain pig one morn to market went. He was a pig whose taste it was to roam. A brother pig, I wot of, stayed at home. He, smoking by the fire, followed his bent; Another pig was, I am sure, content To sup on sweets sweeter than honeycomb, On nectar made of cream whipped to a foam; While to another naught but husks were sent. The fifth pig in our history was one Who cried, " Wee, wee!" whatever was his
fate, Never Elia laugh and ne'er had any fun. All I well, it takes all sorts of pigs to make A world, and it takes, too, ev'ry estate;— Let's dance our jig in time, for pity's sake.

Out on the mountain over the town, All night long, all night long, The trolls go up and the trolls go down. Bearing their packs and crooning a song; And this is the song the hill-folk croon As they trudge in the light of the misty moon: Gold, gold I ever more gold— Bright Jed gold for dearie I "
Deep in the. hill the yeoman delves,
All night long, all night long; None but the peering, furtive elves

See his toil and hear his song; Merrily over the cavern rings I As merrily over his pick he swings, And merrily over his song he sings: "Gold, gold! ever more gold— Bright red go 4 for dearie I " Mother is rocking thy lowly bed, All night long, all night long— Happy to smooth thy curly head And to hold thy hand and to sing her song; 'Tis not of the hill-folk, dwarfed ,and old, Nor the song of the yeoman, stanch and bold, And the burden it beareth is not of gold; But it's " Love, love—nothing but love— Mother's love for dearie ! " —Eugene Field, in "Chicago News."

div.head: POSTAL AND SAVNGS BANK REGULATIONS
div.p: POSTAL AND SAVNGS BANK REGULATIONS
For farther partionlars see " Post oMce Guide," at any Post aline. POSTAGE STAMPS..
Books containing 12 ponny and 23 halfpenny stamps are now on sale at each post office. Price 2s.
INLAND CORIZESPO.NDENCE.

The term "Inland Correspondence " means cor- respondence posted within the United Kingdom, including the Isle of Man and the Channel Islands. "Inland Correspondence " is divided into the following classes : (a) Letters (d) Newspapers (b) Postcards (e) Parcels (c) Halfpenny packets Not only letters, but any document or article (with a few trifling exceptions) which can be trans- mitted by post at all, may be sent by letter post, the only limitation being that of size.

LETTER POST. The prepaid rate of postage is as follows Not exceeding 4 ozs. in weight ... Id. For every additional 2 0z5.... A letter posted unpaid is chargeable on delivery with double postage; a letter insufficiently paid, with double the deficiency. No letter may exceed two feet in length, one foot in width, or one foot in depth.

POST-Ci.RDS. The prepaid rate of postage on every post-card is one half-penny, and on every reply post-card one penny. A post-card posted unpaid is chargeable on delivery with one penny. Cards used as post-cards must be made of ordinary card-board, not thicker than the material used for the thickest official post-card. They may not exceed 5i inches in length by 3 inckes in width, or be less than 31 inches iu length by 21 inches in width. A gummed label (not to exceed 2 inches long and i-inch wide) bearing the address may now be affixed to the address side of card. If any of the rules relating to a post-card be infringed, the card will be treated as a letter. HALFPENNY PACKET POST. _ _ _
The Halfpenny Packet Post can be used only for packets not exceeding 2oz. in weight. Printed matter, &c., not in the nature of a letter, may be transmitted by this method. NEWSPAPER POST. . .

The prepaid rate of On-aregistered news- paper, including any supplement thereto, whether posted singly or with others is id. Newspapers not registered at the General Post Office are treated in the pcst like any other printed matter.

PARCEL POST. The rates of postage on parcels areas follows: For a parcel ... ... not exceedinig 1 lb. 0 3 9, exceeding 1 lb. 33 2 lb. 0 4 ~ „ 2 lb. „ 3 lb. 0 5 19 „ 3 lb. 7, 5 lb. 0 6 5 lb. t, 7 lb. 0 7 17 >7 7 lb. e 8 lb. 0 8 , I 11l 8 lb, 7, 9 lb. ' 0 9 71 9 f 9 lb. 7, 10 lb. 0 10 10 lb. 11 lb. 0 11 No parcel may exceed 11 lb. In weight. The size allowed for an inland parcel la : Greatest length... ... ... ... 3 ft. G in. Greatest length and girth combined 6 ft. 0 in. For example—A parcel measuring 3ft. Gin, in its longest dimensions as much as 2fl. Gin, round its thickest part ; a short parcel may be thicker •, thus, if it measure no more than 31t. in length, it may measure as much as 3ft. round its thickest part. The postage on a parcel must be prepaid. Mark each parcel " Parcel Post." A parcel must not he posted in a letter box, but presented at the counter of a post oflice, and the sender should see that the weight, size and postage are in order before leaving. PARCELS (FOREIGN AND COLONIAL). Parcels are accepted for parcel post to most foreign countries under conditions similar to the inland regulations, except that for customs require- ments the contents must be declared. The customs charges can be prepaid or collected on delivery. The postage varies to different countries and must be prepaid. MONEY ORDERS (INLAND.) The postal authorities cannot issue a single money order for more than £4O, and will only cash them at the money order office at which they are made payable, unless they are crossed, when they can be paid through a bank. No fractional part of a id. can be contnined in a money order. The rates of poundage are :—Not exceeding Li, 2d. : £3, 3d.; £lO, 41; £2O, lid. ; £3O, Bd. ; £4O, 10d. By paying an additional 2d. and cost of the telegram of advice, a money order can be telegraphed under certain restrictions. MONEY ORDERS (FOREIGN AND COLONIAL.) The maximum amount for which a money order i may be issued for places abroad varies n each particular place. The poundage rates are :—Not exceeding £l,3d. ; £2, Gd. ; and above that, 3d. for each additional £2 or portion of it. A fee of tid. in addition to the ordinary poundage, together with cost of telegram of advice, enables money orders to be telegraphed to certain places abroad. POSTAL ORDERS. -

These are obtaiii;lle-rli:tiTMO-n.ey order orrice in the United Kingdom, and possess the advantage over money orders that they can be cashed at any money order office. If crossed, they can be paid into a bank. They are issue for fixed amounts, rising by Gd., from 6d. to £l-Is. The poundage fees are up to 2s. 6cl. ; id. up to 155.; lAd. up to 21s. Before parting with a postal order, always fill in the name of the person to whom the amount is to be paid. Each order is numbered, as is also the counterfoil attached, which latter should be retained and name of payee filled in. The Post- master-General will entertain no further claim after an order is once paid. Stamps to the amount of sd. can be affixed to make up odd sums.

. - TPLEGRAMS (INLAND). The Postmaster-General possesses,al most entirely, the privilege of transmitting,collecLing and deliver- ing telegrams in the United Kingdom. The charge for a telegram is a minimum amount of 6d.' which covers hi words, and an additional id. for each extra word. This charge includes delivery within the postal district if sent out for delivery from a head telegraph ollice, but if from a sub-office then within three miles only, beyond which a charge of 3d. per mile is made from the office door. All charges are, as far as possible, prepared by affixing stamps to telegram form. Address of person receiv- ing a telegram has to he paid for, but sender's name if written on back of form need not be. Five figures count as one word. The cost of a reply may be prepaid. Telegrams can be repeated on payment of half the original charge, which extra payment is refunded if error is detected. Telegrams may be posted in wall or pillar boxes, or handed to rural postmen, and are wired as soon as received at the nearest telegraph office. Late fees secure attention, in certain cases, to telegrams handed in after the usual hours. The cost of registering an abbrevi- ated address, which must consist of two words, is £ I is. TELEGRAMS (FOREIGN AND COLONIAL) Must be written on special forms and are accepted in the language of any of the principal European countries. The rates vary, and are too numerous to detail here. POST OFFICE SAVINGS BANK. These are established at all money order offices. In ordinary cases the annual deposit must not exceed £5O, and the total amount £2OO. No person can have more than one account. Amounts placed in the bank on behalf of children under seven years of age cannot be withdrawn until the child reaches that age, and then only under his or her own signa- ture. The smallest amount received at a time is Is., and this may take the form of 12 penny stamps affixed to a special form. Each depositor receives a bank book in which the amount of each deposit should he entered at the time of paying in. If the deposit is £1 or over, a special acknowledgment is sent from the head London office. Interest is allowed at the rate of 21 per cent. Any amount up to and including 21 may be withdrawn without previous notice, on presenting a bank book. The bank book should be sent each year, postage free, on the anniversary of the date when the account was opened, to the Controller of the Savings Bank Department for purposes of chocking and adding interest. The withdrawal of money can bee xpedited by telegraphing, the depositor paying cost of telegrams. P.O. TELEPHONE AND TRUNK LINE CHARGES. The fees for the use of the Trunk lines are as follows:
For 2:5 miles or under ... 3d. „ 50 „ Cd 75 11 $, „ 100 „ 1/. „ every additional 40 miles or fraction thereof... _ 6d.
Betvreen the hours of I p.m. and 7 a.m., SIK minutes conversation is allowed for the same price as three minutes between 7 a.m. and 7 p.m., and a reduced charge is made for three minute calls.

MOTOR CAR AND CYCLE REOULATIONS. Each one must be registered with the council of a county or county borough, the fee being £1 fored motor car, and ss. for a motor cycle. A register a number is assigned to each, which it is an offence not to keep affixed when driving. Each driver must possess a license, costing 5 s., to be renewed every 12 months, and obtainable from the county authorities, which may be endorsed or suspended for reckless driving or certain other offences. The highest speed at which a car may be driven on the public highways is 20 miles an hour, which is reduced to 10 miles under special local regula- tions. It is an offence under the Motar Car Act (1903), to drive a car in such a way on a public highway as to be dargerous to the public, having regard to Il the circumstances of the case. In the event of an accident to any person due to he presence of the motor car on the road, the triver must supply his name and address, and the wner and number of the car, under heavy penal- odie The driver roust produce his licence at the Bequest of a police constable.

RUNCORN'S FINE WIN AT LEIGH. At Leigh, before 4,003 spectators. The game was very even, each side attacking in turn. Leigh were penalised for obstruction, and Jolley kicked a goal. The Leigh forwards dribbled finely, but were stopped under the Runcorn goal. The defenders were penalised, and Sam Johnson equalised the scores by placing a goal. A moment later Leigh were again penalised for obstruction, and Jolley added another goal. Passing was neglected, both sides playing the kick-and-rush game. Jolley picked up from among a number ofi players and dropped a goal. At the interval Runcorn led by six points to two. On resuming, Leigh attacked strongly, but were con- fronted by a superb defence. About Live minutes remained for play when the referee blew his whistle for " time," and the spectators left the field. Subse- quently he discovered his mistake, and play was resumed. Winstanley scored a try for Leigh from a scrummage, but Sam Jackson failed at goal. A moment later Leigh were awarded a free kick, but Clarkson failed from a difficult position, and Runcorn won by 3 goals (ii points), to 1 goal and 1 try (5 points).

With a re-arranged team Warrington went to Swinton on Saturday full of determination to improve their dis- appointing record since the opening of the season. They made a very plucky fight and were only narrowly beaten. Beautiful weather prevailed and 5,000 spectators assembled to witness a very exciting and interesting struggle. J. Jenkins made a welcome re-appearance on the NVarrington side, and the teams turned out as follows : Warrington : Tilley, back ' • Fish, Dickenson, Cart- wright and Jordan, threequarter backs ; Jenkins and Brooks' half-backs ; P. Boardman, A. Boardman,Naylor, Hewitt, Chester and Belton, forwards. Swinton : Townson, back ; Wallwork, Griffin, Kewin, and Wharton, threequarter back ; Jones and Fairhurst, half-backs ; Barnett, Bailey, Lloyd, W. Preston, J. Preston and Vicars, forwards. Referee, Mr. J. C. Lumley. Leeds ; touch judges, Messrs. T. King, Salford ; and J. Edwards, St. Helens. A. E. Boardman started, and it was soon apparent that a stiff struggle for supremacy would soon take place. Give-and-take play ensued, and it was not until Cartwright and Jordan got smartly working that Town- son's charge was in jeopardy, and the Warrington for- wards were almost over as the result of a tine burst. Again did a free kick givo the Swintonians welcome relief, and headway was made by Jack Preston and Bar- dett, but the home side never really became dangerous. The Warrington backs again handled the ball very smartly, and Swinton were compelled to adopt defen- sive tactics. An attempt by liewiu and Jones to raise the siege was well met by Tilley, who subsequently marked in a favourable position, only to see Dicken- son's shot at goal go wide of the mark. A sharp run by Wallwork gave Swinton a footing inside the War- rington quarters, and progress being made by the home forwards' Tilley had all his work cut out to save. He emerged from the ordeal with flying colours, and Fish seconing the effort with a fine run, the Warring- tonians once more played the part of aggressors. A good effort by Cartwright caused Wallwork trouble, and Warrington were unfortunate in not crossing, after Fish and Dickenson had tested the defence. Warrington continued to display superior form, and after Jenkins and Brooks had once more shown flue combination, Fish missed a glorious chance. It was not for long, however, for the ball again travelled towards the left, and accepting splendidly he dashed past Townson in all his old style and scored a grand try. The goal kick was a failure. Swinton rallied slightly after this, and , Kewin and Fairhurst were conspicuous in an effort which lodged the game at the Warrington end. The 1 interval arrived with the score in favour of Warrington by three points to nil. Resuming, the hot pace which characterized the first half was displayed, aad after Cartwright and Jordan had combined well, Brooks opened out the game and some brilliant passing was seen amongst the Warrington rear division. The visiting forwards were just a shade too premature in forcing the game and were penalized. Preston's kick caused Warrington to boat a hasty retreat, and Jones and Fairhurst getting the better of the Warrington half-backs, Kewin was given possession, and a lofty punt travelled to Jordan, who was tackled. A splendid movement by the Swinton backs culminated in Wallwork scoring a beautiful try. The goal kick was again abortive, and the scores were thus equalled. Swinton now warmed to their work, and on several occasions the Warrington line was threatened. Griffin marked, and from the place kick near the centre J. Preston gave his side the lead with a fine goal. The subsequent play was of an exciting character, each end being visited in rapid succession. Result :—Swiriton, one goal and one try (five points) ; Warrington, one try (three points.)

div.head: WIDNES v. OLDHANI: THE REFEREE ESCORTED OFF.
div.p: WIDNES v. OLDHANI: THE REFEREE ESCORTED OFF.

Played at Widnes, before 4,000 spectators. The game opened in favour of Oldham, and in the first few minutes Cook had the line at his mercy, but in trying to gather the ball he knocked on. smith, the New Zealander, made several gallant attempts to cross the line, but he as well watched, and tha tackling of the home three-quarters was particularly keen. At half- time there was no score.

Early in the second half Widnes were penalised for off-side, and Ferguson gained the lead for his side by kicking a goal. A few minutes later the Oldham baclis got going, and Tyson scored an unimproved try at the corner. rowards the finish, when play was at half-way, Widnes were penalised for obstruction, and Ferguson kicked a goal from short range. Just before the finish Lloyd, one of the Widnes forwards, was ordered oft' Result :—Oldham 2 goals 1 try (7 points), Widnes nil. Referee, Mr. Mainwaring' Salford. Touch judges, Messrs. Platt (Swinton) and Lowe (Broughton). Some of the decisions of the referee displeased the spectators, and at the conclusion of the game great hostility was shown towards him, and ha had to be escorted to the dressing-rooms.
WIDNES REPORTED AND CAUTIONED.
THE SC ENE AFTER THE;MATCH WITH OLDHAM.

A portion of the business before the committee of the Northern Rugby League at Huddersfield last night was conducted publicly. This was a complaint by Mr. Mainvrarin,,' (Salford), the referee in the Widnes v. Oldham match played on the Widnes ground on Saturday last. The referee stated that at three-quarter time a Niidnes player was ordered off for kicking an opponent. Up to that time the match had been splendidly contested, and then there was a good deal of shouting and hooting. After he blew his whistle he had to be escorted to his dressing-room by seine men in plain clothes and ofilcials of the club. He had to cross a field to get to his dressing-room, and although he was not molested in any way he considered that had he not been so pro- tected he would have been, and he thought it necessary that he should bring the matter before the League, so that other referees might be protected. Mr. F . . Wright, the treasurer of the Widnes club after additional evidence had been given, said there was a hooting crowd during the last ten minutes of the game and seeing that the crowd was a little excited, arrange- ments were made by the club officials to have the referee guarded when he went off the ground. After the matter had been discussed in private the committee intimated that the Widnes club should post warning notices on the ground, and they recommended that a dressing-room should be provided for referees under the grandstand, and if the recommend ttions were not carried out very likely the club would be ordered to carry out the recommendations. The Widnes club was ordered to pay expenses.

div.head: NORTHERN RUGBY UNION.
div.p: NORTHERN RUGBY UNION.
FRIENDLY MATCHES. STOCKTON HEATTI V. HEATON MOOR.

IThe Stockton Heath club opened their season on , Saturday with a visit to Heaton Moor and returned home with honours, winning by eight points to seven. In the first half the visitors had the better of matters, the forwards playing a brilliant combined game and affording the Heaton Moor backs little scope to main- tain any lengthened period of aggression. Turning ' round, Stockton Heath soon attacked, and forcing the pace the backs indulged in some effective passing which I caused Heaton Moor serious trouble. Eventually ! Ferguson got hold from some loose work and raced over for the first try of the season Following this commend- able effort the Heaton backs,especially Bainbridge (who I is the Warrington cricketer and formerly assisted. I Leicester), Williams, Powell-Jones and Emmett , struggled hard to place the sides on a level footing, but all tone purpose, for the defence prevailed. It was not until Burns dropped a goal that Eaton Moor were able ' to record a tangible point. Ins visitors speedily retaliated, and after Langley and Ferguson had been held up Warren scored rather cleverly, and Langley placed his side further ahead when he negotiated the goal. Again in 11 rroa rs the home side strenuously attacked and T. Tunsley got over. The goal kick failed. The Moor tried hard but unsuccessfully. Powell-Jones, Bainbridge and Croxfield making gallant, but futile, efforts to cross the Stockton Heath line, which was cleverly kept intact. Final: Stockton Heath, one goal one try (eight points) ; Heaton Moor one dropped goal one try (seven points).

div.head: ASSOCIATION FOOTBALL.
div.p: ASSOCIATION FOOTBALL.
WARRINGTON CUP. ALBIONS VICTORIOUS IN RE-PLAYED FINAL.

Great interest was taken in the re-played final tie for the above cup which took place last Saturday, and several thousands of spectators assembled. The teams were as follows :—Warrington Albion : J. Wyatt, goal ; H. Osborne and G. H. Short, full-backs ; I'. Dilworth, 0. Dickenson and R.Hamblett, half-backs; C. F. Trow, W. H. Hunter S. Gregsota, E. Ball and J. Pendlebury, forwards. Caslner-Kellner : Dobson,goal ; Knight and Proffitt, full-backs ; Briggs, Bell and Black- burn, half-backs ; T. Senior, H. Senior, Stott, Brookes and Acton, forwards. Referee, Mr. Hargreaves, Liverpool. From the start the Albions were on the attack and Pendlobury registered a goal after eight minutes' play. The Cestrians now played up briskly but their repeated efforts to score were frustrated by the fine work of their opponents. Before the interval, goals were scored for the Albions by Hunter, Dilworth and Trow. Half-time: Albions, four goals ; Castner-Kellner, nil. Stott restarted and Castner's seemed to brighten up a little, showing plenty of dash. The Cestrians ran the ball down the left wing and Acton passed to Brookes, who saw his opportunity and banged the ball in, completely beating Wyatt with a cross-shot three minutes after the interval. Play was kept in the centre, but Hunter seeing his chance, broke clean away and fired straight at goal. It was a splendid shot, the ball bouncing to the top of the net. This put the Albion five up. Dobson saved splendidly three minutes later from the same player at about four yards range. Both teams played a good hard game but the Albion's combination outclassed that of their opponents. Result : Warrington Albion, 5 goals; Castner-Kellner, one goal. WARRINGTON PLAYERS FOR EVERTON. Two Warrington Albion F.C. players have been signed by Everton and will probably play to-day with the reserves. One is Webb, a centre half, who played in the friendly fixture on Saturday last and shaped very well, and the other is Orborae,a right full back.

div.head: WARRINGTON STABBING CASE.
div.p: WARRINGTON STABBING CASE.
Prisoner Committed for Trial.

At the Warrington Police Court, on Tuesday, before Mr. H. Roberts and other magistrates, Joseph Marriott, of Foundry-street, was charged on remand with wounding Isabella Mannion, a married woman, residing in Foundry-street, on Bank Holiday, August 3. Mr. W. H, J. Jenkins prosecuted and Mr. T. S. Steel defended. Mr. Jenkins said that about eight o'clock on the night in question the complainant, along with another neighbour, were gossiping at the front door. The prisoner passed along the street, and hearing some laughter he thought the merriment was directed at him. He rushed at the complainant's sister and " butted "her, aftervgrds striking bar a severe blow on the face. The complSinant, seeing her sister assaulted went to her assistance, when the defendant rushed into his shop, and came back flourishing a large pocket knife with which he stabbed the complainant under the left breast, causing a very serious wound which necessitated her detention in the infirmary for seven weeks. The complainant, who had to be assisted into Court, gave evidence bearing out this atatement. She said the blow struck by the prisoner was deliberate. In reply to Mr. Steel she said she had known • prisoner for a good many years' and she bad never quarrelled with him before. He had been falling out and " carrying on " with his wife all day on the date in question. She knew no reason rthy prisoner should stab her. Edward James Dandy, 3, Haydock-street, spoke to seeing the prisoner rush out of his shop with a knife in his hand and strike Mrs. Maunion on the left side. Dr. Russell, of the Infirmary, stated that when Mrs. Mannion was admitted to the institution, she was suffering from a wound in tho left side. The clothes about the wound were saturated with blood. Judging ' from her appearance when he first saw her lying on the ambulance, she appeared to be very excited. Sha also smelled of drink. The wound was situated about 2,111. to 3in. from the centre of the left breast. It was about lin. long and penetrated the chest wall. It passed through the ribs. The wound was a very serious one and following upon it serious chest troubles arose, which required two operations. She had been confined to the institution for 7 weeks. Her present condition would necessitate her receiving further attention from the infirmary. In answer to. r. Steel, he said the wound might have been caused by the woman falling upon the knife, while she was hi the act, of striking prisoner Margaret Howard, wife of John Howard, Foundry- street, gave evidence to the effect that at about 8.15 o'clock, she stood in the roadway talking to Sarah Anne Stokes. div.head: WORKS BOWLING ASSOCIATION. Captain Crosfield Presents the Prizes'
div.p: WORKS BOWLING ASSOCIATION. Captain Crosfield Presents the Prizes'

The Warrington Works Bowling Association brought a highly successful season to a close on Monday even- ing, when the presentation of prizes gained in the recent individual merit handicap took place at the Bowling Green Inn, Bank Quay. There was a large attendance. and the evening was pleasantly spent in music and short speeches. Captain Crosfleld (president of the Associa- tion) attended to distribute the awards, and amongst others present were :-Messrs. J. Willett (chairman of the committee), G. Ball, jun. (vice-chairman of the committee), \V. Holbrook (treasurer), W. Patrick (secretary), and several members of the committee. The PRMIDENT submitted the toast of "The King." At the outset he said he sincerely appreciated the courtesy of the members in putting off that function until he returned from his holidays. He travelled back through Germany and Holland,and whenever he got into touch with the Germans or the Dutch, every one of them expressed the greatest admiration for our King. (Applause.) It behoved us all to back him up by serv- ing him right loyally as good citizens. (Applause.) The toast was cordially honoured. The PeesinENT said he was delighted to hear they had had such an excellent competition and he was sure it reflected the greatest credit upon the officials and members of the committee that everything had passed off so smoothly and amicably. On previous occasions be had uttered prc tests against the excessive amount of football playing that went on, but he hoped none of them would think he was opposed to games themselves. He was absolutely for games; he thought they were splendid. The longer he lived, the more he saw the good results of playing games, but there was all the difference in the world between playing and simply looking on. To his mind, the great advantage of the game of bowls was that they all played their hardest and there was very little looking on. He did not believe in making a regular business of games. Con- tinuing, Captain Croefleld entertained the company with a graphic account of his recent mountaineering experi- ences in the Tyrol. Again referring to the value of games, he impressed upon his hearers that there was not only the game of pleasure but the game of life. Many mottoes which they drew from games could be very rightly and properly used in ordinary, every-day life, and there was no finer motto than " Play the game." (Applause,) They should play it honestly, fairly end squarely, to the best of their ability, no matter whether they won or whether they were beaten. He was afraid we Britishers were perhaps not quite playing the game at the present time. We were being warned by men who had given their lives to the Empire, about our want of preparation and there were very few who troubled to think about it. He was afraid those eloquent words of Mr. Rudyard Kipling might come true if -me did not wake up and play the national game. He referred to the following lir.es from" The Recessional " :- Far called our navies melt away, On dune and headland sinks the fire ; Lo, all our pomp of yesterday, Is one with Nineveh and Tyro ! Judge of the Nationsopare us yet, Lest we forget, lest we forget. In presenting the prizes on that occasion he would ask them to remember the motto which he was sure they all had very much at heart -"Play the game"-and also ‘ those eloquent words of Mr. Kipling's, 'Lest we forget, lest we forget." (Applause.) The PRESIDNNIT then presented the first prize to Jack Gleave, Whitecross, who received a clock and gold chain, value .£ 1, and also holds the handsome cep, pre- sented by Lady Greenall, for twelve months. The other prise winners were :-2nd, IV Torukinson, Crosfields' ; 3rd, W Bibby, Greenings ; 4th, G. Shaw, Rylands ; sth, A Warburton, Whitecross ; oth A Middleton, Crosfields' ; 70). Judging by the , enthusiasm at present displayed, he did not think the I association had depredated, and they looked forward to is long continuance of Captain Crosfield's services as President. (Applause.) The toast was drunk with musical honours.

Captain CRWSFIZ‘ID, "In responding, thanked the assembly very sincerely for the kind way in which they had received the toast. If they did him the honour to re-elect him next year—and he could assure them he thought it was a high honour to be president of an Association of all the works in this important town,— he hoped he might be able to help them more than he bad done, lie wished their excellent a sociatica all success in the years to come. (Applause.) Mr. J. WILLETr proposed' Ile Prize Donors "and expressed the indebtedness of the Association to all who had contributed.
