div.head: LETTERS TO THE EDITOR. NOTICE TO CORRESPONDENTS. Authors of letters intended for publication mn.t in all cases send their names and addresses to the Editor al a guarantee of good faith.
div.p: LETTERS TO THE EDITOR. NOTICE TO CORRESPONDENTS. Authors of letters intended for publication mn.t in all cases send their names and addresses to the Editor al a guarantee of good faith.

Governments and Unemployment. Sir,—The subject of" Gasworker's" discourse in your last week's issue is one of vital importance at present. The subject of "bad trade" is one which ought to occupy everyone's attention and deliberations, which, unfortu- nately, is not o. I must join in agreement with the arguments expressed in the aforesaid letter, that Governments are not responsible for either bad trade or good. But I Wa9 sorry he did not investigate the matter more closely and analyze for the cause. A chapter in Mr. Edward Bellamy' book "Equality" simply explains the cause, I think. The chapter is entitled " The parable of a water tank," which I will endeavour to condense in the smallest,possible space. A , certain community is stricken with water famine and they go seeking water, which they find in a tank. The water and tank belong to men who allow the famine-stricken people to use the water if they will keep the tank full. • 'They must bring the water in buckets from the sur- rounding districts to the tank and place it therein. For every bucketful brought they will receive a penny, and for every bucketful drawn from the tank they must pay twopence. It is easily seen that the people will only consume half of what they produce. In time the tank overflowed and the people were thrown idle by their own diligence, and that is the exact position of the English people to-day. They produce in excess of their purchasing power, and we have the excruciating ! spectacle of people out of employment and working short time, which entails short rations, because they have pro- duced too much. On the other hand we see a small section of the community taking more than they require with- out giving in return any adequate services. According to Mr. Chiozza Money, M.P., 5 million persona take from the annual wealth produced in England £B3O millions from the aggregate £1,710 millions.£BBo millions going to 43 million people. It is the extortion from the masses by the classes that curtails the purchasing power of the producer ; that produces the "bad trade" complained of. The logical remedy for the people in the parable would be the common ownersh.js of the tank, and the remedy for the British people as the common ownership of the source of wealth production—the land, which is Nature's gift to all men, from which men's sustenance is derived; and the machinery for pro- ducing man's sustenance from the land, must become the property of the people, controlle4 by the people, in the Interest of the people. But that would 'be Socialism : —Yours truly, LABOR OMNIA VINCIT.

div.head: -- The Home Office and Daisy Lord.
div.p: -- The Home Office and Daisy Lord.

--- Sir,—Enclosed is a copy of an oEcial letter I have just received from the Home Office referring to the " Daisy Lord" Petition.—Yours, etc., CHARLES WALKER (Sec. Warrington 1.L.P.) Whitehall, 19th September, 1908. Sir,—l am directed by the Secretary of State to say that he bas had under his consideration your applica- tion regarding the case of Daisy Lord and many other similar petitions on her behalf, and that he thinks that he can best answer these appeals--by stating briefly what is the usual practice of the Home Office in cases where a mother is convicted of the murder of her infant child. He must say by way of preface that he Ina observed in some cases a tendency to underrate and even to ignore the serious- ness of the crime o f infanticide. Doubtless this arises from the imposition of the death sentence under the present law—a law which Mr. Gladstone hopes it may be possible to amend—and from natural indigna- tion at the escape of the father from legal responsi- bility ; but he cannot regard these circumstances as justifying him in treating lightly so grave an offence as the murder of an infant child. It appears to him however that all, or nearly all, those who have petitioned him on behalf of Daisy Lord have done so without knowledge of the practice of the Home Office, and under a mistaken impression as to the sentence she ‘vill have to serve. The polctice in such cases is that the death sentence should always be commuted in the first instauce to penal servitude for life. This is not done with the intention that the prisoner should in any case serve for life, but because it a?lows the Home Secretary as a free hand subsequently to modify the sentence in accordance with the circumstances of the case,and the disposition and progress of the progress of the prisoner. To fix at once a definite term would give rise to mis- understanding, and might lead in some cases to a longer detention than ultimately proves to be necessary. • The prisoner then undergoes a longer or shorter period of detention in a convict prison under discipline and with the best training and guidance which can be given by humane officers with speCial experience of such cases. In the prison there is also a Committee of Ladies who, without holding any official position, take a keen interest in the prisoners, and give valuable assistanee in the work of their reformation. There can be no doubt of the advantage both physical and moral, which most prisoners of this class derive from this training. In the case of the hardened criminal it may be ineffective : but women who have been convicted of infanticide are rarely of that class, and are generally amenable to good influence and capable of having their character improved and strengthened. The term of detention varies, but it now, save in exceptional circumstances, rarely exceeds three years. And it may be shorter if the prisoner is of previous good character, or if she responds readily to whole- some influences, and if she has friends who can under- take the responsible care of her on her release, or a home can be found where she can be received and cared for. As soon as these conditions are fulfilled, she is released conditionally to her friends or to the Home ; her further progress is carefully watched, and as soon as it is seen to be to her advantage the condi- tions of her release are cancelled and she is restored to complete freedom. This is the course which the Secretary of State proposes to follow in the case of Daisy Lord, and he feels sure that it will satisfy the reasonable hopes of those who have so earnestly appealed to him on her behalf.

div.head: I am, Sir, Your obedlent servant. C. E. TROUPE. Tariff Reform Meeting. "Red Rose " and Councillor Broadhurk.
div.p: I am, Sir, Your obedlent servant. C. E. TROUPE. Tariff Reform Meeting. "Red Rose " and Councillor Broadhurk.

Sir,—A correspondence has recently taken place between Councillor Broadhurst and myself in the columns of one of your contemporaries, which the Editor has now closed. I neither complain of this action nor am I surprised at it, for the points which Councillor Broadhurst has persisted in repeating have been repeatedly answered by me, and for the most part they have been concerned with questions involving nothing more than the consideration of the infinitely little. But as in the " necessary reply " allowed to Councillor Broadhurst, he does not confine himself to the question dealt with in ray last letter, and as it con- tains a number of erroneous conclusions I am emboldened, in the interests of Free trade, to ask for the hospitality of your columns for a rejoinder to it. Considering that in my last letter to the "Guardian" I convicted Councillor Broadhurst of the offence of garbling passages I had written so as to make it appear that I had put forward statements that were not made, his charge against me of using " bluff " exhibits on his part a considerable amount of assurance. I have used no " bluff "in this controversy, and I protest against the offensive imputation. Free Trade no more needs the aid of such means than the multiplication table itself. We who support the system court the fullest inquiry iato it, and we shirk no facts because we know that any fact that can be produced in connection with inter- national commerce can only serve to vindicate the justice and wisdom of a Free Trade policy. If Councillor Broadhnrst will try and formulate some logical proposition in relation to the tin plate trade it will be possible to deal with him, but it is hopeless to discuss the question so long as he will do nothing but beat his head against certain facts which are either not disputed or are irrelevant or insignificant. For instance, in every letter be has written for some time he has i pointed n triumph to the fact that the American tariff has inflicted injury on our tin plate industry. But who said it hadn't, and what if it has? I have always conceded the point that the American tariff inflicted injury upon our tin plates exports to that country. On the other hand I have invited Councillor Broadhurst'a acceptance of some other facts which are just as undoubted, but this he resolutely refuses to do. I have pointed to our increasing tin plate exports to other countries, but he insists on wrangling about the exact figures. The fact that we have increased our exports of tin plates since 1893 by 130,000 tons is nothing to him. It is in vain that he is reminded that year by year our exports of tin plate have steadily increased, that including black plates they rose last year to the highest quantity yet arrived at, and that even excluding black plates they, were within a few thousand tons of any previous record. All this is lost upon him, and he makes no other reply than to cavil about a figure or doggedly to repeat that the American tariff injured our tin plate industry, or occasionally he will lapse into poetry, as when in his last letter he pathetically declares that "the very life blood of the nation is flowing rapidly away." One fact alone which I have mentioned more than once is suMcient to settle this question. It is that in 190 G we made the record production of G 31,000 tons of tin plate. No fair-minded,man after that fact bad been pointed out to him' would have said another word on the subject. But Councillor Broadhurst has steadily ignored the fact and has kept harping upon the reduc- tion in the number of mills. This is beside the question. We are discussing the production of tin plate and not the number of mills engaged in doing it. It would not matter if there were only a single mill left, if that Mill turned out a greater tonnage than all the other mills together had previously done. To attempt to disprove a statement of increased tonnage by saying that the number of mills has decreased, is in Councillor Broad- hurt's elegant style of speech—" bluff."

In connection with our tin plate exports to Canada, Councillor Broadhurst has found a remarkable mare's nest. He says that we have now lost the control of the Canadian market, as from January to May of this year America exported 211,665 tons, whilst Great Britain only sent 101,933 tons. As the largest quantity of tin plate we ever sent to Canada in one year was 23,427 tons, which we sent in 190:3, we are doing extremely well indeed now if we are sending 101,9:33 tons in five months. At that rate it would be a pleasant thing to lose the control of a market. But it is too good to be true. It is, in fact, another of Councillor Broadhurst's stupendous blunders. The quantity we actually shipped to Canada from January to May of this year was not 101,933 tons, but the much , more modest quantity of 5,611 tons. It is 2,433 tons less than we sent in the same period of last year, but 475 tons more than in 1993, so that there are no bones broken yet. If we are sending less tin plate to Canada we are sending more to Ara,:xica. We sent there 8,000 tons more last year than we did in 1933, and this year we are sending still more. From January to August we sent 43,891 tons against 41,133 tons in the same period of last year. To Canada we sent,January to August last year, 13,511 tons, and this year 9,333 tons. Now, if Coun- cillor Broadhurst will attentively consider the figures he will see something very significant indeed. We are sending some 1,000 tons of tin plate less to Canada and some 4,000 tons more to America, At the same time America is increasing her tin plate exports to Canada. Does not Councillor Broadhurst smell a rat ? If not, I will tell him th it it is our tin plate the Americans are sending to Canada. There is no question whatever about that The American Government, finding that they had no tin plate export trade, recently came to the conclusion that the Tariff was the cause. They there- fore decided to reduce the duty by 93 per cent. on all tin plate imported for the purpose of being re-exported. In consequence of that the Americans are now buying increased quantities of tin plate from us, and as it is practically duty free they are able to supply Canada on pretty much the same terms as we ourselves. Thus, if the Americans have now got a tin plato export trade to Canada, it is by buying British goods tariff free and selling them again, and thus Councillor Broad- hurst may perceive that as all roads are said to lead to Rome, so all economic truths whoa they are closely pursued will be found to arrive at the great and invincible principle of Free Trade.—Yours etc., RED ROSE. September 23rd, 1003.

div.head: LOCAL PARLIAMENT. OPENING OF fHE AUTUMN SESSION. Debate on the King's Speech.
div.p: LOCAL PARLIAMENT. OPENING OF fHE AUTUMN SESSION. Debate on the King's Speech.

Our local Parliament—in other words the Warring- ton Parliamentary Debating Society—entered upon its autumn session at the Co-operative Hall, Sankey-street, 03 Thursday evening. It cannot be said that the honourable members as a whole responded with alacrity to the call to resume their duties, for the attendance was sparse in all parts of the House. Apparently there was an expectation that most of the time would be devoted to formal business, but this did not prove to be the case, for after less than an hour spent in electing officers, the discussion on the King's Speech was opened. The debate was not brilliant—at times it was decidedly tame—but it was not without its interesting passages. The Cabinet is exactly the same as that which direoted the nation's affairs last session, with the excep- tion that a new office has been created by the appoint- ment of Councillor Locker as Secretary for India. The Premier (Mr. John Upson) was in his accustomed place, bat owing to indifferent health Councillor Nield has withdrawn from the leadership of the Opposition. His place was taken by Mr. W. H. Stansfleld (Dublin University).

div.head: ELECTION OF OFFICER.
div.p: ELECTION OF OFFICER.

Pending the election of officers, Alderman BENNE'FT (‘V. Birmingham) was voted to the chair. He con- gratulated the society on the admirable start it made last session. It had abundantly justified its existence. He felt that the work of the second session would redound to its credit and the town's. He never knew the time when it was more important that men of all parties should meet together for the purpose of discussion with the sole and sincere view of promoting the best interests of the country and of the Empire. (Applause). The CHANCELLOR OF THE EXCHEcH.TER(Mr. E. England) moved the adoption of the balance sheet which showed an income of £lO 9s. Sd. and 211 Bs. 9d. in hand. This was approved. The PIiENIER proposed the re-election of their speaker (Mr. Charles Plinston). After the admirable way in which he had done his work it would be in gross ingratitude, on their part to refuse to re-elect him unanimously. That the society had coming out with flying colours was largely owing to the wise guidance, and impartial spirit shown to every member of the House. In seconding Mr. SEANSFIELD said that Mr. Plinston had fulfilled the post with conspicuous ability. Councillor O'Toole (Leader of the Nationalists) and Mr. W. Nightingale (Normanton, for the socialists) supported. The Speaker was re-elected unanimously. The SPEA.KER proposed that Councillor Steel be re-elected Deputy Speaker. Mr. J. JARNtA.N (President Board of Trade) seconded, and it was carried.
Mr. F. G. ThYLOTt (Peterstield) proposed Mr. W. Mason's re-election as Clerk of the House. _

Mr. J. F. AWBERY (Secretary for Ireland) seconded and it was agreed to with much cordiality. Mr. BAINES (West Derby), proposed the re-election of Mr. Nathan Cook, jun., as Deputy Clerk of the House. Mr. W. U. SIIERCURN (Secretary for Scotland) seconded. . _ .

The proposal was carried unanimously. Mr. W. L.WlLmams (Oswestry), proposed the re-elec- tion of Mr. E. Osborne as Secretary to the Society. The initial success of Society was largely due to Mr. Osborne's (Alerts and it must have given him great satisfaction. The CLERK OF THE HOUSE seconded and it was carried unanimously. The CHANCELLOR OE' THE EXCHEQUER proposed Mr. Percy Bennett as Hon. Treasurer and Mr. Williams (Owestry), seconded. This was unanimously agreed to. The following were elected to the Council :—Messrs. J. Upson, W. H. Stansfield, E. Plinston, E. England, M. G. Hearne, W. L. Williams, M. Cunningham, R. Pierce Williams, E. G. Burgess, W. H. Sherburn J. McDermid, J. F. Awbery, W. Nightingale, Councillor Ball, Councillor Toole, J. N. Vernon and the oflicers of the House.

_ The SPEAKER then took the chair. Addressing the members, he said their conduct last Session was sufficient proof to him that it was their intention this Session to do all they possibly could to help him in his duties. There was only one word of warn- ing that he would like to give, and that was that at the present time political opinions were apparently getting keener, and as they were all aware politicians got very excited in giving utterance to their arguments and he hoped that they would try to bear in mind that person- alities did not count. He trusted that all of them would endeavour in all matters, whether political or religious questions, to listen attentively to the argu- ments and if they could refute them it would be all the better for them. ite pointed out that at the end of this year the Liberal Ministry, whether defeated or not, would go out of office, and he hoped all parties in the House were considering the formation of a new Government. "I have heard a whisper," he concluded, " that it is to be a coalition, but time alone will show."

div.head: LATE MR. JOHN MAGINN.
div.p: THE LATE MR. JOHN MAGINN.

The Pur.mtrut then moved a resolution expressing the members' deep sense of the loss they had sustained by the death of Mr. John Magian, who was a member of the House. He said it was not his intention to pro- nounce a formal eulogy on Mr. Maginn—there were often, he thought, notes of insincerity in formal eulogies. Mr. Maginn, being mortal like the rest of them, no doubt bad his short-comings, but if he had,the memories of thorn were rapidly passing into oblivion and what was left was the vivid remembrance of a man who was absolutely fearless in the expression of his opinions, kind and courteous in his manners, sympathetic in his actions, virile in his thought and witty in his speech. He went out to fight death alone and with undaunted breast and unflinching courage met the King of Terrors. Although be was finally vanquished, as we all ultimately must be, yet, if he (the speaker) might be allowed the expression, he went down with drums beating and trumpets blaring, and his colours at the mast. Mr. W. H. STANSFIELD (Dublin University), in second;ng, said Mr. Maginn was a worthy citizen who did his best to uplift the town in every way, and the children found in him a sincere friend.

Warm tributes were also forthcoming from Councillor TOOLE (Nationalist Leader), Mr. W. NIGITTINGA.LE (Normanton), and Mr. E. PLTNSTON (Gateshead). The Rev. C. HARVEY CoOK (Ashford, Kent) said he had been in close relationship with Mr. Nfaginn in political and other matters, and if ever the lines were appropriate, they were most appropriate to Mr. John Maginn—" An honest man, the noblest work of God." The resolution was carried, the members standing as a mark of respect whilst the speeches were being delivered.

div.head: KING'S SPEECH.
div.p: THE KING'S SPEECH.

The CLEaK or, TILE fIOUiE then read the King's Speech as follows : GENTLEMEN', His Majesty's Government is pleased to report the continuance of cordial relations with all other Powers. Provocative and irresponsible journalists and others, both in Great Britain and Germany, have imperilled those relations with that country but happily have not succeeded in effecting their purpose. The panic fears they created are rapidly dying down, and the good sense of both peoples has recognised that the best interests of each are promoted by a mutually peaceful policy. Financial proposals will be submitted to you at an early date. The Reforms indicated below will entail the raising of considerable sums of money, and the approval of the House will be asked for proposals by which the necessary funds may be raised. We are gravely concerned by the undoubted evidence of widespread distress arising from lack of employ- ment. We are anxiously considering the difficult

gap.desc: skipped/gap: fewer than 20 non-control characters after cleanup

div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, September 26, 1908.

problem and we hope to submit for your approval I plans which ;V) trust will go far temente the solution of thepressing and diallit pro `dem of unemployment. The continu33 raevemeat amongst railway corn- , peniee towards c3mbia ttioa threatens to become, I ultimately, opposed to the best interests of the State. Wo tailk the time his come when private interests in, and management of, railways should cease, and we shall saenelt proposals for the State ownership of the railways of this country. The question of the valuation of land for taxation and rating fairp asea iS engaging the atteatioe of ministers. Efforts will b 3 made to reduce the glaring anomalies associated with this subject ad you will be asked to approve a Bill dealing drastically with the inequalities and injusticies at prenent existing. Electoral and Registration Reform is urgently neede I. eVe shall ask you to approve of a Bill that will secure the removal of abuses, while at the same time securing for rainy now disfranchised the right to take part in the government of the country. "God save the King." Mr. J. JARM 1.. N (President of the Board of Trade) moved the adoption of the King's speech. The most important question touched upon, he said, was that of unemployment and the Government intended to make a determined effort to deal with it on such lines, that they would preduce a really useful measure and not make it a question of mere doling out of charity. The necessity of taxation of land values had been intensified of late because Acts which had been passed with the object of giving people a greater interest in the land had been rendered almost abortive, owing to the inability to get held of the necessary land. Where a person absolutely refused to use land laimself or to allow others to use it at a reasonable value, the Government intended to place on it the value which the owner him- self estimated it at, and insist that he should be taxed on that value. (Applause.) With regard to the railways, the Government had come to the conclusion that if it were possible for large railway companys to make agreements, pool their earnings and not compete with each other in certain districts, the State might well take over the management of affairs and work the rail- ways economically and in the interests of the public. As to electoral reforms, the Government want to abolish plural voting. It must be "one man, one vote." (Applause.) He was not in the counsels of the Govern- ment on the question of the extension of the franchise to women, but he believed in a measure on the lines of adult suffrage all round. (Applause.) Mr. P. O'BRIEN (St. Pancras) seconded. He expressed himself in harmony with the peace senti- ments in the King's Speech, but pointed out that unfortunately the good relations between Germany and this country might be imperilled by the action of one man—and he not an Englishman—and therefore it behoved us to be prepared. (Opposition applause.) 'lle recent possibility of a railway strike had led men of all parties to the conclusion that the employes on the railways should have security of position at fair wages and that there should be no dislocation of trade. Alluding to electoral reform, Mr. O'Btien, in emphasis- ing the difficulties which beset the claimant of a vote, mentioned the proceedings at the local Revision Court and created roars of laughter by a slip of the tongue which caused him to allude to the Revising Barrister as "the Coroner." Well, he added, he gave the death blow to some of them. (More laughter.) Mn IV. If. STANSFIELD (Dublin University) after a sympathetic reference to the late leader of the Opposi- tion, expressed his agreement with the desirability of maintaining friendly relations with other Powers. His party would not associate themselves with the provoca- tion of strife, and they were at one with the Govern- ment in wishing to preserve peace and goodwill. Taking the Speech as a whole, he should have expected it to come from the Socialists. The whole tone of it was Socialistic. They could see where the masters were. (Laughter). Roferring to unemployment, Mr. Stens- field said Mr. Chanaberlain had been telling them it would come. (Laughter). He had also shown them how to provide against it. (" Question.") If they had Fair Trade they would not have the question of unemployment. The nationalisation:of railways sounded very well, but it wanted carefully looking into. It did not mean that if they nationalised a thine' it was going to be better than it was at present. It all depended upen how they nationalised it. They had nationalised the schools, but he did not think they were what they ought to be. They had only nationalised them in a partial sense. (Hear, bear). With regard to land, he had read that there was a dearth of applicants for the small holdings and allotments. Toucl in; upon votes for women, Mr. Stanstleld warned the Govern- ment that by granting them they would be strengthen- ing the Conservative ranks, because most of the women he knew were of the same views as his party. (Laughter.) He asked the Government to consider not only " one man, one vote," but " one vote, one value." He did not agree that every individual who happened to be 2t years of age was capable of exercising the franchise. Councillor TOOLE (N. Monaghan) expressed regret that there was no mention in the King's Speech of State arbitration which would make suclia dispute as that which was now in progress in industrial Lancashire an impossibility. He was sorry there was no mention of Ireland in the Speech. (A Voice : " You got Home Rule last session.") If that were so, his party had better retire from the House for they would have nothing to fight for. (Laughter.) However, many phases of the laud question in Ireland wanted tackling. (Dear, hear.) He regretted that the King did not severely censure the Prime Minister for the action he took in insulting so many of his Majesty's subjects in conneetioa with the recent Eucharistic pro- cession. He was certain such action was not taken with the consent of the King. He hoped the House would shortly take steps to sae that the obnoxious and antiquated law on the subject was amended so that Roman Catholics should be on the same footing as othee citizens. (Applause). The PREAITER, after joining in the expression of regret at the illness of the late leader of the Opposi- tion, remarked that the .‘ others" referred to in the 11 paragraph about friendly relations included, he was sorry to say, some members of the party with which the Gevernmeut were frequently charged with being in close touch. Every movement the Government made towards reform, every attempt that was made to lessen the burdens upon the people of this country, every step that was taken in the progressive cause, was to be damned with the charge of Socialism. If the Socialists advocated things which were right, good and true, why should the Government be prevented from helping; along , their work, if they were of the same opinion ? 1 (Applause.) But that was not so. They claimed that if the Government programme was Socialistic, they had ' been Socialistic before there was a Socialist party. (Laughter and applause.) The Ematters now brought forward had been on their programme for many years, and they hoped soon to see them on the Statute Book. To charge our present Free Trade policy with unem- ployment was simply to fly in the face of history, as was evidenced by the state of affairs in the times of the Chartist agitation, when we had an extaemely high tariff. He was surprised to hear the remarks of the leader of the Opposition about the land question. There was an undoubted land hunger and that was shown by the large demand for allotments. As to women's franchise, if the Government were convinced that woman was entitled to the vote she should have it, even if she voted Conservative. (Applause). Mr. Upson defended I the action of Mr. Asquith with regard to the Eucharistic I procession. He was astonished to hear a member of a party which professed to be democratic, talk of appeal- I ing to the King above the King's Ministers who were the representatives of the peopre.The Government stood by all they had done. (Applause.) As long as the law of England remained as it was, they would enforce that law irrespective of parties or nationalities. The only proceeding which would meet with approbation would be a proposal on the part of the hon. member who intro- duced the matter to so alter the law of the land that such processions should become legal. So long as the , law said they were illegal, those processions should net be allowed to take place. (Applause). Mr. G. REEVES (Preston) endorsed most of the items , in the speech. He suggested that in raising the necessary I funds the Government should be careful not to tax wages. He would rather they taxed salaries. I (Laughter). With grim humour, the speaker agreed , that the unemployed question was a "grave " questien, as burials were going on very rapidly in consequence of the distress. Alderman BENNETT (W. Birmingham) in a vigorous address, described the King's Speech as a beautiful ; skeleton. It was admirably expressed,extremely vague, I and his own opinion of it depended on the legislation which resulted. The skeleton might be made into a , scare crow or it might become a minister of light. I (Laughter). He would like to know whether the Government included in the "provocative and irrespon- sible journalists and others " men like Mn Blatchford ; and Mr. Hyndman. ('Yes.") It was not his place to speak in their defence, but he thought if ever two men spoke from their hearts and with a full 1 conviction that they were voicing a national danger, it was Mr. Blatchford and Mr. Ifyndman. I When men who devoted their whole lives to the pro- ' motion of peace were convinced that there was some- thing to call for warning we ought to rise from the atmosphere of sentiment, in which the Government was perpetually enveloped, and attempt to look facts in the face. As an Englishman he was not afraid of any power on the face of 'God's earth—(laughter)--but we ought to prepare ourselves for emergenciee. All parties were bound to do what they could to affect a permanent remedy of unemployment, and he taought tariff reform would do something to minimise the curse. He was confirmed in that by the result of the Patents Act, a Protective measure—("no,no") —brought in by Mr. Lloyd George. As to the railways, he was entirely in sympathy with the policy the Government proposed, pro- vided it was embodied in an intelligent and equitable form. He believed some of these questions were probably introdaced with the object of burking tariff reform, but it was bound to triumph in the end. (" No, no" and Opposition applause.) He believed in the necessity for electoral reform, bat not of the one-sided,ierry-mandering style they were accus- tomed to associate with the Liberal party. (Laughter.) He protested against the monstrous injustice of allow- ing Ireland 25 members more than she could fairly claim. Conservative as he was, he was an Englishman first and would be prepared to sum:part good measures from any party. At this stage Mr. AWDERY (Secretary for Ireland) moved the adjournment of the debate until next Tues- day and this was agreed to.

div.head: WARRINGTON GARDEN SUBURBS SCHEME.
div.p: THE WARRINGTON GARDEN SUBURBS SCHEME.

An important forward move is about to be made by the two associations which are cu-operating in the promotion of the above scheme. It will possibly be I remembered that the project first took definite shape I in a letter which appeared in the local papers on the I let December, 1006, signed by the Rev.Caacm. Morley I Stevenson, Alderman Arthur Bennett, Mr. William Long, Mrs. Mary Garnett, Mr. Charles E. Parker, and Miss Trude H. Crosfield. This was followed by a well-attended meeting at the Town Hall on Friday, the 7th December, and that, in turn, by a meeting at the Old Academy, on Friday, the 21st December, at : which it was unanimously resolved to form a local company. Some twenty suitable sites were visited, I and, on Wednesday, the 17th July, 1007, the parent I body, which is known as " Warrington Gardenl Suburbs, Limited," was registered under the Com- panies Acts with a capital of 5;20,000, divided into ' ; 20,000 shares of .£1 each, entitled to a cumulative dividend of 5 per cent. Alderman Bennett, Captain George R. Crosfield, Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., Mr. William Long,llr.F. W.Monks,Mr.Charles E.Parker,Mr. . J. Charlton Parr, Mr. Henry Roberts, Mr. W. Peter Rylands and Canon Stevenson consented to act as: directors ; with Mr. Parker as chairman, Alderman , 'Bennett as secretary, Messrs. Henry Greenall and Co. I and Mr. F. R. Roberts, M.A., L.L.8., as solicitors, and Mr. Louis A. Voisey, chartered accountant, as auditor • Messrs. William and Segar Owen being sub- sequently appointed consulting architects. Over £5,000 were subscribed, and, after much consultation, ' two excellent sites, the first at Great Sankey and the second at Grappenkall were secured at reasonable prices. In October, 1007, two premiums of ;£3O each were offered by the Directors for the best plans for laying , out tbe company's estates. The competition was limited to architects practising within a radius of thirty miles of Market Gate, and to specialists in the planning of Garden Suburbs. Eleven plans were ; sent in for the Grappenhall, and ten for the Great 'Sankey estate, and, after the most careful examination the directors, who had been assisted by the consulting I architects, unanimously awarded both the premiums to Messrs. A. and J. Soutar, Architects, of Wands- worth, London, S.W. The functamental basis of tloo scheme is that, taking the total area of each estate,the 'houses are not to exceed twelve to the acre. The area of the Great Sankey Estate (which is within easy ' distance of the Sankey and Fiddler's Ferry. stations , I and the Sankey trams) is about 20 acres,and provision is made for 240 houses. The area of the Grappenhall I Estate is about 22 acres, and provision is made for 265 houses. Each will, therefore, have a good-sized garden, and, in addition to this, the fortunate 'inhabitants will have the privilege of access to tlae ample public gardens, recreation grounds, and open spaces which are carefully provided for by the Company. The principal recreation ground at , Great Sankey is picturesquely situated on the margin of a pure and pleasant brook, and considerable progress has already been made in laying
IMPORTANT FORWARD MOVE.

it out. There is also a small public garden in the central area, and a second recreation ground in the neighbourhood of the existing pond. The roads are all symmetrical, and will, probably, be lined with grass and trees ; and, as all the houses have to be approved by the Directors of the Company, it is hoped that they will be attractive in design and healthy and convenient in arrangement. At Grappenhall, a spacious triangular recreation ground has been reserved in a gentle hollow near the Railway, and three smaller recreation grounds of : similar shape in other parts of the estate. Provision lis likewise made for allotment gardens. This estate I I is bounded, on the East and West, by winding brooks ' and frequent trees, and some noble beeches add the charm of silver trunk and waving foliage to a ' singularly suitable and pleasant piece of land. It is situated on the lower Thelwall-road, is readily I accessible from the Latchford tram termin-is, close to Thelwall station, and almost opposite the Latchford Locks. Owing to its proximity to the works of Messrs. Pierpoint and Bryant, Messrs. William I Bobertson, Limited, and the Richmond Gas Stove and Meter Co., Ltd., it seems more than likely ; that, if suitable houses are built on this estate, they I will be let at once. .

As the dividends are strictly limited to five per cent., and both estates have been acquired on reason- able terms, the company are able to offer splendid sites at a minimum ground rent of three-halfpence per square yard. The Garden City leases are for 93 years only, subject to renewal on revised terms, and we wish that these short leases could be localized ; but Warrington is not yet ripe for them, and, while the directors reserve the freehold, they are prepared to grant leases for 959 years —the usual term. There seems to still be 901119 misunderstanding as to the com- pany's proposals. Whilst retaining the freehold in every case, together with full right to build them- selves, they are prepared to offer sites on either estate to individual investors, builders or intending residents on highly advantageous terms, and subject only to the understanding that not more than twelve houses to the acre (taking the total acreage of each estate) mast be erected, and that the plans must be approved by the directors. _

But the principal promoters of the Company have likewise assisted in the formation of a co-operative society,which has been registered under the Industrial and Provident Societies Act, 1503, with the title of " Warrington Tenants', Limited." This was con- templated from the outset, and preliminary arrange- ments were in progress practically all last year. The actual registration of the Society was, however,delayed through unavoidable circumstances for close upon six months, and the formal certificate was only issued on the 7th of January last. The Prospectus, which has already been privately circulated, will soon, we understand, be issued broadcast ; and sub- stantial promises of support have been received from the Committee and others. The Society is affiliated with the Co-partnership Tenants' Housing Council,

ANOTHER LETTER BOX NEEDED. It was decided, on the proposition of Mr. F. Jackson, seconded by Mr. E. G. White, that the Clerk write the Warrington Postmaster, suggesting that a pillar letter box be placed in Ellesmere-road, about half way down.

will be able to borrow from the public Works Loan Commissioners at 3} per cent.,_ can issue Loan Stock to any extent at 4 per cent., and is authorized to pay a dividend of 5 per cent, upon its Share Capital. of which no member can hold above £2OO, the remaining profits, after making proper provision for repairs, depreciation, sinking fund, &c, being allocated amongst the tenant members in the shape of extra shares. Each member must invest at least .C2O, and each tenant member at least ..Z5O in the society, but, in the case of the tenant members, this can, of eourse, be paid by small instalments ; and it is hoped that the non-tenant members will eventually be paid out, and the tenant members become absolute owners of all the houses built by the Society. If they leave the district, they can either sell their shares or continue to draw their dividends. The principle is now in operation at Ealing and several other places, and has met with uniform and quite astonishing success. We may add that Hampstead is the only place which has preceded Warrington in adopting a scheme , which combines the principles of First Garden City, Limited, and those of the Co-partnership Societies, and that Warrington has the unique distinction of being the first and only place in England to commence with two distinct sites, and to definitely contemplate a ring of Garden Suburbs which, it is hoped, will ultimately girdle all the town. Owing to a variety of circumstances, there has been some delay in actually commencing building opera- tions, but we understand that sites have been secured and plans prepared for eight houses on the Great Sankey and for four on the Grappenhall Estate, and that other developments are in prospect. The plans for the first four houses, which are being erected by " Warrington Tenants', Limited," have been prepared by Messrs. J. E. Wright, Garnett and Wright, and the contract has been let to Mr. F. W. Wright, builder, Latchford. Work is to commence immediately, and, as will be seen from our advertise- ment columns, two corner stones are to be laid on Thursday next, the Ist October, at 3 pm, one by Lady Greenall, as representing the local phases of the movement, and one by Mr. Ebenezer Howard,the founder of " Garden City " and the pioneer of the great ideal which is making such astonishing pro- gress throughout the country. Mr. C. E. Parker, the chairman of " Warrington Garden Suburbs,Limited," will preside, and the Mayor, Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., Mr. A. H. Crosfield, M.P., and others are expected to take part in the -proceedings. In the evening, at 8 o'clock, Mr. Howard will lecture at the Town Hall on " Garden Cities and Suburbs," with lantern illustrations. The public are cordially invited to be present on both occasions. Full particulars of the scheme may be obtained from the Secretary of " Warrington Garden Suburbs, Limited" (gr. Arthur Bennett, Chartered Accountant, Market Gate Chambers), or from Mr. George H. Smith, of 13, Lovely-lane, the Secretary of" Warring- ton Tenants', Limited.

URBAN POWERS_ OR JOINING WARRINGTON.

On the motion of Air. Deakin seconded by Mr. E. G. White, it was resolved that the question of seeking Urban powers or joining Warrington be taken into con- sideration and that the Parish Council's report be printed and circulated along with the notice convening the next parish meeting.

Crossley be appointed to wait upon the Tramways Committee of the Warring- I ton Corporation to urge upon them that the time has I now arrived when the fare to and from Stockton Heath I should be reduced to one penny, or halfpenny stages I should be fixed.

div.head: DEATH OF MR. R. H. SMOCK.
div.p: DEATH OF MR. R. H. SMOCK.

Warrington his lost another highly respected towns- man by the death of Mr. Reginald Heber Silcock, who passed away at his residence, 13, Museum-street, nu Monday at the age of fifty-seven years. Although he took no prominent part in public life, Mr. Silcock by his business relations and his active work as a member

of several local organizations, was one of the best known inhibitants of Warrington and all who knew him admired him for his many sterling qualities. He was the third son of the late Mr. William Silcoclg,

who commenced business at the King-street Wire Works, Warrington, in the year 1837. He was made partner along with his brother, Mr. Alfred J. Siloock, in the year 1831, and from that time until the present the basiness has been carried on under the name of W. Sitcock and Sons.' The deceased

gentleman was a great lover of music and for over twenty years had been a valuable member of the Warrington Musical Society, serving on the committee and doing everthinff he could to make its work successful. He had long been identified with the Warrington Cricket and Bowling Club and in 1002 the members recognized his enthusiastic . . . .

support of the organization electing him president. He fulfilled the duties most admirably and earned the gratitude and esteem of all who have the interests of the club at heart. Mr. Silcock was a devoted member
of the Wesleyan Methodist Church and was never

happier than -when lending his help to some of the manifold activities of that denomination. Ever regular in his attendance at the services at Bold-street Church, he contributed generously to its funds, and for many years was secretary and treasurer to the church. Ur Silcock never figured in political or municipal affairs. though he was approached several times with a vivi- to entering the Council as a representative of St. Austin's Ward, where he had resided for more than 20 years. He was of an unassuming, kindly and I sympathetic disposition and by his death many hava lost a true friend. THE FUNERAL. The large attendance at the funeral, which took place at the Warrington Cemetery at noon on Thursday, testified to the general respect in which the late Mr. Silcock was held. The first part of the service wag held in Bold-street Wesleyan Church, where a numerous I congregation assembled. The rostrum and Communion table were draped in black. The officiating ministers were the Revs. Theodore Bishop (a former superinten- dent minister of the Warrington Circuit), E. Blanshard Keeling (superintendent), and T. Miller and the Kev.J. Gunnell was also present. Mr:Frank Hickman was at the organ and played "0 rest in the Lord" at the opening g the service and "The Dead March" in Saul at the close: The hymns" Rock of Ages " and "Peace, perfect Peace' were sung, and the beautiful quartette " Yea, though I walk " was rendered by four members of the choir. The Rev. Theodore Bishop delivered a short address

in the course of which he said that his old friend to whom they had gathered to do hnnour, would have been . the last to wish that any words of praise should be I said about him. He was always diffident, not to say shY 4 aid retiring, but they could speak about him as he ' appeared to them and not take his own estimate of , himself, which was a very bumble one. In the beauti- ; i ful words of the lesson which had just been read, there was one sentence which came to them and which they could thank God for—" Death is swallowed up in victory." They could not think of death as ending all. k.. It was not a full stop in a man's life ; it was only a comma. His life continued in another world where he 12reathed, as their hymn book said, " an ampler air." Their brother, whose loss they mourned that day, lived 5 in an atmosphere of prayer and love. He was not one to say much about it, but what he did say was to the , point and there was no mistake about it. The speaker I recalled an incident which occurred when Mr. Silcocii: 1

visited him at Llandudno. Sitting in his study chair, Mr. Silcock said " It would be easy enough to make a ;sermon here," and, taking a pen and a sheet of papor,he at once wrote some words which he (Mr. Bishop) bad treasured ever since. The spirit of them was in this wise : "Oh, hew blessed it is when the heart is full of grief or doubt, to be able to go to Him and unburden itself in prayer." A man could not write that if he did not live it, and it came so spontaneously from him that it gave one an insight into his very heart. He (Mr. Bishop) had known and loved him for nine years or more. He never knew a more genial or kindly man, wondrously kind in his disposition, hospitable, a man who was straight in all his dealings, and won the esteem of all who knew him, while all who knew him well loved him. Ile was esteemed in the town for his integrity, his honesty, his straightforwardness of purpose. He was loved in the church to which he belonged for his kindliness, his generosity,his sympathy with everything that was good, and his death was a distinct loss to the church and to the town. One hardly liked to speak of the private life, yet his home life as he (the speaker) had seen it was beautiful in its simplicity, kindliness and love. He had never known him in all the intercourse he (the speaker) had with him, both social and public,in private or in business meetings, to utter an angry word. Ile was always ready to find good in others and would never traduce. If he could .not praise he would ba hopeful. He (the speaker) loved him as one man loved another when he had found out his sterling, qualitiee and had learnt to appreciate him. Mr. Bishop concluded with an expression of sympathy with the widow and family in their great loss. . The last rites at the graveside were conducted by the Revs. T. Bishop, T. Miller and J. Gunnell. The chief mourners ware :—Messrs IV Silcock, A 3 Silcock, and S P Silcock (brothers), R N Silcock (sea). Bertram Silcock and W A Silcock (nephews), II if Evans (Manchester), A W White (Sale), Dr GI Rogers (Gorton), E A Connor, H Roberts, and T Fairhurst (Altrincham). Ur DEAR CHILDRMN, PUSSY IN THE WITNESS-BOX. . to y, . .: BY THOS. W. CRITTENDEN. Although animals were not unfrequenfl, summoned in judicial proceedings, in days gone by, it is not now a common thing for animals to be formally summoned by a court of justice, either to stand trial themselves or to give evidence against or in behalf of liti- gants. Nevertheless, such an instance has just occurred in this country, and the testi- mony of a fine Maltese cat summarily de- cided a case that had puzzled judge and jury for a week. The circumstances of this novel occurrence were as follows: Two men living in a Western city each owned a young Newfoundland dog, and the two animals resembled each other so strongly in all points that it was not possible for even the respective owners to distinguish them. By some means one of the dogs was lost, and his owner seeing, as he supposed, his missing pet in the street one day, about a month after the loss, naturally took posses- sion of him, and led him home. We wit). call 1 this dog " Major " to distinguish him. The I Proprietor of Major objected strongly to this proceeding, and laid claim to the animal, his title being promptly disputed by the first, who insisted that the dog belonged to him, and I added that, as "possession was nine points I of the law," he proposed to keep him, let the other do what he might. Argument and per- suasion failing, suit was brought to recover Major, and the case was regularly brought into court and came to trial about Christmas time, before a judge and a jury. Witnesses on both sides testified positively that it was Major, and that it was not Major— the animal himself, meanwhile, going freely to either of his claimants, and leaving one readily at the call of the other, seeming quite ' indifferent as to which one might finally secure him. A whole week was taken up with conflicting testimony, and even then neither judge nor jury were the wiser, or better pre- pared to render a true decision concerning the case. , At this point a woman living in the same house with Major's ownr declared that her cat could settle the question as to which dog it was, since the cat and Major were on terms of great friendship, eating and playing to- gether, and sleeping on the same- rug, while ,the cat was a sworn foe of all other canines, and had worsted many in fair fight. Here was a solution by which, all parties to the controversy were willing to abide, and a' formal writ was accordingly issued in the name of the people of the State commanding "all and singular, the owner or owners of a certain Maltese cat to produce the living body of the said anithal before the Hon. So- and-So, a justice duly and legally commis- sioned by the people of the commonwealth aforesaid," at a given time and place duly specified in the writ, and " thereof to fail not at their own proper peril." At the time appointed the momentous cat was duly produced before the honourable court, Major and his claimant being on hand, as well as a, large assembly attracted by the novelty of the proceedings. The record does not state whether Puss was duly sworn to tell "the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth," nor whether his owner was required to act as proxy for him in this re- spect. However this - may have been, he proceeded to vindicate his mistress's assertions, first with regard to his fighting qualities, for, on the introduction of some strange animals of the canine species, brought by. direction of the dignified court, he dilated his tail to most majestic proportions, arched his back in monu- mental style, and gave battle, to the satisfao tion of the spectators, if not to that of his adversaries, clearing the room in fine style, and in an exceedingly brief space of time. Next, Major was brought in, whereupon Puss/s warlike mood and demeanour were speedily changed to demonstrations of acquaintance and good-fellowship, the ani- mals recognising each other to the satisfaction of all concerned, and immediately terminating by this conclusive evidence a suit which, ex- cept for the shrewd thought of a woman, might have dragged on interminably and led to rancour and strife.. —4—.._. . THE CHILDREN OF THE SUN. A sunflower tall, by the garden wait, Scornfully nodded his head To a brilliant poppy, whose cheeks below Were all aflame with a crimson glow. -" I am the child of the sun," he smiled; " His colour is mine, you see, , While you are drinking his warm rays in, You never once try his tints to win." But the poppy gay, still blushing away (And laughing a _little, too), Quietly answered, " The sun has told Me to be red and you to be gold. ' The morning's hush and the poppy's blush Are dear to the heart of day As the noontide hour, with its triumphs won, And the flower that rivals the glowing sun. Heaven is large, and its chiefest charge Is that life shall be broad and free, And it bids the children of sun and storm \ Ne'er to a single type conform." The sunflower wise looked down in surprise At the bold little flower below, But he learned a lesson there and then' That neels to be learned by many men.
